en: Then, after some time had passed, King Daśaratha, the joy of the Raghus, spoke to his son Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Sarga 1, Verse 1)
"O dear son, this is the son of the King of Kekaya who dwells here; O hero, he is your maternal uncle Yudhājit, who has come to take you away."
Having heard this from Daśaratha, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī,
then set out for the journey together with Śatrughna.
Having taken leave of his father, of Rāma who performs deeds without weariness,
and of his mothers as well, that hero, the best among men, departed accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having received Bharata along with Śatrughna, the heroic Yudhājit entered his own city filled with joy; his father was indeed well-pleased.
There he lived with his brother, honored with hospitality,
and cherished by his maternal uncle Aśvapati out of affection for his son.
Dwelling there as well and gratifying their desires at will,
those two heroic brothers remembered King Daśaratha, who had grown old.
The king, possessed of great majesty, also remembered his two sons who were away from home—
both Bharata and Śatrughna, who resembled Mahendra and Varuṇa.
Indeed, all four of those bulls among men were dear to him,
like his own four arms issuing forth from his body.
Among them, Rāma, possessed of great splendor and most virtuous, became the source of his father’s delight,
just as the Self-Existent One is for all living beings.
Once Bharata had departed, Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa then paid their respects to their father, who resembled a god.
Placing his father’s command foremost, the righteous Rāma performed all the affairs of the citizens, both what was pleasing and what was beneficial.
Having performed his duties toward his mothers with the utmost self-restraint,
he attended to the needs of his elders from time to time.
Thus Daśaratha was pleased, as were the brahmins, the merchants,
and all the inhabitants of the realm by Rāma’s character and conduct.
For he is always tranquil in soul and speaks with gentleness;
even when addressed harshly, he does not offer a retort.
He is satisfied by even a single benefit rendered in some way;
yet, through his self-possession, he does not remember even a hundred injuries.
He would always remain conversing with virtuous men who were advanced in conduct, advanced in knowledge, and advanced in age, even during intervals between his practice of weaponry.
Of noble lineage, virtuous, undaunted, truthful, and upright,
he was well-disciplined by elders— twice-born men who perceive the true meaning of dharma.
He knew the true nature of dharma, artha, and kāma; he possessed mindfulness and eloquence;
he was skilled and confident in worldly conventions and conduct.
He is learned in the scriptures, grateful, skilled in discerning the character of other men,
and wise in bestowing both restraint and favor according to what is right.
He was skilled in the means of acquiring wealth and well-acquainted with the management of expenditures;
he had attained preeminence among the collections of scriptures, even those of a miscellaneous nature.
Having mastered both wealth and dharma, he was devoted to happiness yet not indolent;
he was an expert in the arts of recreation and a knower of the distinctions among objects.
Skilled in the mounting and training of both elephants and horses,
he was the foremost among those who know the science of archery and was esteemed in the world as an Atiratha.
An assailant and a striker, skilled in the leadership of armies,
he was invincible in battle even by the enraged gods and asuras;
free from malice, having conquered anger, he was neither arrogant nor envious.
He did not despise living beings, nor was he subject to the power of time.
Thus endowed with such excellent qualities, the prince was esteemed by his subjects; he was honored throughout the three worlds for his virtues of forbearance like those of the Earth,
equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect and to the Lord of Śacī in prowess.
Thus, with qualities beloved by all the people and generating joy for his father,
Rāma shone like the radiant sun with its rays.
The Earth desired him as her lord— he who was thus endowed with perfect conduct, possessed of invincible prowess, and comparable to the Guardians of the World.
But seeing his son endowed with these many incomparable virtues, King Daśaratha, the scorcher of foes, fell into deep reflection.
For this supreme longing revolves within his heart:
"When indeed shall I see my beloved son consecrated?"
For he desires the prosperity of the world and has compassion for all beings; he is dearer to the world than I am, like the rain-bearing cloud.
Equal to Yama and Śakra in vigor, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect,
and equal to the mountains in fortitude, he is even more virtuous than I am.
"Seeing my son established over this entire earth at such a young age, may I attain heaven. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.1.32)
Having observed that he was endowed with all combined virtues, the great king,
after deliberating together with his ministers, decided upon him as the crown prince.
The lord of the earth summoned from the world the foremost men, both those residing in various cities and commoners from different provinces.
Then, upon various seats provided by the king,
the disciplined monarchs sat down facing the king himself.

Surrounded by kings who had come to pay their respects and were endowed with humility, as well as by the people of the cities and the countryside seated nearby, the king shone like the thousand-eyed Lord Indra surrounded by the immortals.
Then, having addressed the entire assembly, the lord of the earth spoke these incomparable words, which were both beneficial and heartening: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 2.1.1.
With a great voice, deep and resonant like the sound of a drum,
the king roared like a thundercloud.
Therefore, desiring to endow this entire world— which is worthy of happiness— with the highest good, I shall follow that which was protected by the former Ikṣvākus, the lords of men.
I too have acted by following the path trodden by my predecessors,
constantly and unweariedly protecting my subjects to the best of my ability.
This body of mine has grown old in the shade of this white parasol, which was moved about for the benefit of the entire world.
Having lived for many thousands of years and reached the end of my lifespan,
I desire rest for this worn-out body.
For, bearing the heavy yoke of dharma for the world— a burden endowed with royal majesty and difficult to carry for those who have not conquered their senses— I am now exhausted.
Therefore, desiring rest, I shall appoint my son to the welfare of the subjects,
having obtained the consent of all these eminent brahmins who are present here.
For my eldest son Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, is born with all my virtues; he is equal to Purandara in valor.
I shall joyfully appoint that bull among men, the best of the upholders of dharma, to the position of crown prince, like the moon joined with the constellation Puṣya.
That illustrious elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa is a worthy protector for you;
by having him as your lord, even the three worlds would become more truly possessed of a protector.
"By immediately uniting this earth with such excellence through the installation of that son, I shall indeed become free from affliction."
As the king spoke thus, the kings rejoiced in response,
like peacocks crying out at a great rain-cloud pouring down its showers.
Having fully understood the disposition of that king who was learned in both dharma and worldly affairs,
and having perceived it with their minds, they spoke to the aged King Daśaratha.
"O King, you have grown old for many thousands of years;
therefore, consecrate Rāma as the crown prince and king."
Having heard those words, which were pleasing to their hearts, the king, as if not knowing and desiring to learn more, spoke these words: (Rāmāyaṇa 2.2.16)
"How is it that while I am ruling the earth according to dharma,
you gentlemen wish to see my own son as the crown prince?"
Together with the people of the city and the countryside, they said to that great-souled one:
"O King, your son possesses many auspicious virtues."
O lord of the people, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, is equal to Śakra in divine qualities and is indeed more deeply devoted than all the other Ikṣvākus.
Rāma is a virtuous man in this world, devoted to truth and righteousness;
he knows the dharma, is true to his word, possesses good character, and is free from malice.
Patient, consoling, gentle, grateful, and having his senses conquered;
mild, firm of mind, always auspicious, and free from envy.
Rāghava speaks kindly to all beings and is a speaker of truth;
he is a devoted servant of the learned and aged Brāhmaṇas.
Because of that, his incomparable fame, glory, and splendor increase here;
he is skilled in all weapons among gods, asuras, and humans.
Whenever he goes forth to battle for the sake of a village or a city,
having set out accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, he never returns without being victorious.
Having returned from battle on either an elephant or a chariot,
he always inquires after the welfare of the citizens as if they were his own kinsmen.
Toward his sons, his sacred fires, his wives, and his groups of servants and disciples,
he behaved entirely and in due order like a father toward his own biological sons.
"O tiger among men, Rāma always asks us: 'Do your disciples serve you, and are they diligent in their duties? (Rāmāyaṇa 2.2.27)
He becomes deeply distressed at the misfortunes of men,
and at all their festivals, he rejoices like a father.
A speaker of truth, a great archer, a servant of the elders, and one who has conquered his senses—
by good fortune, O Rāghava, this Vatsa has been born for your welfare;
by good fortune, he is endowed with the virtues of a son, like Kaśyapa’s son Mārīca.
All the people in the kingdom and likewise in the excellent city hope for the strength, health, and long life of Rāma, who knows his own self.
Both the people of the city and the countryside,
as well as women— both old and young— were composed in mind morning and evening.
They pay homage to all the gods for the sake of the illustrious Rāma;
O Lord, may their prayer be fulfilled through your grace.
We behold Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, the destroyer of all enemies,
your son, O best of kings, established in the position of crown prince.

O Giver of Boons, you ought to joyfully consecrate this son of yours— who is like a god among gods and devoted to the welfare of the entire world— for our benefit, as he is soon to be invested with the noble [status].
Having accepted their lotus-like hands joined in reverence from all sides, the king spoke these words, which were both pleasing and beneficial, to them: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 3.1.1.
"Aha! I am supremely delighted, and my power is incomparable, since you desire that my eldest and beloved son be established in the position of crown prince."
Having thus honored those brahmins, the king spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva while they were listening.
"This month of Caitra is glorious and auspicious, with its forests in full bloom;
let everything be prepared for Rāma’s consecration as crown prince."
Approaching the Lord of the World, those two bulls among the twice-born, filled with joy and delight, spoke as they had been instructed: "It is done."
Then the radiant king spoke these words to Sumantra:
"Let the self-disciplined Rāma be brought here by you immediately."
Having promised "So be it," Sumantra, by the king's command,
brought Rāma— the best among chariot-warriors— to that place by means of his chariot.
Then, while King Daśaratha was seated there,
the rulers of the earth from the east, the north, the west, and the south [approached him].
Mlecchas, Aryas, and others who dwell in forests and mountain fastnesses—
all of them paid him homage, as the gods do to Vāsava.
In their midst, that royal sage, standing upon his palace like Vāsava among the Maruts,
beheld his son approaching in a chariot.
Resembling a king of the Gandharvas, renowned for his prowess in the world,
long-armed, a great being with the gait of an elephant in rut.
Rāma, whose face was like the moon, was exceedingly lovely to behold; by his beauty, magnanimity, and virtues, he captivated the sight and the hearts of men.
Like subjects scorched by the heat longing for the rain-cloud that brings refreshment,
the lord of men could not look enough at him as he approached.
Having helped that descendant of Raghu descend from his excellent chariot,
Sumantra followed behind him with joined palms as he proceeded toward his father.
That bull among men, Rāghava, ascended that palace, which resembled a peak of Mount Kailāsa, together with his charioteer in order to see the king.
Approaching with palms joined in reverence and bowing low before his father,
Rāma announced his own name and paid homage at his father's feet.
Seeing him standing by his side, bowing with palms joined in reverence,
the king took him by the hands, drew him close, and embraced his beloved son.
And for him, the illustrious king directed a beautiful, supreme seat, adorned with jewels and gold, which had been prepared for Rāma.
Having obtained that excellent seat, Rāghava illuminated it with his own radiance,
like the stainless sun at its rising illuminating Mount Meru.
Illuminated by him, that assembly hall shone forth brilliantly,
like the autumnal sky with its stainless planets and stars when graced by the moon.
Beholding his beloved son, the king rejoiced as if he were seeing his own self adorned, reflected upon the surface of a mirror.
Addressing his son with a smile, that king, the best among those who possess sons, spoke these words,
just as Kaśyapa spoke to Devendra.
"In my eldest wife, who is worthy of me,
you, my son Rāma, have been born as a worthy child, preeminent in virtues and dear to me."
"Since these subjects have been won over by you through your own virtues,
therefore, under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, receive the office of heir apparent."
"By your very nature you are disciplined and possessed of virtue;
yet, O son, because of my affection for you who are already virtuous, I shall speak what is for your benefit."
Furthermore, remaining steadfast in discipline, always keep your senses conquered,
and abandon those vices that arise from desire and anger.
Conducting yourself through both indirect and direct means,
win over all the subjects, beginning with the ministers.
When a king protects the earth with his subjects satisfied and devoted to him,
his friends rejoice as if the immortals had obtained the nectar of immortality;
therefore, my son, conduct yourself by restraining yourself.
Having heard that, his friends, who acted for the welfare of Rāma,
quickly approached and informed Kausalyā.
That Kausalyā, the most excellent of women, bestowed gold, cattle, and various kinds of jewels upon those who brought her pleasant news.
Then, having saluted the king and mounted his chariot,
Rāghava departed for his own radiant residence, honored by throngs of people.
And those citizens, having heard those words of the king, felt as if they had attained a desired gain;
taking leave of the lord of men and returning to their homes, they worshipped the gods with exceeding joy.

When the citizens had departed, King Daśaratha, who was skilled in making decisions, consulted further with his ministers and then reached a firm resolution. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Sarga 4, Verse 1)
"Tomorrow Puṣya will be in the ascendant; tomorrow my son Rāma, whose eyes are as copper-red as lotuses, shall be consecrated by me as the heir apparent," so said the lord.
Then, having entered the inner apartments, King Daśaratha at that time commanded the charioteer: "Bring Rāma back here once more."
Having accepted those words, the charioteer returned once more to Rāma’s palace in haste to bring Rāma back again.
The gatekeepers announced his arrival once more;
and upon hearing that he had arrived, Rāma became filled with apprehension.
Having quickly ushered him in, Rāma spoke these words:
"Tell me in full once more what the purpose of your arrival is."
Then the charioteer said to him: "The king wishes to see you;
having heard this, you are the authority here regarding whether to go or otherwise."
Having heard these words of the charioteer, Rāma then, filled with haste,
set out for the royal palace to see the lord of men once again.
Having heard that Rāma had arrived, King Daśaratha,
desiring to see his most beloved son, caused him to enter the palace.
As soon as the illustrious Rāghava entered his father’s palace,
he saw his father from afar and, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself before him.
Raising him up as he was bowing down and embracing him, the lord of the earth offered him a splendid seat and spoke to him again.
"O Rāma, I am old and long-lived; I have enjoyed all the pleasures I desired, and likewise performed hundreds of sacrifices provided with abundant food and profuse sacrificial fees."
"O best of men, today you have been born as my incomparable offspring on this earth;
by you, I have truly given, sacrificed, and studied."
O hero, I have experienced desired pleasures;
thus, I am free from debt to the gods, sages, ancestors, brahmins, and to myself.
"There is nothing whatsoever that must be done by me for you other than your consecration;
therefore, you ought to do for me whatever I shall tell you."
"Today all the subjects desire you as their lord;
therefore, my son, I shall consecrate you as the crown prince."
Moreover, O Rāma, today I see inauspicious and terrible dreams;
great meteors, accompanied by thunderclaps, fall here with a mighty roar.
O Rāma, the astrologers report that my birth star has been seized by cruel planets— the Sun, Mars, and Rāhu.
For generally, when such omens arise,
a king either meets his death or encounters a terrible calamity.
Therefore, O Raghava, consecrate yourself while my mind is not yet deluded; for the intellect of living beings is fickle.
"Today the moon has entered Punarvasu, which precedes Puṣya;
the astrologers declare that tomorrow the conjunction with Puṣya is certain."
"Therefore, perform your consecration during the Puṣya asterism; my mind seems to urge me on.
Tomorrow, O scorcher of foes, I shall consecrate you as the crown prince."
Therefore, you, observing your vow today with a self-restrained mind,
must fast together with your wife, sleeping upon a bed of darbha grass.
Let your friends, remaining vigilant, protect you today on all sides;
for indeed, undertakings of this kind are beset by many obstacles.
As long as Bharata remains away from this city,
so long do I consider the time for your consecration to have arrived.
Indeed, Bharata, your brother, stands firm in the conduct of the virtuous;
he follows his elder brother, is righteous in soul, compassionate, and has conquered his senses.
But it is my opinion, O Raghava, that the minds of men are impermanent, whereas for the virtuous who are constant in dharma, their conduct is beautiful through its fulfillment.
Having been addressed thus and granted permission for the consecration to take place on the following day,
Rāma saluted his father, saying "I depart," and went home.
Having entered his own quarters for the consecration appointed by the king,
he departed at that very moment and went to his mother’s inner apartments.
There, in the temple of the deity, he saw his mother, dressed in linen, restrained in speech, and devotedly praying for the goddess Śrī.
Sumitra and Lakshmana had already arrived there,
and Sita was summoned upon hearing the pleasant news of Rama’s consecration.
At that time, Kausalyā stood with her eyes closed,
attended by Sumitrā, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard that her son’s consecration as crown prince would take place under the asterism Puṣya,
she meditated upon Janārdana, the Supreme Person, while practicing breath control.
Having approached her while she was thus observing her vow and having saluted her,
Rāma then spoke these words to her, gladdening her.
"Mother, I have been appointed by my father to the task of protecting the subjects;
tomorrow my consecration shall take place, according to my father's command."
"Sītā must also fast this night along with me;
thus did my father speak to me together with the officiating priests and preceptors."
"Whatever auspicious rites are appropriate here for tomorrow's consecration, perform them today for me and for Vaidehī."

Having heard this, Kausalyā, whose long-cherished desire was fulfilled, addressed these words to Rāma, choked with tears of joy: etac chrutvā tu kausalyā cirakālābhikāṅkṣitam / harṣabāṣpakalaṃ vākyam idaṃ rāmam abhāṣata // RamS_2,4.38 //
Child Rāma, live long; those who stand as your adversaries are slain.
Endowed with glory, bring joy to my kinsmen and to Sumitrā.
"O son, you were born under an auspicious constellation,
since by your virtues you have gratified your father, Daśaratha."
"Truly, my patience toward the lotus-eyed man has not been in vain,
O son, for this royal glory of Ikṣvāku shall now rest upon you."
Having been addressed thus by his mother, Rāma, looking at his brother who was seated before him with joined palms and bowed head, spoke as if smiling.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, rule this earth together with me;
for you, who are my very second self, this royal fortune has arrived."
O Saumitri, enjoy the pleasures you desire and the fruits of sovereignty;
for both life and the kingdom I seek only for your sake.
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, and having saluted his two mothers and taken leave of Sītā, Rāma went to his own dwelling.
Having instructed Rāma regarding the consecration to take place on the following day, the king summoned the family priest Vasiṣṭha and spoke these words: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Sarga 5, Verse 1).
"O ascetic, today cause Kakutstha,
who is firm in his vows, to observe a fast along with his bride for the sake of attaining prosperity, fame, and the kingdom."
Having said "So be it" to the king, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the best among the knowers of the Vedas, went in person to Rāma’s residence.
Having reached Rāma’s palace, which shone like a mass of white clouds,
that best of sages entered through three courtyards by means of his chariot alone.
When the seer had arrived, Rāma, as if in haste and full of agitation,
went out from his residence to honor him who was worthy of honor.
Having approached the vicinity of the wise man's chariot with haste,
he himself took hold of him and helped him down from the vehicle.

Seeing him so humble, and having conversed with him and inspired his confidence, the family priest spoke thus to Rāma, who was worthy of affection and gladdened him: sa cainaṃ praśritaṃ dṛṣṭvā sambhāṣyābhiprasādya ca / priyārhaṃ harṣayan rāmam ity uvāca purohitaḥ // RamS_2,5.7 //
"O Rāma, your father is pleased; you shall obtain the position of crown prince.
You should observe a fast today together with Sītā."
For tomorrow morning, King Daśaratha, your father, will affectionately consecrate you as the crown prince, just as Nahuṣa did for Yayāti.
Having spoken thus, the sage then caused Rāma, who was restrained by his vows, to observe a fast along with Vaidehī according to the prescribed mantras.
Then, having been duly honored by Rāma,
that preceptor of the king took leave of the descendant of Kakutstha and departed from Rāma’s residence.
There, Rāma also, having taken leave of his friends in every way and being honored by them,
entered [the city] after having dismissed them all.
Then Rāma’s residence, filled with joyful men and women,
shone like a lake of blooming lotuses frequented by flocks of intoxicated birds.
Having emerged from that residence of Rāma, which resembled a royal palace,
Vasiṣṭha beheld the road crowded with people.
In Ayodhyā, the royal highways on all sides became congested, crowded with throngs upon throngs of curious people.
Then, due to the joyful sounds arising from the friction of the waves of the crowds of people,
the roar of the royal highway became like that of the ocean.
For on that day, the city of Ayodhyā, garlanded with groves, had its streets sprinkled and swept, and the banners upon its lofty houses were raised high.
For at that time, the people residing in Ayodhyā— including women, children, and the elderly—
longed for Rāma’s consecration, just as they long for the rising of the sun.
And as he was the ornament of the people and the increaser of their joy,
the populace became eager to witness that great festival of Ayodhyā.
Thus, as if clearing away the throng of people, the domestic priest proceeded slowly toward the royal palace along that royal highway crowded with folk.
Having ascended the palace, which resembled the peak of a white cloud,
he met with the lord of men as Bṛhaspati meets with Śakra.
Seeing that he had arrived, the king left his royal throne and questioned him; and he reported to him that the task had been accomplished.
Having been permitted by his preceptor and having dismissed that multitude of people,
the king entered the inner apartments like a lion entering a mountain cave.
Illuminating that residence, which was crowded with women in exquisite attire and resembled the palace of Mahendra,
the king entered as the moon enters the sky filled with hosts of stars.
When the family priest had departed, Rāma, having bathed and with his mind restrained, approached Nārāyaṇa together with his large-eyed wife. *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 6.1.
Then, taking the vessel of oblation upon his head according to the prescribed rite,
he offered the clarified butter into the blazing fire for the great deity.
Having consumed the remainder of that sacrificial oblation and having prayed for his own welfare,
he should meditate upon the god Nārāyaṇa while lying on a well-spread bed of kuśa grass.
Restraining his speech and keeping his mind disciplined, the son of the best of men lay down with Vaidehī in the glorious sanctuary of Viṣṇu.
When one watch of the night remained, he woke up and had the entire decoration of his palace carried out.
There, listening to the pleasant words of the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards,
he performed his morning devotions and recited his prayers with a restrained mind.
Bowing his head, he praised Madhusūdana,
who was clothed in spotless linen garments, and he caused the twice-born to recite benedictions.
Then, the deep and sweet sound of their proclamation of an auspicious day,
resonating with the sound of musical instruments, filled Ayodhyā.
When all the people residing in Ayodhyā heard that Rāghava, together with Vaidehī, had observed the fast, they were all filled with joy.
Then all the citizens, having heard of Rāma’s consecration and seeing that the night had turned to dawn, once again prepared the city with supreme splendor.
In temples resembling the peaks of white clouds, at crossroads, on carriage-roads, at shrines, and on watchtowers; ||| RamS_2,6.11 |||
And he saw the marketplaces of merchants, abounding with various articles for sale,
as well as the prosperous and magnificent mansions of householders.
Then, in all the assembly halls and upon the visible trees,
colorful banners and flags were raised on high.
And here and there, they heard the voices of troupes of actors and dancers, and of singers singing words that were pleasing to the mind and ear.
And as the consecration of Rāma drew near, the people engaged in conversations with one another regarding Rāma’s installation,
both in the public squares and within their homes.
Even the children, playing in groups at the doors of their houses,
were talking among themselves about Rāma’s consecration.
And for Rāma’s consecration, the citizens prepared the magnificent royal highway, strewn with offerings of flowers and perfumed with the scent of incense.
And for the purpose of providing illumination, fearing the arrival of night,
they likewise placed lamp-trees everywhere along the streets.
Having thus decorated the city, the inhabitants of that city awaited the consecration of Rāma as the crown prince.
Having gathered together in groups at all the crossroads and assembly halls,
they conversed with one another there and praised the lord of men.
"Oh, how great-souled is this King, the joy of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
who, knowing himself to be old, will consecrate Rāma in the kingdom!"
For we have all been favored in that Rāma, the lord of the earth—
who has perceived the higher and lower truths of the world— will be our protector for a long time.
The wise Raghava, whose mind is undisturbed, who is righteous in soul and devoted to his brothers,
is as affectionate toward us as he is toward his own brothers.
"May the righteous King Daśaratha live long, O sinless one,
by whose grace we shall behold Rāma consecrated."
While the citizens were speaking in this manner,
people from the countryside, who had heard the news from all directions, arrived there.
Having arrived at the city from all directions to witness the consecration of Rāma,
those people from the countryside filled the city of Rāma.
From those surging throngs of people, a roar was heard there like the roar of the ocean when its momentum is unleashed during the change of the moon.

Then that city, resembling the abode of Indra, appeared agitated and filled with noise on all sides by the country folk who had arrived, desiring to see it, like the waters of the ocean teeming with sea-monsters.
Since she was born as a slave of her kinsmen and had lived with Kaikeyī, she ascended by chance to the palace that resembled the moon. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 7.1)
From that palace, Mantharā gazed down upon the entire city of Ayodhyā, its main roads sprinkled with water and strewn with lotuses and water-lilies.
It was beautifully adorned with banners worthy of the best and with flags;
it was sprinkled with sandalwood water and filled with people who had performed their head-baths.
Seeing the nurse standing nearby, Mantharā,
who was devoted to her own interests, questioned her while filled with the highest joy.
"Why is Rāma’s mother distributing wealth to the people?
Tell me, why is there such excessive joy among the populace?
Or what will the delighted lord of the earth have them do?"
Torn asunder by joy and with supreme delight,
the nurse then announced to the hunchback the even greater fortune of Rāghava.
Tomorrow, under the asterism Puṣya, King Daśaratha will consecrate the sinless Rāghava, who has conquered anger, as the crown prince.
Having heard the words of the nurse, the hunchback, quickly provoked to anger,
descended from the palace which resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
Burning with rage, the evil-sighted Mantharā approached Kaikeyī as she lay on her bed and spoke these words.
"Arise, you fool! Why do you lie there? Fear assails you;
why do you not realize that you are being overwhelmed by a surging flood?"
You boast of your good fortune regarding this undesirable form of beauty;
for your good fortune is as fickle as the current of a river during the summer heat.
Thus addressed with harsh words by the angry and evil-minded Kubjā, Kaikeyī fell into a state of extreme despondency.
Kaikeyī, however, said to the hunchback Mantharā: "Is all not well, Mantharā?
For I perceive you with a dejected face, exceedingly distressed."
But Mantharā, having heard Kaikeyī’s words spoken in sweet syllables,
being herself skilled in speech, spoke these words filled with anger.
Becoming even more despondent, that hunchback, though wishing her well,
spoke to her in a way that caused her distress and sowed discord within Rāghava.
"O Queen, a very great misfortune has begun that will lead to your destruction:
King Daśaratha intends to consecrate Rāma as the crown prince."
I am submerged in bottomless fear, overwhelmed by pain and sorrow;
as if being consumed by fire, I have come here for the sake of your welfare.
O Kaikeyī, through your sorrow my own sorrow shall become great;
and through your prosperity my prosperity shall likewise increase—of this there is no doubt.
Born into a lineage of sovereigns, you are the queen of a lord of the earth;
O Goddess, how is it that you do not perceive the severity of royal duties?
Your husband speaks of righteousness but is deceitful; he speaks gently but is cruel.
Because you did not recognize this in your pure-heartedness, you have been thus deceived by him.
Employing toward you consolations that are now useless,
your husband will today unite Kausalyā with wealth alone.
Having sent Bharata away among your kinsmen, that evil-minded one will establish Rāma in the kingdom at daybreak, once all obstacles have been removed.
O young woman, you have embraced an enemy under the guise of a husband, out of a desire for his welfare like that of a mother, while he was like a venomous serpent held in your lap.
Just as one would treat a snake or an enemy if neglected,
so have you and your sons been treated today by King Daśaratha.
By establishing Rāma on the throne through evil means and false conciliation, you, who were always accustomed to happiness, have indeed been destroyed along with your kin, O child.
O Kaikeyī, whose appearance is so wondrous, perform now what is for your own welfare, as the time has come; save your son, yourself, and me.
Having heard Mantharā’s words, she of the beautiful countenance rose from her bed and gave those auspicious ornaments to the hunchbacked woman.

Having given that ornament to the hunchbacked woman, Kaikeyī, the most excellent of women, being delighted, spoke this again to Mantharā: "Having given that ornament to the hunchbacked woman, Kaikeyī, the most excellent of women, being delighted, spoke this again to Mantharā."
"O Mantharā, this which you have told me is most pleasing to me. What more may I do for you who has told me this pleasant news?"
"I perceive no difference between Rāma and Bharata;
therefore, I am pleased that the king will consecrate Rāma in the kingdom."
"O you who deserve what is dear, there is nothing further that could be more pleasing to me than this well-spoken and excellent word from you;
for you have spoken thus, most dear and superior, so I grant you another supreme boon—choose it."
Then Mantharā, filled with envy, resentment, anger, and sorrow, cast off those ornaments and spoke these words to her: (Ramayana 2.8.1)
"O foolish woman, why have you displayed this joy at an inappropriate time? Do you not perceive that you yourself are situated in the midst of an ocean of grief?"
Fortunate indeed is Kausalyā, whose son shall be consecrated tomorrow with the great office of heir apparent by the best of the twice-born under the asterism Puṣya.
Having slain your enemies, you shall wait upon Kausalyā— who has attained great joy and is now confident— with palms joined in reverence like a maidservant.
The supreme wives of Rāma will surely be joyful,
while your daughters-in-law will be dejected at the downfall of Bharata.
Then, seeing Mantharā speaking with great joy,
Queen Kaikeyī praised the very virtues of Rāma.
Knowing the Dharma, self-controlled by his elders, grateful, truthful in speech, and pure—
Rāma, the eldest son of the king, therefore deserves the position of crown prince.
"O long-lived one, he will protect his brothers and servants like a father;
why then, O hunchback, do you grieve upon hearing of Rāma’s consecration?"
And Bharata, that bull among men, will certainly obtain his father’s and grandfather’s kingdom after Rama has completed a hundred years.
Since prosperity has arrived, Mantharā, and is currently present and will continue in the future, for what reason do you grieve?
He indeed serves me even more than he does Kausalyā.
Having heard Kaikeyī’s words, Mantharā was deeply distressed;
sighing long and hot, she spoke this to Kaikeyī: RamS_2,8.11 //
Out of folly, you do not perceive what is harmful and do not understand yourself,
as you sink into an ocean of suffering, vast with grief and calamity.
Rāghava shall become king, as will the son of Rāghava;
but Bharata, O Kaikeyī, shall be excluded from the royal lineage.
For not all the sons of a king remain in the kingdom, O beautiful lady;
if all were installed, a very great disorder would arise.
Therefore, O Kaikeyī of faultless limbs, kings establish the affairs of state with their eldest sons, even if they possess other virtuous qualities as well.
O affectionate lady, this son of yours will become utterly broken; like one who is helpless, he shall be deprived of pleasures and from the royal lineage.
I have come here for your sake, yet you do not recognize me;
you wish to give me what is due to me only when my co-wife has prospered.
Once Rāma has obtained the kingdom free from all obstacles, he will certainly cause Bharata to be sent away to another country— or even to the other world.
For Bharata was indeed led by you to his maternal uncle while still a child; and from proximity, affection arises even among inanimate things.
For Saumitri is the protector of Rāma, and Rāghava is likewise the protector of Lakṣmaṇa;
their brotherly affection is renowned throughout the worlds, like that of the Aśvins.
Therefore, Rāma will not do anything harmful to Lakṣmaṇa;
however, there is no doubt that Rāma might do harm to Bharata.
"Therefore, let your son go from Rājagṛha itself to the forest;
for this pleases me greatly and is also highly beneficial for you."
In this way, there will be welfare for your kinsmen as well,
if Bharata obtains his paternal kingdom in accordance with dharma.
How shall that boy, accustomed to comfort and born as Rama’s natural enemy, live under your control— he who has lost his wealth while you have attained all your aims?
Just as a leader of an elephant herd might be pursued in the forest by a lion,
you ought to protect Bharata, who is being overwhelmed by Rāma.
How could your co-wife, the mother of Rāma, whom you previously slighted out of pride due to your own good fortune, not seek to avenge her enmity?
For when Rāma shall obtain the earth, Bharata will certainly be ruined;
therefore, deliberate now upon the kingdom for your own son and the cause for the exile of the other.
Thus addressed, Kaikeyī, her face blazing with anger,
sighed long and hot and spoke this to Mantharā. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 9.1)
Today I shall swiftly dispatch Rāma from here to the forest,
and I shall have Bharata consecrated as the heir apparent with all speed.
But now consider this, Mantharā: by what means can Bharata obtain the kingdom, and not Rāma, by any means whatsoever?
Thus addressed by the queen, the evil-minded Mantharā, seeking to harm Rāma’s interests, spoke these words to Kaikeyī: ||| RamS_2,9.4 |||
Now, O Kaikeyī, I shall tell you; listen to me how your son Bharata shall obtain the kingdom in its entirety.
Having heard these words of Mantharā, Kaikeyī rose slightly from her well-spread bed and spoke as follows.
"Tell me, Mantharā, what means there is by which Bharata may obtain the kingdom, and by no means Rāma."
Thus addressed by the queen, the hunchbacked Mantharā, who perceives only evil,
spoke these words while seeking to harm Rāma.
In the war between the gods and the asuras, your husband, accompanied by the royal sages,
went forth taking you with him to provide assistance to the king of the gods.
O Kaikeyī, taking your stand in the southern direction toward the Daṇḍaka forest,
there is a city known as Vaijayanta where Timidhvaja resides.
That great asura, known as Śambara, possessed of a hundred illusions and undefeated by the hosts of gods, gave battle to Śakra.
In that great battle, O Queen, King Daśaratha was then carried away from the field by you while he was unconscious.
There too, when your husband was wounded by weapons, he was protected by you;
pleased with you, O lady of auspicious appearance, he granted you two boons.
"O Goddess, you said to your husband, 'Whenever I desire, I shall take two boons'; that was agreed upon as 'so be it' by that high-souled one.
For I was unaware of this, O Goddess, though it was told by you yourself long ago."
Ask your husband for these two boons: the consecration of Bharata, and the exile of Rāma for fourteen years.
"Having entered the chamber of wrath today like one enraged, O daughter of Aśvapati, lie down on the ground while remaining invisible, wearing soiled garments;
do not look up at him, nor speak to him."
"You are always beloved by your husband; of this I have no doubt.
For your sake, the great king would even enter the fire."
He is unable to provoke you to anger, nor can he even look upon you when you are angry;
for the sake of your pleasure, the king would indeed sacrifice even his own life.
For the lord of the earth is not able to transgress your word;
O woman of weak character, realize the power of your own good fortune.
King Daśaratha may give you jewels, pearls, gold, and various kinds of gems; do not set your mind upon them.
O highly fortunate lady, remind him of those two boons which Daśaratha granted during the war between the gods and the asuras; let that purpose not pass you by.
But when Rāghava, having raised you up himself, offers you a boon, O great king, you should choose this boon after having established him firmly in his position.
Exile Rāma to the forest for nine and five years;
let Bharata be made king upon the earth, O bull among monarchs.
Thus, once Rāma has been exiled, he will no longer be a source of delight;
and Bharata, having destroyed his enemies, will become your king.
By the time Rāma returns from the forest,
your son will have established his roots;
he will be self-possessed, having gathered a circle of men together with his friends.
I believe the time has come for you, free from fear, to restrain the king’s resolve regarding Rāma’s consecration and turn him back from it.

Having been made to perceive that which was harmful as being beneficial by her, Kaikeyī, delighted and convinced, then spoke this to Mantharā: *anartham artharūpeṇa grāhitā sā tatas tayā / hṛṣṭā pratītā kaikeyī mantharām idam abravīt //* RamS_2,9.27 *//* "Having been made to perceive that which was harmful as being beneficial by her, Kaikeyī, delighted and convinced, then spoke this to Mantharā."
O Kubjā, I did not know you as one who is truly excellent yet speaks of herself as inferior;
on this earth, you are the best among the hunchbacked in the certainty of your intellect.
"You alone, however, are ever intent on my welfare and desire my benefit;
O Kubjā, I would not have understood what the King intended to do."
There are those who are ill-formed, hunchbacked, crooked, and exceedingly wicked;
you, however, are lovely to behold, bending like a lotus under the wind.
Your chest is indeed well-set, rising as high as your shoulders;
and below it, your belly is tranquil, with a beautiful navel that seems almost bashful.
Your hips resound with beauty, adorned by a girdle of bells;
your thighs are perfectly set, and both your feet are long and well-formed.
O Mantharā, dressed in linen, with your long thighs,
you shine like a royal swan as you walk ahead of me.
This is your hump, long and extended like the front of a chariot;
within it dwell your thoughts, your knowledge of the Kṣatra, and your powers of illusion.
"O Kubjā, when Bharata has been consecrated and Rāghava has gone to the forest, I shall place this golden garland upon you."
O beautiful one, with pure gold that has been well-refined,
and having achieved my purpose and gained your trust, I shall smear your hump.
"And on your face, O hunchback, I shall have a beautiful, auspicious tilaka made of gold, as well as other auspicious ornaments."
Having donned two beautiful garments, you shall move about like a goddess;
with a face that rivals the moon, O lady of incomparable countenance,
you shall go along the most excellent path, putting your enemies to shame.
Your hunchbacks as well, adorned with all ornaments,
shall serve at the feet of Kubjā, just as you always serve mine.
Thus being praised, she spoke these words to Kaikeyī,
who lay upon a white couch like a flame of fire upon a sacrificial altar.
"O auspicious lady, it is not fitting to build a dam once the water has already flowed away.
Arise, do what is beneficial, and present yourself before the king."
Thus encouraged by Mantharā,
the large-eyed queen, proud with the intoxication of her own good fortune, went and entered the chamber of wrath.
The beautiful woman took off her pearl necklace worth many hundreds of thousands,
as well as her excellent and auspicious ornaments.
Then Kaikeyī, who resembled molten gold and had fallen under the influence of Mantharā’s words, lay down upon the ground and spoke thus to her: Ramāyaṇa 2.9.44.
"Or else, O hunchback, you shall report me as dead to the king;
for when Rāghava has reached the forest, Bharata will obtain the earth."
Then, having spoken these most cruel words and casting off all her ornaments,
that beautiful woman lay down upon the bare earth, uncovered by any bedding, like a fallen kinnarī.
With her face shrouded by the darkness of rising fury, and having cast off her finest garlands and ornaments,
that queen of the king became despondent, like the sky when its stars have vanished and are enveloped in gloom.

Having given orders for the consecration of the descendant of Raghu, the self-controlled Great King entered the inner apartments to tell the pleasant news to his beloved wife, who was worthy of such affection. *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 10.1.
There the lord of the earth beheld her fallen upon the ground, lying in a manner unaccustomed to her, as if scorched by grief.
That sinless old man beheld his young wife, who was dearer to him than life itself, lying upon the surface of the earth with sinful intent.
Like a great elephant in the forest, he caressed her out of affection, as a hunter in the woods might stroke a female elephant pierced by a poisoned arrow.

Having touched her with both hands, his mind filled with trepidation, the lover spoke these words to the woman whose eyes were like lotus petals: *parimṛśya ca pāṇibhyām abhisaṃtrastacetanaḥ / kāmī I do not recall you ever harboring anger within yourself;
O Queen, by whom have you been assailed, or by whom have you been insulted?

"Since you lie here in the dust for my sorrow, O auspicious one; why do you lie upon the ground while I am well-disposed toward you? Like one whose mind is possessed by a spirit, you are tormenting my heart."
"I have skilled physicians who are entirely well-pleased; they will bring you back to health. Tell me your ailment, O beautiful lady."
Whose dear wish must be fulfilled, or by whom has an offense been committed?
Who shall receive what is pleasing today, or who shall suffer a most grievous misfortune?
Who that is not to be killed should be killed, or who that is to be killed should be released?
Who should become poor, or who, though possessing wealth, should become destitute?
I myself and all my followers are subject to your will;
I do not venture to thwart any of your intentions.
"Tell me what you desire in your mind, even at the cost of my own life:
as far as the wheel turns, so far is the earth mine."
Thus addressed and comforted, she, desiring to speak that unpleasant news,
began once more to afflict her husband.
"I have not been treated with hostility by anyone, O King, nor have I been insulted;
however, I have a certain desire which I wish to have fulfilled by you."
Make a formal pledge if you wish to act;
then I shall declare that which has been requested by me.
Thus addressed by his beloved wife, the king, who had fallen under the sway of women,
replied to Kaikeyī with a slight smile, his great majesty undiminished.
O proud woman, you do not realize that there is no human being dearer to me than you; indeed, no other man exists who is dearer to me than Rāma, that tiger among men.
"O blessed lady, reflect upon this very heart of mine and draw it out;
having considered this, O Kaikeyī, speak what you deem to be right."
Perceiving my own strength, you ought not to doubt me;
I shall do what pleases you, I swear it to you by my very merit.
Delighted by those words, she spoke of her own most terrible intention, as if Death himself had arrived.
"Since you swear by your word in due order and grant me this boon,
let the thirty-three gods, led by Indra, hear it."
The moon and the sun, the sky, the planets, night and day, the quarters of space,
the world, and the earth itself, along with the Gandharvas and the Rākṣasas.
May the night-roaming spirits, the household deities in the houses,
and whatever other beings there may be, take note of what you have spoken.
"True to his promise, possessed of great splendor, knower of dharma, and perfectly composed—
let the deities hear from me that he shall grant me a boon."
Having thus embraced and reproached the great archer,
the queen then spoke these words to the boon-granter who was deluded by passion.
"O God, O Lord of the Earth, those two boons which were granted to me by you at that time—those very ones I shall speak of this very day; listen to my words."
"The preparations for Rāghava’s consecration have been made;
let Bharata be consecrated by me with this very same consecration."
Let Rāma become an ascetic, dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest for nine and five years, wearing bark garments, skins, and matted hair.
"Let Bharata enjoy the thornless sovereignty of the heir-apparent today;
for this very day I shall see Rāghava departing for the forest."
Then, O Great King, having heard Kaikeyī’s cruel words,
he was distressed and lamented, like a deer that has seen a tigress.
Seated upon the bare ground, sighing deeply, the lord of men, filled with indignation, uttered the words, "Alas! Shame!
and, his consciousness stricken by grief, fell once more into a swoon.
After a long time, the king regained consciousness and, being deeply distressed,
spoke to Kaikeyī in anger, as if burning her with his eyes.
O cruel woman of wicked conduct, you who are the destroyer of this lineage!
What wrong has Rāma done to you, O sinful woman, or what wrong have I done as well?
Rāghava always maintains toward you a conduct equal to that toward his own mother;
for what reason, then, are you now intent upon his ruin?
Out of ignorance, you were made by me to enter my own home for my own destruction, like a sharp-venomed female serpent, O princess.
When the entire world of living beings here is singing the praises of Rāma’s virtues,
on account of what offense shall I abandon my beloved son?
I might abandon Kausalyā or Sumitrā, or even my royal fortune, or even my own life; but I would never abandon Rāma, who is so devoted to his father.
Supreme joy comes to me upon seeing my eldest son;
yet when I do not see Rāma, my consciousness is lost.
The world might endure without the sun, or crops without water;
but my life cannot remain within this body without Rāma.
Therefore, enough! Let this resolve be abandoned, O woman of evil resolve;
I even touch your feet with my head—be gracious to me.
Lamenting like one who is helpless, that protector of the earth was seized in his heart by his wife with excessive intensity;
he fell upon her outstretched feet, failing to touch them both, just as a dying man fails to reach his goal.
The Great King, undeserving of such a fate and unaccustomed to it, lay there like Yayāti fallen from the world of the gods at the exhaustion of his merit. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 11.1)
Though her purpose was unfulfilled, she had achieved her aim; though fearless, she appeared to see danger.
Once more, that woman urged him toward that very same boon.
O Great King, you proclaim yourself a speaker of truth and one firm in his vows;
why then do you wish to withhold this boon from me? (Rāmāyaṇa 2.11.3)
Thus addressed by Kaikeyī, King Daśaratha then replied,
enraged and as if distraught for a moment.
When I am dead and Rāma, that bull among men, has gone to the forest— alas,
O ignoble woman, my enemy, Rāma has been exiled to the forest!
If I speak this truth, it will become a falsehood;
there will surely be incomparable infamy in the world and my certain humiliation.
As he was thus lamenting with a bewildered mind,
the sun set and night approached.
Thus, for the king who was lamenting in such distress, that night— though adorned by the orb of the moon— did not shine.
In that very manner, sighing hotly, the aged King Daśaratha lamented in distress like one afflicted, his eyes fixed upon the sky.
"I do not wish for dawn to break while you are here; I join my palms in supplication to you.
Or rather, depart quickly; I have no desire to see the pitiless and cruel Kaikeyī, on whose account this great calamity has occurred."
Having spoken thus, the king, with palms joined in reverence, again sought to appease Kaikeyī and spoke to her as follows.
O Queen, show favor to one who is of virtuous conduct, yet now wretched, whose life is spent, and who has turned his heart toward you— especially for the sake of the king, O blessed lady.
"O lady of beautiful hips, this has indeed been uttered by me in jest;
O young girl, please show me favor, for you are truly kind-hearted."
For, hearing the various and piteous lamentation of her husband— the king whose nature was pure, whose eyes were copper-red, and who was choked with tears— that cruel woman did not heed his words.
Then that king, seeing his beloved wife again dissatisfied and speaking with hostility regarding the exile of his son, fell to the ground unconscious and distressed.
Seeing the descendant of Ikṣvāku afflicted by grief for his son, fallen senseless upon the ground, and writhing there, that wicked woman spoke these words to him: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 12.1.
Having made a promise and then broken it, why do you lie thus, dejected, upon the surface of the earth as if you had committed a sin? You ought to remain steadfast in your station.
Those who know the Dharma say that truth is indeed the supreme Dharma;
for it is by relying upon truth that I have exhorted you to righteousness.
Having made this promise, O King, Śaibya, the lord of the earth, gave his own body to the hawk and attained the supreme goal.
For instance, the radiant Alarka, when a Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas requested them,
plucked out his own eyes and gave them away without any hesitation.
The lord of rivers, however, being devoted to truth, does not transgress his own boundary at the appointed time out of regard for truth, even though that boundary is very small.
And if you do not fulfill this noble agreement with me,
I shall abandon my life right before your eyes.
Thus urged by Kaikeyī, who was free from hesitation,
the king was unable to release himself from the snare, just as Bali could not escape the one set by Indra.
With a bewildered heart and a pale face,
he became like a draft animal struggling within the space between the yoke and the wheels.
With his eyes agitated as if unable to see, the lord of the earth steadied himself with great effort and fortitude, and spoke this to Kaikeyī: *RamS_2,12.10*
O wicked woman, that hand of yours which was grasped by me before the fire with the recitation of mantras—
that I now renounce, along with your own son, yourself.
Then Kaikeyī, of evil conduct, skilled in speech and overwhelmed with rage, addressed these harsh words once more to the king.
"O King, why do you speak these words that are like the pain of poison?
You ought to have Rāma, your unblemished son, brought here."
Having installed my son in the kingdom and having made Rāma a dweller in the forest,
and having made me free from rivals, you will have fulfilled your duty.
Like a noble horse pricked by a sharp goad, the king, being repeatedly urged on, spoke thus to Kaikeyī: "RamS_2,12.15"
"I am bound by the bond of dharma and my consciousness is lost;
I wish to see my eldest son, the beloved and righteous Rāma."
Having heard these words of the king, Kaikeyī immediately spoke herself to the charioteer: "Go, bring Rāma here."
Then that illustrious and righteous king, his joy regarding his son vanished and his eyes reddened with grief, looked up at the charioteer and spoke.
Having heard those piteous words and seeing the king so despondent, Sumantra joined his palms in reverence and withdrew slightly from that place.
When the lord of the earth was unable to speak himself due to his dejection,
then Kaikeyī, skilled in counsel, replied to Sumantra.
"Sumantra, bring the handsome Rāma quickly so that I may see him.
Thinking this was auspicious, he rejoiced in his heart.
Urged by her, Sumantra reflected quickly:
"Clearly, Rāma, the knower of dharma, will come here for the sake of his consecration."
Having thus formed this resolution, the charioteer of great splendor went forth once more with immense joy, desiring to behold Rāghava.
Then, having suddenly emerged from the front, looking at the lords of the earth stationed at the gate,
he beheld various citizens of great wealth who had approached and were standing at the entrance.
Having spent that night there, those Brahmins, masters of the Vedas, together with the royal priest, presented themselves at the assembly hall. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 13.1)
The ministers, the military commanders,
and the leading members of the merchant guilds gathered together, full of joy, for the sake of Raghava’s consecration.
When the stainless sun had risen and the day of Puṣya had arrived,
the lords of the twice-born prepared for Rāma’s consecration.
There were golden water-jars and a well-adorned auspicious throne;
and Rāma was properly seated upon it, covered with a shining tiger-skin.
Water brought from the holy confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
as well as from other sacred rivers, lakes, wells, and ponds.
The waters flowing eastward, upward, and across were gathered together;
and from them, as well as from all the oceans, water was drawn.
Honey, curd, ghee, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers, along with milk;
jars made of gold and silver, covered with leaves of milk-exuding trees and filled with parched grain, shone, adorned with lotuses and water-lilies and brimming with the finest water.
Resembling the radiant rays of the moon, white and adorned with jewels,
that excellent yak-tail fan stands ready for Rāma.
And there was a white parasol, resembling the orb of the moon,
ready, radiant, glorious, and placed in front for the consecration.
The white bull is ready, the white horse stands firm,
and the majestic royal elephant Prasruta awaits.
There were eight auspicious maidens adorned with all kinds of ornaments,
as well as all types of musical instruments, and likewise other bards.
Having gathered the materials suitable for the consecration of a prince, just as they are prepared for the royal consecration in the kingdom of the Ikṣvākus.
Having assembled there at the king’s command, they did not see the lord of the earth and said, "Who indeed shall announce us to the king?"
We do not see the king, yet the sun has risen,
and the consecration for the wise Rāma as crown prince is ready.
While they were speaking thus to the sovereign lords of the earth,
Sumantra, honored by the king, addressed all of them with these words.
"By your word I ask this: Is it well with the venerable ones? And what is the reason for the arrival of King Saṃpratibuddha?"
Having spoken thus, the knower of ancient lore approached the gate of the inner apartments and praised Rāghava with blessings endowed with virtuous qualities.
The blessed night has passed and an auspicious day has arrived;
awaken, O tiger among kings, and perform what must be done next.
"O King, the brahmins, the military chiefs, and the merchants have arrived;
they long for an audience. Wake up, O Raghava!"
Then, having awakened, the king spoke these words to Sumantra, that charioteer skilled in counsel, who was thus praising him.
"And while I am still fast asleep, bring Rāghava here quickly"—
thus King Daśaratha commanded the charioteer there once again.
Having heard the king's words and honored them with a bow of his head,
he departed from the royal residence, considering it a great favor.
Having reached the royal highway, which was adorned with banners and flags,
the charioteer there heard stories concerning Rāma.
Then Sumantra beheld the beautiful residence of Rāma, which possessed a splendor like that of Kailāsa and a radiance equal to the palace of Śakra.
It was closed with great doors, adorned with hundreds of balconies,
featuring a single golden statue and gateways of jewels and coral.
Resembling a dense mass of autumnal clouds, radiant like the interior of Mount Meru,
it was adorned with magnificent garlands of choice flowers.
Driving his chariot yoked with swift horses, the charioteer surveyed the royal palace crowded with men;
then, having approached that great and wealthy place, the charioteer’s hair stood on end with joy.

Like a sea-monster entering the ocean filled with abundant jewels, the charioteer entered unopposed that supreme mansion within the great celestial palace, which resembled a mountain peak or a mass of clouds.
Having passed through that gate of the inner apartments which was crowded with people,
he, the knower of ancient lore, then reached a secluded courtyard.
It was guarded by youths bearing spears and bows, wearing polished earrings,
who were vigilant, one-pointed in attention, and deeply devoted.
There he saw the superintendents of the women's quarters stationed at the gate— wearing saffron robes, elderly, holding canes in their hands, well-adorned, and composed in mind.
Seeing him approaching, those who wished to do what was pleasing to Rāma immediately informed Rāma, who was accompanied by his wife.
Having learned from the messenger that [the charioteer] had been announced, Rāghava, desiring to please his father, had him brought right there into his father's presence.
The charioteer beheld him, who resembled Vaiśravaṇa, well-adorned and seated upon a golden couch covered with a fine spread.
The scorcher of foes was anointed with the finest sandalwood paste, which was pure, fragrant, and possessed the hue of boar’s blood.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by Sītā standing at his side with a fly-whisk in her hand, appearing like the moon joined with the constellation Citrā.
To him, who was like the scorching sun, endowed with his own brilliance,
the bard— who knew the rules of conduct— paid homage like a humble servant to the granter of boons.
Having comfortably inquired about the prince’s well-being regarding his dwelling, bed, and seat, Sumantra, who was honored by the king, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
"O Lord, Kausalyā and the illustrious Kaikeyī, the queen, desire to see you; please go there without delay."
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Narasiṃha was delighted;
he then paid honor to Sītā and spoke these words.
The goddess and the god, having come together in my presence,
are surely deliberating on something concerning my consecration.
Having perceived his intention, Sudakṣiṇā, who desires his pleasure and possesses intoxicating eyes, urged the king on my behalf.
As is the assembly there, so is the messenger who has arrived;
surely the king will consecrate me as the crown prince this very day.
"Come now, having gone quickly from here, I shall see the lord of the earth;
you, however, remain here with your retinue and enjoy yourself in happiness."
Having been thus honored, the dark-eyed Sītā followed her husband as far as the gateway, invoking auspicious blessings.
Having seen all those seeking his favor, and having approached and greeted them,
he then ascended that excellent chariot which resembled fire.
With a golden luster, he seemed to steal away the eyes with his radiance,
and was yoked to excellent horses that resembled young female elephants.
Mounting a swift chariot yoked with bay horses, Rāghava, blazing with splendor, departed quickly like the thousand-eyed Indra.
Resounding like a rain-cloud in the sky,
that glorious one went forth from his dwelling, making it echo, like the moon emerging from a great cloud.
But Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, holding a parasol and a fly-whisk in his hands,
protected his brother from behind while standing upon the chariot.
Then, as he was departing, a tumultuous roar of "halahala" arose from the mass of people on all sides.
There Rāghava heard the chatter of the people gathered together—
the various words concerning himself from the citizens of the city who appeared joyful.

"Today this descendant of Raghu attains glory, desiring vast dominion through the favor of the king; we too have all our desires fulfilled, for he shall be our ruler. It is a gain for these people that he shall obtain this entire kingdom for a long time."

Honored by horses with resonant voices, by elephants serving as precursors, by bards and panegyrists chanting auspicious verses, and by the finest musicians, he proceeded like Vaiśravaṇa being extolled.

Rāma beheld the beautiful main road, crowded with female elephants, male elephants, chariots, and horses; its crossroads filled with throngs of people, abounding in jewels, and stocked with many articles for trade.
Mounting his chariot, the glorious Rāma— whose friends were filled with joy— beheld the city teeming with various people. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 15.1)
Rama proceeded along the royal highway, which was adorned with white houses resembling clouds and perfumed in the center with the smoke of aloe-wood.
He beheld that excellent royal road, shining and unconfined,
lined with various wares and diverse kinds of foods.
Hearing many blessings uttered by his friends and honoring all the men according to their merit, he departed.
That path which was practiced by your grandfathers and likewise by your great-grandfathers— from this day forward, O consecrated one, protect that very way.
Just as we were cherished by our father and as we were by our ancestors, the grandfathers,
so shall we all dwell even more happily under King Rāma.
Enough indeed with food today, and enough for us with the highest truths,
so that we may see Rāma returning and established in his kingdom.
For there will be nothing else more dear than this:
namely, the consecration of Rāma, who possesses immeasurable splendor, into the kingdom.
Listening to these and other auspicious stories concerning his friends— narratives that celebrated his own excellence— Rāma proceeded along the great highway.
Indeed, no man was able to withdraw his mind, or even his eyes, from that best of men,
even after Rāghava had already departed.
For that righteous-souled one shows compassion toward all four castes who are in their prime; therefore, they are devoted to him.
Having reached the royal palace, which resembled the abode of Mahendra,
the prince, blazing with splendor, entered his father’s residence.
Having passed through all the courtyards and turned back all the people, that son of Daśaratha entered the inner apartments.
Then, when the prince had entered his father’s presence, all that people were filled with joy and awaited his departure again,
just as the lord of rivers awaits the rising of the moon.
Rāma saw his father seated upon a beautiful throne together with Kaikeyī, looking dejected with a parched face. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 16.1)
Having first saluted his father’s feet with humility, he,
being well-composed, then paid homage to the feet of Kaikeyī.
Having uttered the word "Rāma," the king, his eyes overwhelmed with tears,
being dejected, was unable either to look at him or to speak.
Beholding that unprecedented and terrifying form of the king,
Rāma too was seized with fear, as if he had stepped upon a serpent with his foot.
With his senses uncheered, emaciated by grief and torment,
sighing deeply, the great king was distressed and agitated in mind.
Like an ocean garlanded with waves that is normally unshakeable yet appears to be agitated,
like the sun eclipsed, or like a seer who has uttered a falsehood.
Reflecting upon that inconceivable grief of his father,
he became even more agitated, like the ocean on a full-moon day.
And then Rāma, who was devoted to his father’s welfare, reflected:
"Why is it that the king does not greet me with joy this very day?"
On other occasions, even when my father was angry upon seeing me, he would become gracious;
why then does distress arise in him today at the sight of me?
Like one dejected, afflicted by grief, and with the luster of his face dimmed,
Rāma saluted Kaikeyī and spoke these words.
Tell me if I have committed some offense through ignorance for which my father is angry; and you yourself must appease him.
With a pale face and dejected, he does not speak to me;
is some physical or mental ailment afflicting him? Is it distress or intense fever? For constant happiness is indeed difficult to find.
I hope that no misfortune has befallen the dear-to-beholden prince Bharata,
nor the great-souled Śatrughna, nor my mothers.
If I do not satisfy the great king or carry out my father’s word,
I would not wish to live for even a moment while the monarch is angry.
Since a man perceives the very root from which his own manifestation here arises,
how could he not conduct himself toward that which is a manifest deity?
I hope that nothing harsh was said by you to my father out of arrogance or anger, such that his mind has been disturbed?
Tell this to me in truth, O Goddess, as I ask you:
for what reason has this unprecedented transformation occurred in the lord of men?
For at the word of the king— by whom I am commanded as my teacher, father, monarch, and benefactor— I would even fall into the fire, consume virulent poison, or drown in the ocean.
"O Queen, speak those words which the king desires; I shall do them, I promise you. Rāma does not speak twice."
To that Rāma, who was endowed with sincerity and speaking the truth, the ignoble Kaikeyī spoke these exceedingly cruel words.
Long ago, O Rāghava, during the war between the gods and the asuras, my father,
who was wounded by a dart in that great battle, granted two boons while being protected by me.
There, O Raghava, I requested from the king the consecration of Bharata and your departure for the Daṇḍaka forest this very day.
"O best of men, if you wish to make your father true to his promise and yourself as well, then listen to these words of mine."
Abide by your father’s command exactly as he promised:
you must enter the forest for fourteen years.
Abandoning this consecration, dwell for seven times seven years in the Daṇḍaka forest, wearing matted hair and bark garments.
Let Bharata rule this earth,
filled with various jewels and abounding in horses, chariots, and elephants, from the city of Kosala.
Having heard those unpleasant words from Kaikeyī, which were like death itself, Rāma, the slayer of enemies, was not distressed and spoke this to her: RamS_2,16.27 //
"So be it; from now on, I shall go to dwell in the forest, wearing matted hair and bark garments, fulfilling the king's promise."
But this I wish to know: for what reason does the lord of the earth, that invincible subduer of enemies, no longer greet me as he did before?
"O Goddess, you should not feel anger; speak before me.
I shall go to the forest wearing bark garments and matted hair; be well-pleased."
Being confidently enjoined by my father— who is well-wishing, venerable, grateful, and a king— what dear service would I not perform?
But this one falsehood in my mind burns my heart as it were—
that the King himself did not tell me of Bharata’s consecration.
Indeed, even without being prompted, I would joyfully give Sītā, the kingdom, my own life, and all my cherished wealth to my brother Bharata.
How much more so when he has been personally urged by his father, the lord of men,
and is fulfilling his promise for the sake of doing what is pleasing to you?
Therefore, comfort him; for why is it that the lord of the earth, with eyes fixed upon the ground, slowly sheds these tears?
And let messengers go on swift-footed horses this very day, by the king's command, to bring Bharata from his maternal uncle’s house.
"I am going from here in haste to the Daṇḍaka forest,
without deliberating over my father's command, in order to dwell there for fourteen years."
Having heard those words of Rāma, Kaikeyī was delighted; trusting in his departure, she indeed urged Rāghava to hasten.
"So be it; let men go as messengers on swift-footed horses to bring Bharata back from his maternal uncle's house."
But I consider it appropriate for you, O Rāma, that there should be no further delay for one who is eager; therefore, you ought to depart from here for the forest quickly.
O best of men, it is because he is overcome with shame that the king does not speak to you himself; this is nothing, so let your anger be dispelled.
O Rāma, as long as you have not departed from this city in haste for the forest,
your father will neither bathe nor eat.
"Alas, what misery! sighing thus, the king, overwhelmed by grief, fell unconscious upon that gold-adorned couch.
Rāma, too, having raised up the king who had been urged by Kaikeyī,
made haste to go to the forest like a horse struck by a whip.
Having heard those unpleasant words of the ignoble woman, which were harsh in their core, Rāma remained free from distress and spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
"O Queen, I do not venture to dwell in this world intent upon worldly gain;
know me to be equal to the seers, established solely in dharma."
Whatever kindness you, sir, might wish to do for me, that shall be accomplished by me in every way, even at the cost of my own life.
For there is no practice of dharma greater than this:
namely, service to one's father or the carrying out of his word.
Even though it has not been said by your honor,
I shall dwell in this lonely forest for fourteen years at your word.
Surely you do not perceive any virtue in me, Kaikeyī,
since you have spoken thus to the King, even though you are my sovereign.
"As soon as I have taken leave of my mother and entreated Sītā,
I shall depart this very day for the great Daṇḍaka forest."
"Bharata must protect the kingdom and serve his father;
this is how you must act, for that is the eternal dharma."
Having heard Rāma’s words, his father, deeply stricken by grief and unable to restrain his tears out of sorrow, wept aloud with a great sound.
Having then bowed at the feet of his unconscious father and also of the ignoble Kaikeyī, the immensely radiant Rāma departed.
Having circumambulated his father and Kaikeyī,
Rāma emerged from that inner apartment and beheld his circle of friends.
With eyes filled with tears,
Lakṣmaṇa— the enhancer of Sumitrā’s joy— followed behind him, burning with supreme indignation.
Having performed the circumambulation of the vessels used for the consecration, Rāma walked away slowly, looking back with longing and not withdrawing his gaze from that spot.
And the loss of his kingdom did not diminish his great splendor;
for the world-beloved one, his loveliness remained as that of the cool-rayed moon during the night.
In him who desires to go to the forest and renounce the earth, no sign of mental agitation is perceived, as if he were one who has transcended all worlds.
Bearing his sorrow in his mind and restraining his senses,
the self-possessed prince entered his mother’s chamber, intending to announce the unpleasant news.
Having entered his palace, which was filled with extreme joy, and beholding that calamity regarding his wealth that had arrived,
Rāma did not undergo any change of state there, due to his apprehension for the welfare of his kinsmen.
But Rāma, deeply distressed and sighing like an elephant, went with his brother to his mother’s inner apartments, though he was one who possessed self-mastery. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 17.1)
There he saw an elderly man, most highly honored,
seated at the door of the house, while many others stood nearby.
Having entered the first courtyard, he beheld in the second elderly brahmins, perfected in the Vedas, who were being honored by the king.
Having bowed to those elders, Rāma beheld on the third day women— both old and young— as well as men, all intent upon guarding the gate.
Having increased [the size of the cake] and entered their home, those women, filled with joy,
quickly announced that pleasant news to Rāma’s mother.
Then Queen Kausalyā, having remained composed throughout the night,
performed worship to Viṣṇu at dawn, desiring the welfare of her son.
Clad in linen garments, joyful and ever devoted to her vows,
she then offered oblations into the fire with sacred mantras, having performed the auspicious rites.
Having then entered his mother’s auspicious inner apartments, Rāma beheld his mother there, making oblations into the sacrificial fire.
Having seen her son, the delighter of his mother, returned after a long time,
she rushed toward him in great joy, like a mare toward her foal.
Out of maternal affection for her son, Kausalyā spoke these words, both pleasing and beneficial, to her own son, the invincible Rāghava.
Obtain long life, fame, and the dharma established in your lineage from these aged, virtuous, and high-souled royal sages.
Behold your father, O Raghava, the king who is true to his promise;
for this very day, that righteous soul shall consecrate you as the crown prince.
Rāghava, naturally humble and bowed down by respect, spoke to his mother while slightly extending his joined palms.
O Queen, you surely do not realize that a great danger has arrived;
this will bring suffering for you, for Vaidehī, and for Lakṣmaṇa.
"For fourteen years I shall dwell in the lonely forest,
subsisting on honey, roots, and fruits like a sage, having abandoned meat."
The great king bestows the status of crown prince upon Bharata,
but he exiles me to the Daṇḍaka forest to live as an ascetic.
Seeing his mother fallen like a plantain tree, unaccustomed to suffering,
Rāma raised her up as she lay unconscious.
Having turned back, he stroked with his hand the distressed woman who had risen like a weary mare,
her entire body covered in dust.
Afflicted by sorrow though accustomed to comfort, she spoke to Raghava,
that tiger among men, as he sat nearby while Lakshmana listened.
O Rāghava, if you, my son, had not been born to cause me grief,
I would not have experienced such further suffering as one who remains childless.
For a barren woman, O son, there is only one human sorrow:
the anguish that "I am childless"; no other exists.
"Never before have I seen such auspiciousness or happiness in my husband's manliness;
thinking that I might see it even in my son, I have remained devoted to Rāma."
"As the most excellent wife, I shall have to hear many unpleasant words from my inferior co-wives that pierce the heart; what indeed could be more painful for women than this?"
Even while you were present, I was thus rejected;
how much more so now that you have departed, my father? Surely my death is certain.
For whoever serves me or follows me,
that person does not speak to me, having regard for the son of Kaikeyī.
O Raghava, seventeen years have passed since you were born, while I,
longing for the end of my suffering, have waited.
Indeed, you have been raised in vain by me through fasts, yogic practices, and many arduous labors, for you are destined for a miserable state.
I consider this heart of mine to be firm indeed, since it does not shatter,
like the bank of a great river struck by new waters during the rainy season.
Surely death does not exist for me alone, nor is there any room for me in the abode of Yama,
since Death does not wish to carry me off this very day by force, as a lion seizes a weeping doe.
"Surely my heart is made of iron, for it remains firm, neither breaking nor rending upon this earth;
and though my body is surrendered to this suffering, it is certain that death does not occur before its time."
