But this is my sorrow: that my vows, gifts, and self-restraints, as well as the ascetic penance I have practiced for the sake of offspring, are utterly fruitless—like seed sown in saline soil.
For if anyone, emaciated by heavy sorrow, could obtain death at will even before their time,
I would have gone this very day to the assembly of the departed, like a cow deprived of her calf, without you.
Then, beholding Rāghava and perceiving that great calamity, she lamented intensely and with indignation,
like a kinnarī seeing her son bound.
While Kausalyā, the mother of Rāma, was thus lamenting, the dejected Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words appropriate to the occasion. (Ramāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 18.1)
Noble lady, it does not please me either that Rāghava,
having fallen under the influence of a woman's words, should abandon the glory of the kingdom and go to the forest.
Perverted, aged, and assailed by the objects of the senses,
what indeed would the king not say when urged on by passion?
I see no offense in him, nor any such fault,
by which Rāghava should be exiled from the kingdom to dwell in the forest.
I do not see anyone in this world, even behind his back,
who— whether an enemy or one cast out— could point out his fault.
Who, observing his son who is like a god, upright, self-controlled, and kind even toward his enemies, would abandon him for no reason?
What son, mindful of the conduct of kings, would take to heart these words of the king, who has once again fallen into childhood?
As long as no man understands this matter,
for that long alone establish my teaching within yourself along with me.
O Rāghava, while you stand protected at my side with my bow, who would be capable of doing you harm, any more than one could against Death himself standing ready?
"O bull among men, I shall make this entire Ayodhyā devoid of people with my sharp arrows, if you persist in what is disagreeable to me."
"Furthermore, whoever is on Bharata's side or whoever desires his welfare—all these I shall slay; for one who is mild is treated with contempt."
"O subduer of enemies, having created this unsurpassed enmity with both you and me,
who has the power to give the sovereignty to Bharata?"
"O Queen, I am truly devoted to my brother in spirit;
I swear this to you by my truth, by my bow, and by the gifts and sacrifices I have offered."
O Queen, if Rāma should enter a blazing fire or the forest,
consider me as having entered there before him.
"By my prowess, I shall dispel your suffering as the risen sun dispels the darkness;
let the Goddess behold my valor, and let Rāghava behold it as well."
Having heard these words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
Kausalyā, weeping and overwhelmed with grief, spoke to Rāma.
"My son, you have heard what your brother Lakṣmaṇa has said;
do now whatever you deem appropriate in this matter, if it pleases you."
Having heard the unrighteous words spoken by my co-wife,
you ought not to depart from here, abandoning me while I am consumed by grief.
O knower of dharma, if you are most righteous and wish to practice dharma, then remain here and serve me; thus practice the unsurpassed dharma.
O son, while living in his own home, self-restrained and devoted to serving his mother,
Kāśyapa, endowed with supreme austerity, ascended to heaven.
Just as the king is to be honored by you with reverence, so indeed am I;
I do not give you permission, for you must not go from here to the forest.
"Separated from you, I have no need for life or for happiness;
it would be better for me to eat even grass if I were with you."
If you go to the forest, abandoning me while I am consumed by grief, I shall sit here awaiting death by fasting; for I shall not be able to live.
Then, O son, you shall fall into a hell renowned throughout the world,
just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, fell through the unrighteousness of the murder of a Brahmin.
Then the righteous Rāma spoke these words, consistent with dharma, to his mother Kausalyā, who was thus lamenting in distress.
I have no power to transgress my father’s word;
I entreat you with my head bowed low, for I wish to go to the forest.
And even by the wise seer Kaṇḍu, while observing his vows and carrying out his father’s command, a cow was killed despite his knowledge of the Dharma.
And in our own lineage, in former times, while digging for treasure by the command of their father Sagara,
the sons of Sagara met with a very great slaughter.
By Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, acting in obedience to his father’s command, his own mother Reṇukā was herself cut down with an axe in the forest.
"Indeed, this command of my father is not being carried out by me alone;
rather, I am following the path intended and traversed by my ancestors."
Therefore, this very task must be performed by me on earth and not otherwise;
for no one indeed suffers loss by carrying out the word of their father.
Having spoken thus to his mother, he spoke again to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, I know your unsurpassed affection for me;
yet you do not understand my intention regarding truth and tranquility."
For Dharma is supreme in the world; truth is established upon Dharma;
and this most excellent speech of my father is itself founded upon Dharma.
O hero, having heard the words of one's father, mother, or a Brahmin, one who stands firm in dharma must not act in vain.
Therefore, O hero, I shall not be able to transgress my father’s command;
for it was at my father’s word that I was urged on by Kaikeyī.
Therefore, abandon this ignoble resolve that relies on the conduct of a warrior; take recourse in righteousness, do not resort to harshness, and let my counsel be followed.
Having spoken thus to his brother out of affection, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa spoke again to Kausalyā with joined palms and head bowed low.
"O Goddess, grant me leave as I am about to depart from here for the forest.
You are bound by my life-breaths; perform the rites of blessing for me.
Having fulfilled my vow, I shall return from the forest to the city once more."
For I am not able to cast behind me this great prosperity for the sake of mere sovereignty;
O Queen, while life is not yet long, I do not choose an inferior kingdom today through unrighteousness.
Pacifying his mother, that bull among men, desiring to depart for the Daṇḍaka forest by means of his prowess,
then gave firm instructions to his younger brother and, keeping his mother in his heart, performed a circumambulation around her.
Then [he saw him] dejected with grief, exceedingly indignant, panting like a lordly elephant, his eyes wide with rage. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 19.1)
Having approached his beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā and his dear friend, the self-possessed Rāma,
maintaining his composure with fortitude, spoke these words.
O Saumitri, let this flurry of preparations for my consecration be turned instead into a flurry of preparations for the cessation of that consecration.
Act in such a way that our mother, whose mind is tormented for the sake of my consecration, may not be filled with apprehension.
O Saumitri, I cannot endure for even a moment the pain born of doubt that has arisen in my mind regarding her; I must not neglect it.
I do not recall ever having done anything, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
that was even slightly displeasing to my mother or my father.
Truthful, faithful to his word, and ever possessing the prowess of truth,
may my father— who was once afraid out of fear of the next world— now be free from fear.
For if this deed of his remains unretracted,
he will surely suffer the mental torment of thinking "it was not true," and that torment of his will burn me as well.
Therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, having concluded the ritual of consecration,
I desire to depart from here for the forest immediately thereafter.
"Today, through my renunciation, the princess has fulfilled her purpose;
she will then consecrate her son Bharata without distraction."
When I have gone to the forest, wearing bark garments and deerskins and bearing a mass of matted hair, Kaikeyī will find peace of mind.
I ought not to cause distress to him by whom this intellect has been so well-guided and whose mind is so perfectly composed; I shall go forth into the religious life without delay.
O Saumitri, it must indeed be regarded as the work of Fate alone— both my exile and the subsequent reversal of the kingdom that had already been granted.
For how could Kaikeyī’s resolve toward my torment have come to pass,
were it not for this divine disposition ordained by destiny?
For you know well, O gentle one, that there was never any distinction in my mind between my mothers,
nor any difference in my past conduct toward her or toward my own son.
I do not attribute her harsh and terrible words— spoken for the sake of preventing my consecration and intended to drive me away— to anything other than fate.
"How could a princess endowed with such noble nature and virtues speak of her suffering before her husband like an ordinary woman?"
That which is inconceivable is destiny, and it cannot be thwarted even among living beings;
it is manifest in me and in her, for indeed a reversal has fallen upon us both.
O Saumitri, what man dares to fight against destiny,
for which no cause other than past action is ever observed?
Pleasure and pain, fear and anger, gain and loss, existence and non-existence—
whatever such things as these occur, are they not indeed the work of destiny?
"Even though my consecration has been thwarted, I feel no distress;
therefore, you too, being free from distress, should comply with me and quickly withdraw the preparations for the consecration."
O Lakṣmaṇa, in this obstacle to my kingdom, my younger mother is not to be suspected;
for those struck by fate speak what is undesirable, and you know that such is the power of destiny.
While Rāma was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, with his head bowed, repeatedly listened and, as it were, entered into the middle of both sorrow and joy with his mind. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 20.1)
Then, knitting his brows together in the middle of his forehead, that bull among men hissed like an enraged great serpent within its hole.
Then his face, together with its frown, shone like the face of an enraged lion; it was difficult to look upon.
Shaking him off like an elephant shakes its own trunk, he threw him down across his body, bending his neck both sideways and upwards.
Looking askance at his brother with the corner of his eye, he said:
"This very great agitation has indeed arisen in him at an improper time."
Because it would entail a fault in the Dharma and because the world would not fail to suspect it,
how could one such as you, being free from delusion, speak this?
Since fate is not heroic, why do you, a heroic bull among Kshatriyas, praise that wretched and powerless fate?
But how indeed can there be no suspicion regarding those two evildoers?
O you whose soul is devoted to dharma, do you not perceive that there are subtle deceptions in the guise of righteousness?

O Lord of the Earth, this consecration of someone other than you— an undertaking loathed by the world— has been commenced by him because of whom your mind has fallen into this dilemma; for that very dharma is hateful to me, on account of which you have become deluded.
Even though your conduct is divine and that is the opinion of those two [sages], nevertheless it must be disregarded by you; even that does not please me.
He who is cowardly and devoid of vigor follows fate;
heroes who esteem themselves do not wait upon fate.
The man who is capable of counteracting fate through human effort does not despair when his purpose is frustrated by fate.
Today they shall behold both divine power and human prowess;
today the distinction between the divine and the human shall become manifest.
Today people shall indeed behold destiny struck down by my prowess,
for they have seen today that your consecration to the kingdom was brought about by destiny.
Like an unrestrained elephant, intoxicated by the strength of its rut and rushing forward beyond the goad, I shall turn back destiny through human effort.
Even all the world-protectors together could not today prevent the consecration of Rāma, nor could all the three worlds; how much less so his father?
O King, those by whom you were persuaded to dwell in the forest without clothing shall likewise dwell in the forest for fourteen years.
I shall shatter that hope of your father and of her,
which exists for the sake of your son’s kingdom by obstructing his consecration.
The power of destiny will not prevail against one who opposes me with my own strength; rather, it will lead to suffering, just as my fierce human effort shall do.
O noble sons, after you have gone to dwell in the forest, at the end of a thousand years, they shall thereafter protect the subjects.
For dwelling in the forest is ordained as the conduct of former royal sages,
after having entrusted their subjects to their sons for protection as if they were their own children.
O righteous-souled Rāma, if you do not desire the kingdom for yourself in this way because the king is distracted and you fear a disturbance in the realm, [then consider this].
And I promise you, O hero, that I shall not fail to attain the world of heroes;
I shall protect your kingdom as the shore protects the ocean.
Be consecrated with auspicious rites; apply yourself there.
I alone am sufficient to restrain the rulers of the earth by force.
These two arms are not for the sake of beauty; this bow is not for my adornment; this sword is not for the purpose of binding; nor are these arrows intended to serve as pillars.
All these four are for the purpose of subduing my enemies;
yet I do not desire anything excessively, even regarding one who might be considered my foe.
Even with a sharp-edged sword, possessing the brilliance of flashing lightning,
held aloft, one should not consider an enemy to be like the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The earth shall become impassable and difficult to traverse for me, strewn with the trunks, thighs, and heads of elephants, horses, and men, crushed by the clashing of swords.
Struck today by the edge of my sword, the elephants will fall upon the earth like blazing mountains or like clouds accompanied by lightning.
With my finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on and my bow grasped,
how could any man claim the title of "man" while I stand here?
Overpowering the one with many, and the many people with one,
I shall discharge my arrows into the vital spots of men, horses, and elephants.
Today, O Lord, the power of my weapon’s majesty shall prevail;
it shall bring about the king’s lack of authority and establish your own sovereignty.
Today is the day for the application of the essence of sandalwood, for the removal of armlets,
for the relinquishing of wealth, and for the protection of friends.
These two arms of Rāma are worthy of performing the task of warding off those who would create obstacles to his consecration.
"Tell me, who today shall be separated by me from his life, his fame, and his kinsmen—your enemy—so that this earth may come under your control? Command me accordingly; I am your servant."
Having wiped away his tears and consoled Lakṣmaṇa repeatedly, that enhancer of the Raghava lineage said:
"Listen to me, for I am established in my father’s word; indeed, O gentle one, this is the path of the righteous."
Seeing him thus intent on carrying out his father’s command, Kausalyā, her voice choked with tears, spoke these most righteous words: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 21.1.
How could he, whose nature is dharma, who has never known suffering, and who speaks kindly to all beings—
having been born from Daśaratha through me— subsist by gleaning?
How shall this lord, whose servants and slaves eat choice foods, now subsist on roots and fruits in the forest?
Who, having heard this, would believe it? Or who would not be struck with fear—that Rāghava, virtuous and beloved of the king, is being exiled?
Deprived of you here, this incomparable and great fire of grief will consume me,
just as a blazing fire consumes dry grass at the end of winter.
For how could a cow not follow her own calf as it departs?
I shall follow you, my son, wherever you go.
Having heard those words spoken by his mother, Rāma, the bull among men, addressed his deeply distressed mother with these words.
Deceived by Kaikeyī, and having taken refuge in the forest while I am away,
the king will surely not survive once he is abandoned by you as well.
Indeed, the abandonment of a husband is a cruel act for a woman alone;
it must not be committed by you even in thought, for it is utterly contemptible.
"As long as my father, the descendant of Kakutstha and lord of the earth, lives, let service be rendered to him; for that is the eternal dharma."
Thus addressed by Rāma, the beautiful Kausalyā,
being well-pleased, said "So be it" to Rāma, the doer of effortless deeds.
Thus addressed, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
spoke these words once more to his mother, who was deeply afflicted with grief.
Both you and I must carry out the word of our father;
for the king is the husband, the supreme elder, and the sovereign lord of all.
Having dwelt in this great forest for these fourteen years,
I shall remain most joyful in obedience to your word.
Having been addressed thus by her beloved son, Kausalyā, who was devoted to her son, then spoke with a face filled with tears, being herself deeply afflicted.
"O Rāma, it is not fitting for me to dwell among these co-wives.
O descendant of Kakutstha, take me as well to the forest, like a wild doe;
if you have resolved to go out of regard for your father."
To her who was weeping thus, Rāma, weeping himself, spoke these words:
"For a living woman, the husband is indeed her deity and her lord;
today, the King, as my sovereign, holds authority over both you and me."
And Bharata too, whose soul is righteous and who speaks kindly to all beings, will follow you; for he is always devoted to dharma.
Therefore, being vigilant, act in such a way that the king does not suffer any distress from grief for his son once I have departed.
That most excellent woman who is devoted to vows and fasting,
yet does not follow her husband, shall go to an evil destiny.
She should indeed perform service, devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband;
this is the dharma seen of old, heard in the Veda, and recorded in the Smṛtis.
"O Goddess, those Brahmins of firm vows are worthy of worship on my account;
thus, wait for the time, longing for my return."
"You shall attain your supreme desire once I have returned,
provided that the best among the upholders of dharma continues to hold onto his life."
Thus addressed by Rāma, Kausalyā, her eyes clouded with tears and afflicted by grief for her son, spoke these words to Rāma:
"Go, my son, with a focused mind; may it ever be well with you, O Lord."
For, beholding Rāma resolved upon dwelling in the forest, the queen, with a supreme heart,
spoke auspicious words to Rāma and became intent on seeking his well-being.
Having dispelled that distress and sipped pure water, the high-minded mother performed auspicious rites for Rāma. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 22.1)
May the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts, along with the great ṛṣis, grant well-being;
may Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ grant well-being, and may Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Aryaman grant well-being.
May the seasons, the fortnights, the months, the years, the nights,
the days, and the moments always grant you well-being.
May mindfulness, fortitude, and righteousness protect you on all sides, my son,
as well as the blessed Lord Skanda, Soma, and Bṛhaspati.
May the Seven Sages and Nārada protect you on all sides,
as well as all the constellations and the planets together with their presiding deities,
for you who are wise and wander in the guise of a sage through the great forests.
May there be no monkeys, scorpions, gadflies, or mosquitoes in the forest for you, nor any reptiles or insects in that thicket.
May the great elephants, lions, tigers, bears, fanged beasts,
and fierce horned buffaloes not harm you, my son.
O son, let those who eat human flesh, the fierce ones, and whatever other species of beings there may be, not harm you; for they have been fully honored here by me.
May your sacred scriptures be auspicious, may your heroic endeavors be successful, and may all prosperity attend you, O Rāma; go forth in well-being, my dear son.
May there be well-being for you from the beings of the intermediate space and from those of the earth, again and again;
and likewise from all the gods, and from those who stand as obstacles to you.
May Brahmā, the lord of all worlds, the sustainer of beings, as well as the sages and all the remaining gods, protect you while you dwell in the forest.
Thus the illustrious, large-eyed lady honored the hosts of gods with garlands, perfumes, and fitting hymns of praise.
Whatever auspiciousness arose at the destruction of Vṛtra for the thousand-eyed one who is honored by all the gods— may that auspiciousness be yours.
Whatever auspicious blessing Vinatā formerly invoked for Suparṇa as he sought the nectar of immortality, may that same blessing be yours.
Kausalyā also prepared the auspicious *oṣadhī* known as *siddhārthā*, which removes all pain, and she performed protective rites while reciting sacred mantras.
Having bowed her head and smelled it, the illustrious lady embraced him and said, "O son, Siddhārtha; go, Rāma, as you please."
"O child, I see you returned safely to Ayodhyā, free from illness, with all your goals accomplished, dwelling happily and securely in the royal palace."
O Raghava, may the hosts of gods headed by Śiva, the great seers, the spirits, the great asuras, and the serpents— worshipped by me—
desire your welfare as you depart for the forest for a long time, and likewise may the quarters of the sky do so.
Thus, with her eyes filled with tears, having completed the rites for well-being according to the prescribed rules,
she circumambulated Rāghava and embraced him again and again, pressing him close.
Having thus performed a circumambulation of the queen and having repeatedly pressed his mother’s feet,
that highly illustrious Rāghava, blazing with his own splendor, went to Sītā’s dwelling.
Having paid homage to Kausalyā, Rāma, having performed the rites for his safe journey and remaining steadfast on the path of righteousness, set out for the forest. *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 23.1.
Illuminating the royal highway crowded with men, the prince seemed to churn the hearts of the people with his excellence.
And the ascetic Vaidehī did not hear any of that;
her mind was fixed solely upon his consecration as the crown prince.
Having performed her duties for the gods, grateful and joyful in heart, she—
well-versed in the laws of kings— waited upon the prince.
Then Rāma entered his own well-adorned residence,
which was filled with joyful people, while his face was somewhat cast down with shame.
Then Sītā, springing up and trembling,
beheld her husband tormented by grief, his senses agitated by anxiety.
Seeing him with a pale face, perspiring and impatient, she, tormented by grief, said: "O Lord, what is this now?"
"O Raghava, today the auspicious Puṣya constellation is joined with Bṛhaspati, as declared by wise Brahmins; why then are you dejected?"
Your lovely face, though covered by a parasol with a hundred ribs that resembles the foam of water, does not shine forth.
And why is your face, with eyes resembling the hundred-petaled lotus, not fanned by those two excellent fans which possess the brilliance of the moon and the swan?
O bull among men, the eloquent bards and the heralds and genealogists, who used to praise you with auspicious hymns, are not seen today, filled as they once were with joy.
Those Brahmins, masters of the Vedas, did not, according to the prescribed rite, place honey and curds upon the head of the consecrated king.
Neither all the subjects, nor the adorned leaders of the guilds, nor likewise the people of the city and the countryside, desire to follow you.
Why does your principal flower-chariot, yoked with four excellent horses adorned with gold and endowed with great speed, not go before you?
O hero, as you set forth, no glorious elephant, adorned with auspicious marks and possessing the luster of a dark cloud or a mountain, is seen before you.
And yet, O one of lovely appearance, I do not see you going ahead with the golden,
variegated throne placed before you, preceded by your heroic attendants.
When the consecration is ready, why is this now with you?
Your facial complexion is unprecedented, and no great joy is observed.
To her, who was thus lamenting, the joy of the Raghus said:
"O Sītā, my noble father is sending me away to the forest."
Born of a great lineage, knower of dharma, and practitioner of dharma—
listen, O daughter of Janaka, to how this has come upon me in due course.
In the past, my father King Daśaratha, who was true to his promise, joyfully granted two great boons to Kaikeyī.
Therefore, today, while this consecration has been prepared for me and undertaken by the king,
that time has been impelled by Dharma and utterly defeated.
"For fourteen years must I dwell in Daṇḍaka;
my father has also appointed Bharata as the heir apparent.
Thus, having come to see you, I am setting out for the lonely forest."
"You must never speak of me in Bharata’s presence;
for men endowed with great power cannot endure the praise of others.
Therefore, my virtues must not be recounted before Bharata."
Nor should you ever be supported by him in any special way;
it is possible to remain near him only by being compliant.
And I too, fulfilling that promise of my elder, shall depart for the forest this very day; remain firm, O wise lady.
And when I have departed for the forest frequented by sages, O auspicious and sinless lady, you must remain devoted to vows and fasting.
Having risen early in the morning and performed the worship of the gods according to the prescribed rites,
my father Daśaratha, the lord of men, must be saluted.
And my mother Kausalyā, aged and emaciated by grief,
deserves honor from you, having placed dharma foremost.
And you must always pay homage to those who remain, my other mothers; for they are equal to me in affection, endearment, and shared enjoyment.
Furthermore, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, who are dearer to me than my own life, should especially be regarded by you as equal to your own brothers and sons.
One must never do anything displeasing to Bharata,
for he is indeed the king and the lord of both the country and the lineage.
For kings, when propitiated by virtue and served with diligent efforts, become well-disposed; in the opposite case, they become enraged.
For kings abandon even their own biological sons if they act against their interests, yet they accept even strangers if they are capable.
"I shall go to the great forest, my dear; you must remain right here, O beautiful lady. You must act according to these words of mine, so that you do not cause offense to anyone."
Thus addressed, Vaidehī— who was worthy of affection and spoke with kindness— became enraged out of very much love and spoke this to her husband: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 24.1).
Noble son, father, mother, brother, son, and likewise daughter-in-law,
each enjoying their own merits, experience their respective fortunes.
O bull among men, a wife alone receives the fortune of her husband;
for this reason, I have been commanded that I must dwell in the forest as well.
Neither father, nor son, nor self, nor mother, nor circle of friends—
here on earth and after death, for women, the husband alone is always their refuge.
O Rāghava, if you are setting out for the difficult forest this very day,
I shall go before you, treading down the kusha grass and thorns.
Casting aside envy and anger like water left over after drinking, lead me confidently, O hero; no sin exists within me.
Whether by means of the tops of palaces, celestial chariots, or traveling through the sky,
the shadow of the Lord’s feet is superior in every situation.
I have been instructed by my mother and father in various matters;
I need not now be told how I ought to conduct myself.
I shall dwell happily in the forest, just as if in my father’s palace,
not thinking of the three worlds, but contemplating only my devotion to my husband.
Constantly serving you, self-restrained and observing the vow of celibacy,
O hero, I shall enjoy myself with you in the forests fragrant with honey.
For you, O Rāma, are indeed capable of providing protection in the forest for any other person here, let alone for me, O bestower of honor.
I shall always subsist on fruits and roots; of this there is no doubt. Dwelling together with you, I will cause you no suffering.
With you as my wise protector, I desire to behold rivers, mountains, ponds, and forests everywhere, free from fear.
Accompanied by you, O hero, I wish to behold with joy the lotus ponds, filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks and beautifully in bloom.
"O large-eyed one, with you I shall sport, supremely delighted;
thus may I spend a hundred thousand years together with you."
And even if my dwelling in heaven were to occur without you, O Rāghava, tiger among men, I would not find even that desirable.
I shall go to the forest, so difficult to traverse, filled with deer and abounding in monkeys and elephants;
there I will dwell as if in my father’s house, devotedly clinging to your very feet.
"Take me, who am devoted to no other, whose heart is full of love for you, and who am resolved to die if separated from you;
please fulfill my request, for I shall not be a burden to you."
Even though she spoke thus, that best of men, who was devoted to righteousness, did not wish to take Sītā away;
and he spoke many words to her, who was distressed regarding the dwelling in the forest, in order to turn her back.
To Sītā, who was speaking thus, the righteous-souled Rāma— knower of dharma and lover of dharma— spoke these words for the sake of her returning. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 25.1)
"Sītā, you are born of a noble lineage and are always devoted to dharma;
practice your own duty here, and not merely for the sake of your heart's pleasure."
"O Sītā, O frail woman, you must act exactly as I tell you;
for there are many dangers in the forest—listen to me as I describe them."
O Sītā, let this intention to dwell in the forest be abandoned;
for the wilderness, known as the forest, is said to be full of many perils.
Indeed, these words are spoken by me out of a desire for your welfare;
I do not know of any constant happiness, for the forest is always nothing but suffering.
The roars of lions dwelling in mountain caves, produced by the mountain torrents, are painful to hear; therefore, the forest is a place of suffering.
One sleeps on the ground upon beds of leaves broken off by oneself during nights exhausted by fatigue; therefore, the forest is more miserable than that.
And a fast must be observed according to one's strength, O Maithilī;
and a mass of matted hair must be worn by one clad in garments of bark.
There is an excessive wind, constant darkness, and perpetual hunger; there are also great terrors therein—therefore, that forest is more painful than all else.
And many reptiles of various forms roam the earth out of pride, O beautiful lady; therefore, this forest is even more painful.
Snakes that dwell in rivers and move as crookedly as rivers stand blocking the path; therefore, the forest is even more painful than this.
Moths, scorpions, insects, gadflies, and mosquitoes constantly afflict the weak; therefore, the forest is entirely suffering.
O beautiful lady, because of the thorny trees, the *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses,
and the branches of the forest trees tangled together, this forest is exceedingly painful.
Therefore, enough of your going to the forest; for the forest is not suitable for you.
Reflecting upon it here, I see the forest as having many greater evils.
When the high-souled Rāma had not yet resolved to lead her to the forest, Sītā did not heed his words; thereupon, deeply distressed, she spoke this to Rāma.
Having heard these words of Rāma, Sītā, distressed and with her face covered in flowing tears, spoke these words softly: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 26.1.
Those defects you have enumerated regarding dwelling in the forest— know them, rather, to be virtues, prompted as they are by your affection for me.
"I must go with you, O Rāma, by the command of my elders;
for without you, my life must be abandoned here."
And even while I am standing right here beside you, O Raghava, Śakra, the lord of the gods, is not able to overpower me by his might.
But a woman who is deprived of her husband will not be able to live;
O Rāma, you have indeed shown me such a state as this.
Moreover, O one of great wisdom, I have heard from the Brahmins that in former times, while in my father’s house, it was said that I must truly dwell in the forest.
O mighty one, having heard these words from the twice-born experts in omens while at home, I have always been intent upon dwelling in the forest.
"I must indeed receive the command for forest-dwelling;
therefore, O beloved, I shall go there with you, and not otherwise."
Having received your command, I shall go; I will accompany you.
This moment has arrived; let the words of the twice-born man prove true.
For I know, O hero, that many kinds of sufferings are indeed certainly encountered in forest life by men who have not disciplined themselves.
And while I was still a maiden in my father’s house, I heard of the forest exile from a virtuous female mendicant here before my mother.
O Lord, you have indeed been propitiated by me in many ways previously;
for my desire was to dwell in the forest together with you.
I am ready to depart, may you be blessed, O Raghava;
for the life of forest-dwelling appeals to me, O hero.
"O pure-souled one, through this state of love I shall indeed become stainless;
for as I follow my husband, my husband is indeed my deity."
"Even in the life hereafter, may my union with you be auspicious;
for such a holy tradition is heard from the illustrious Brahmins."
O high-minded one, in this world, whatever woman has been given by her kinsmen to a man according to the sacred law with the pouring of water, she belongs to him even in the state beyond death.
Thus, for what reason here do you not find it pleasing to take me with you— me, your own wife, who is virtuous and devoted to her husband?

O descendant of Kakutstha, you ought to take me with you— me, your devoted and faithful wife, who am now distressed and equal to you in both joy and sorrow, sharing equally in your happiness and suffering.
If you do not wish to take me, who am thus afflicted with grief, to the forest,
I shall resort to poison, fire, or water for the sake of death.
Though she thus entreated him in many ways regarding her departure,
the mighty-armed one did not consent to lead her to the lonely forest.
Thus addressed, Maithilī was overcome with anxiety,
as if bathing the earth with the warm tears falling from her eyes.
As Vaidehī was thus reflecting and overcome with anger, the self-possessed descendant of Kakutstha endeavored to turn her back and consoled her in many ways.
While being consoled by Rāma, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, spoke these words to her husband regarding the cause of their forest exile: *Ramāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 27.1*
Utterly agitated, Sītā, out of both affection and pride, rebuked that broad-chested descendant of Raghu.
"What did my father, the King of Mithilā and Lord of Videha, think of you,
O Rāma, when he obtained you as a son-in-law— a woman in the form of a man?"
This world is untruthful because of its ignorance; for it speaks thus, though there is no splendor superior to Rāma, who blazes like the sun in the sky.
What indeed have you done that you are despondent, or from what does your fear arise, that you wish to abandon me, who have no other refuge?
O hero, know me to be devoted to Satyavanta, the son of Dyumatsena,
and under my own control, just as Sāvitrī was to the Sun.
But I shall not look upon anyone else even in my mind, O sinless one, except for you; with you, O Raghava, I would go, unlike any other woman who brings disgrace to her family.
But you, O Rāma, wish to give me away to others— me, who am your own wife, a virtuous woman who has lived with you since my youth, like a stage-player handing over his role.
"You ought not to depart for the forest without taking me with you;
whether it be asceticism, the wilderness, or heaven itself, it shall be shared with you."
And as I follow behind you, there shall be no fatigue for me on the road, even while resting and sleeping in monasteries.
The kuśa grass, kāśa, śara, and iṣīkā reeds, as well as the thorny trees along the path,
shall feel to me like cotton or deerskin when I am with you.
O lover, I consider that dust which, stirred up by a great wind, shall fall upon me, to be like the most precious sandalwood.
If I, a forest-dweller, shall lie upon the grassy meadows at the edge of the forest, what could be more pleasant than that, even compared to beds spread with woolen rugs?
Whatever leaf, root, or fruit you shall give me yourself, having gathered it— whether it be little or much— that will be like the taste of nectar to me.
There, while enjoying the seasonal flowers and fruits, I shall not remember my mother, nor my father, nor my home.
And having gone there, you shall not see anything unpleasant;
on my account, you need have no grief, for I shall not be a burden to you.
"That which is with you is heaven; that which is without you is hell"—knowing this, O Rāma, go to the highest joy together with me.
If you do not lead me, who am thus undistracted, to the forest,
I shall drink poison this very day, lest I fall under the power of my enemies.
For even afterwards, there would be no life for me in the midst of suffering;
O Lord, it would have been better to die at that very moment when I was abandoned by you.
Indeed, I cannot endure this grief even for a moment;
how much less can I bear it in misery for fourteen years?
Thus, tormented by grief, she lamented piteously at great length; then, overcome with distress, she embraced her husband tightly and wailed aloud.
Pierced by many words like a female elephant by poisoned arrows,
she released her long-restrained tears as the fire-drill releases fire.
From her eyes flowed water resembling crystal, born of her intense anguish, like water from two lotuses.
Embracing her with both arms as she lay there unconscious and sorrowful,
Rāma then spoke these words to reassure her.
"O Queen, I do not desire even heaven because of your sorrow;
for I have no fear from any quarter, just as the Self-Existent One has none."
O lady of auspicious countenance, without knowing your entire intention,
I do not find pleasure in dwelling in the forest, even though I am capable of protecting you.
Since you were created by me to dwell in the forest together with me, O Maithilī,
I cannot abandon you, just as a self-possessed man cannot abandon his reputation.
But as for the dharma practiced by the virtuous in the past, O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, I follow it today just as Suvarcalā follows the Sun.
O lady of beautiful hips, this is indeed the law: obedience to one's father and mother.
Therefore, having transgressed their command, I have no desire to live.

"I wish to act exactly as my father, who stands upon the path of truth and righteousness, commands me; for that indeed is the eternal dharma. Follow me, O timid one, and become my partner in the practice of dharma."
Give jewels to the Brahmins and food to the mendicants; bestow these upon those who desire them, and hasten—do not delay.
Realizing that her departure was favorable to her husband,
the queen, greatly delighted, immediately began to give them away.
Then, her heart filled with joy upon hearing her husband's words, that illustrious woman,
high-minded and devoted to righteousness, began to bestow wealth and jewels.
Then the immensely radiant Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood before him, a hero ready to depart, with palms joined in supplication. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 28.1)
"O Saumitri, if you go to that forest with me today,
who will support Kausalyā or the illustrious Sumitrā?"
Like Parjanya raining upon the earth with desires,
that lord of the earth, possessed of great splendor, was ensnared by the noose of desire.
For having obtained this kingdom, that daughter of King Aśvapati will not act kindly toward her suffering co-wives.
Thus addressed by Rāma with gentle words, Lakṣmaṇa,
who was skilled in speech, then replied to Rāma, who was himself an expert in discourse.
O hero, by your very splendor, Bharata will, with self-restraint, honor both Kausalyā and Sumitrā; of this there is no doubt.
The noble Kausalyā could support even a thousand people like me,
she for whom a thousand villages have been obtained as a means of subsistence.
Taking up my bow along with arrows and carrying a spade and a basket,
I shall go before you, showing you the way.
"I shall constantly bring for you roots and fruits,
as well as other forest products that serve as the proper food for ascetics."
But you, together with Vaidehī, shall take delight upon the mountain ridges;
I shall do everything for you, whether you are awake or asleep.
Rāma, highly pleased by these words, replied to him:
"Go, O son of Sumitrā, and take leave of all your friends."
And those two divine bows of fierce appearance, which the high-souled Varuṇa himself gave to King Janaka at his great sacrifice—
There were two divine, impenetrable armor-plates, two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
and two swords, bright as the sun and adorned with gold.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, all this has been deposited with due honor in the preceptor’s residence; therefore, take up your weapons and return quickly."
Having taken leave of his friends and being resolved upon dwelling in the forest,
he took leave of the preceptor of the Ikṣvākus and seized his excellent weapon.
Then that tiger among kings had Saumitri show him all those divine weapons, which were honored and adorned with garlands.
The self-possessed Rāma spoke with affection to the arrived Lakṣmaṇa:
"O gentle Lakṣmaṇa, you have come at the very time I desired."
"O scorcher of enemies, I wish to bestow this wealth of mine upon ascetic Brahmins together with you."
O best of the twice-born, those who dwell here with firm devotion toward their gurus—
for them, as well as for all my dependents, [I shall provide sustenance].
"Bring quickly the noble Suyajña, the son of Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent among the twice-born;
having honored all the other remaining learned brahmins, I shall depart for the forest."
Then, having received his brother’s most auspicious and pleasing command,
he went and quickly entered the residence of Suyajña.
Having saluted that brahmin who was staying in the fire-sanctuary, Lakṣmaṇa said:
"Friend, come here and behold the dwelling of him who performs difficult deeds."
Then, having quickly performed the twilight devotions, he went with the son of Sumitrā and entered that beautiful residence of Rāma, which was filled with splendor.
As he approached, Rāghava, together with Sītā and with palms joined in reverence, went toward Suyajña, the knower of the Vedas, as one approaches a consecrated fire.
With principal armlets made of gold, auspicious earrings,
gems with golden threads, as well as bracelets and bangles;
And with many other jewels, Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, honored Suyajña; then, urged by Sītā, he spoke to him.
"O gentle friend, give this necklace and golden chain to your wife;
now Sītā also wishes to give you this girdle, my friend."
Vaidehī also desires to establish upon you that couch with its excellent coverlet, adorned with various jewels.
O bull among the twice-born, I give to you that elephant named Śatruñjaya, my maternal uncle, whom he gave to me; I give him to you along with a thousand other elephants.
Having been addressed thus by Rāma, Suyajña accepted those words and offered auspicious blessings for Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā.
Then Rāma, who speaks kindly, addressed his beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, with composure, just as Brahmā addresses the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.
O son of Sumitrā, having summoned both Agastya and Kauśika, those two best of brahmins, honor them with jewels as one nourishes crops with water.
And he who, devoted, attends upon Kausalyā with blessings—
the preceptor of the Taittirīyas, handsome and a knower of the Veda.
O Saumitri, provide him with a vehicle, female slaves,
and silken garments, until that twice-born man is satisfied.
The noble Sūta Citraratha has been staying here as a counselor for a very long time;
please gratify him with highly precious jewels, garments, and wealth.
O son of Sumitrā, provide a thousand draft-oxen and two hundred auspicious bulls for the purpose of condiments.
Then that tiger among men, Lakṣmaṇa himself,
bestowed that wealth upon the foremost of the Brahmins as he had been instructed, just like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Then, having bestowed much wealth upon each of his dependents who stood there with tearful faces, he spoke to them.
Both the dwelling of Lakṣmaṇa and this house of mine must each be kept occupied until my return.
Having spoken thus to all those distressed dependents, he said this to the treasurer: "Let the wealth be brought.
Then his dependents brought all of his wealth to him.
Then that tiger among men, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
caused that wealth to be distributed among the brahmins, the young, the old, and the destitute.
There was a certain twice-born man named Trijaṭa, a descendant of Garga who had reddish-brown hair;
no one stopped him even as far as the fifth courtyard.
Having approached the prince, Trijaṭa spoke these words:
"O prince of great renown, I am poor and have many sons;
I live constantly on gleanings in the forest—please look upon me with favor."
Then Rāma spoke to him with a touch of jest:
"Not even a single thousand cows has been bestowed by me;
you shall receive as many as you can encompass with your staff."
Hurriedly and in great agitation, he wrapped that garment around his waist;
then, whirling his staff, he hurled it with all his might and speed.
Then Rāma, consoling Gārgya, said to him:
"Indeed, you should not be angry; this was merely a joke of mine."
Then the great sage Trijaṭa, accompanied by his wife, having accepted the herd of cows, was filled with joy;
he then pronounced blessings upon that high-souled one which increase fame, strength, affection, and happiness.
Having given much wealth to the brahmins along with Vaidehī, the two descendants of Raghu, together with Sītā, went to see their father. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 30.1)
Then, having been taken up, those two weapons, difficult to behold, shone forth;
they were adorned with garlands fastened by Sītā and thus beautifully decorated.
Then, having ascended the palaces, the mansions, and the turrets of the celestial chariots, the illustrious people looked on with indifference.
For the streets, crowded with many people, could not be traversed;
therefore, having climbed onto the palaces, the wretched ones gazed upon Rāghava.
Then, seeing Rāma on foot and deprived of his umbrella, the people,
their hearts stricken with grief, uttered many kinds of words.
Lakṣmaṇa followed him alone, together with Sītā, whereas formerly a great fourfold army used to follow him as he went.
Though he is an appreciator of sovereign power and a granter of desires to those who seek them,
out of reverence for dharma, he does not wish to make his father a liar.
Sītā, whom in the past even the beings who travel through the sky could not behold, today the people on the royal highway see her.
Sītā, who is accustomed to body unguents and uses red sandalwood paste,
will quickly be reduced to a state of discoloration by the rain, the heat, and the cold.
Surely today Daśaratha speaks as if possessed by some spirit;
for a king ought not to exile his beloved son.
How could even a son devoid of virtues be banished?
How much more so one by whose conduct alone this entire world has been conquered?
Kindness, compassion, learning, virtuous conduct, self-restraint, and tranquility—
these six qualities adorn Rāghava, the supreme among men.
Therefore, by his injury, all creatures are exceedingly afflicted,
like aquatic beings in summer when the water has dried up.
The entire world is afflicted by the suffering of this Lord of the World,
just as a tree bearing flowers and fruit is destroyed when its root is damaged.
Like Lakṣmaṇa, we shall quickly follow Rāghava as he goes, accompanied by our wives and kinsmen, along the path by which the descendant of Raghu departs.
Abandoning our gardens, fields, and homes,
let us follow the righteous Rāma, sharing in his single sorrow and joy.
Their hidden treasures have been unearthed, their courtyards are in ruins,
their wealth and grain have been seized, and their very essence has been stripped away from every side.
Let Kaikeyī take possession of these dwellings, strewn with dust, abandoned by the gods, and deserted by us.
"Let the forest where Raghava goes become the city itself,
and let the city abandoned by us turn into a forest."
May all fanged creatures take refuge in holes, and beasts and birds in mountain peaks;
may they abandon what we have left behind, even while it is being enjoyed by others.
Thus Rama heard these various words uttered by different people; and having heard them, his mind was not disturbed.

Then Rāma, appearing unperturbed and as if smiling, went toward his father’s residence while observing the distressed members of his family; desiring to see his father, he wished to carry out his father's command according to the prescribed rule.

Then, seeing Sumantra standing there in a state of distress, the high-souled Rāma, son of the Ikṣvāku line, who was about to depart for the forest, stood still so that his father’s great-souled doorkeeper might be informed.
But Rāghava, who was devoted to dharma and had firmly resolved upon entering the forest at his father’s command, looked at Sumantra and said, “Inform the king of my arrival.”
Sent by Rāma, the charioteer, his senses clouded with distress, quickly entered and beheld the king sighing deeply. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 31.1)
But having observed Rāma, who was of great wisdom, deeply distressed in mind and grieving for him alone, the charioteer approached him with palms joined in reverence.
"O tiger among men, here at the gate stands your son,
who has given away all his wealth to the brahmins and to those who depend upon him."
May that Rāma, whose prowess is truth, behold you—may prosperity be yours!
Having taken leave of all his friends, he now desires to see you.
He will go to the great forest; behold him, O Lord of the World, endowed with all royal virtues like the sun with its rays.
That truthful and righteous king, like the ocean in depth and as stainless as the sky, replied to him.
"O Sumantra, bring my wives—whosoever among them are here;
surrounded by all my wives, I wish to see Rāghava."
Having passed through the inner apartments, he spoke these words to those women:
"The noble king summons you; go there without delay."
Thus addressed by Sumantra at the king's command, all the women set out for that palace, having understood their husband’s instruction.
Then those six hundred and fifty women, their eyes copper-red,
having surrounded Kausalyā, proceeded slowly, firm in their vows.
When his wives had arrived, the lord of the earth looked at them and said to the charioteer, "Sumantra, bring my son to me."
Then that charioteer, taking Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the princess of Mithilā,
went quickly toward the presence of the lord of the earth.
Seeing his son approaching from afar with palms joined in reverence, the king,
surrounded by his women, rose quickly from his seat in distress.
Seeing Rāma, the lord of the people rushed toward him with speed;
but failing to reach him, he fell to the ground in a swoon, afflicted by grief.
Then Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa quickly approached the king, who was then filled with grief and rendered as if unconscious by his sorrow.
And in the royal palace, a cry from thousands of women suddenly arose:
"Alas, alas, O Rāma!"—a sound that overwhelmed the tinkling of their ornaments.
Embracing him with both their arms, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
weeping, laid him down upon the couch together with Sītā.
Then, after a moment, Rāma, having joined his palms in reverence, spoke to the lord of the earth, who had regained consciousness but was submerged in an ocean of grief.
"I take my leave of you, O Great King; you are the lord of us all.
As I depart for the Daṇḍaka forest, look after me with your blessings."
And give leave to Lakṣmaṇa; Sītā follows me to the forest.
Though they are dissuaded by many truthful reasons, they do not wish to stay behind.
O giver of honor, casting aside your grief, grant leave to us all—
to Lakṣmaṇa, to me, and to Sītā— just as Prajāpati grants leave to his creatures.
Beholding Rāghava waiting with composure for the permission of the lord of the earth, the king addressed him regarding his forest exile.
O Raghava, deluded by the granting of boons to Kaikeyī, I say this:
seize me and become you the king of Ayodhyā today.
Thus addressed by the king, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma and skilled in speech,
replied to his father with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, may you be the lord of the earth for a thousand years;
as for me, I shall dwell in the forest—I have no concern with your falsehood."
For the sake of your welfare, your prosperity, and your return once more,
O dear one, go now with an undistracted mind upon a path that is auspicious and free from all fear.
But today, my son, do not depart for the night by any means;
dwell this very night beholding me, your mother,
and being satisfied with all your desires, you shall accomplish your purpose tomorrow at the proper time.
Then Rāma, having heard those words spoken by his distressed father,
spoke these words in dejection along with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Who will give me tomorrow those virtues which I shall attain today? Therefore, I choose departure from all desires.
"This earth, along with its kingdom and its people, abounding in wealth and grain, has been relinquished by me; let it be given to Bharata."
"Let your sorrow depart; do not be overwhelmed by tears.
For the invincible ocean, the lord of rivers, does not become agitated."
I desire neither sovereignty, nor pleasure, nor even Maithilī;
O bull among men, I desire only you in truth, and not in falsehood.
"The city, the kingdom, and the entire earth have been relinquished by me; let them be given to Bharata.
Following your command, I shall go to the forest to dwell there for a long time."
"Let Bharata rule this auspicious earth, with its mountains, cities, and forests, which has been relinquished by me; O King, let it be exactly as you have said."
O King, my mind is not set upon great pleasures nor upon what is dear to myself as much as it is upon your command, which is honored by the wise; O sinless one, let your sorrow on my account depart.

Therefore, O sinless one, today I would not choose the eternal kingdom, nor all objects of desire, nor happiness, nor Maithilī, nor even life itself, by joining you with untruth; let your vow remain true.
Eating fruits and roots in the forest, beholding the mountains, rivers, and lakes, and having entered the forest filled with diverse trees, I shall become happy; may you find peace of mind.
Then the descendant of Ikṣvāku, distressed by his vow, sighed deeply with tears and spoke these words again and again to Sumantra. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 32.1)
"O Sūta, let an army, well-filled with jewels and consisting of the fourfold forces,
be quickly prepared for the purpose of escorting Rāghava."
And let beautiful courtesans who live by their beauty, and wealthy merchants, adorn the prince’s procession as they spread themselves out.
And those who depend upon you, and those by whom you take delight through their valor— to them give various gifts and employ them as well in this task.
Killing deer and elephants, drinking wild honey,
and beholding various rivers, he will not remember his kingdom.
Whatever storehouse of grain and whatever treasury of wealth I possess,
let both of them follow Rāma as he dwells in the desolate forest.
Sacrificing in holy places and bestowing abundant sacrificial fees,
he will meet with the seers and dwell happily in the forest.
"The mighty-armed Bharata shall rule Ayodhyā;
meanwhile, let the illustrious Rāma be provided with all his desires."
When the descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus, fear came upon Kaikeyī;
her face grew parched and her voice was choked.
Dejected and terrified, Kaikeyī spoke these words:
"O virtuous one, Bharata will not accept a kingdom from which its people have departed— a realm as utterly tasteless and empty as wine from which the scum has been drunk."
While Kaikeyī, having cast off all shame, was speaking these most cruel words,
King Daśaratha addressed the large-eyed woman with these words:
"Why do you pierce me, having yoked me to this burden that I cannot bear?"
Kaikeyī, her anger redoubled, said this to the king:
"In your own lineage, Sagara exiled his eldest son, known as Asamañjas; likewise, this man ought to go."
Thus addressed, King Daśaratha said, "Fie!
and all the people were ashamed; but she did not understand that.
There, an elderly high minister named Siddhārtha by name—pure and highly esteemed by the king—spoke these words to Kaikeyī: ||| RamS_2,32.14 |||
But Asamañja, having seized children on the road, would play by throwing them into the waters of the Sarayū; thus did that evil-minded one take his delight.
Seeing him, all the citizens, filled with anger, said to the king:
"O increaser of the kingdom, choose either Asamañja alone or us."
Then the king asked them, "What is the cause of this fear?
And being thus questioned by the king, those subjects spoke these words.
But this man, his mind deranged, finds incomparable pleasure out of folly in throwing our young sons, who were merely playing, into the Sarayū.
Having heard those words of the subjects,
the lord of men abandoned that harmful son in his desire to do what was pleasing to them.
Thus did the highly righteous King Sagara renounce [his son];
what sin, however, has Rāma committed that he should be thus obstructed?
Having heard Siddhārtha’s words, the king, his voice exceedingly weary,
spoke thus to Kaikeyī with speech stricken by grief:
Today I shall follow Rāma, renouncing kingdom, pleasure, and wealth;
you, together with the king and Bharata, may enjoy the kingdom happily for a long time.
Having heard the words of the high minister, Rāma, who knew the rules of propriety, then addressed King Daśaratha with humility, like one well-disciplined.
O King, for me who have renounced enjoyments, who live on forest produce in the woods,
and who have abandoned all attachments, what need is there for a retinue?
For one who, having given away the best of elephants, sets his mind upon its girth-rope—
what need has he for affection toward the cord when he is relinquishing that supreme elephant?
Likewise, O best of virtuous men, O Lord of the World, what is the use of an army to me?
I grant you all leave; let them bring me only bark garments.
"Bring both the spade and the basket for me as you go;
I am to dwell fourteen years in the forest."
Then Kaikeyī, having herself brought the bark garments, spoke shamelessly before the multitude of people to Rāghava: "Put these on!"
Having accepted those rags from Kaikeyī, that tiger among men cast aside his fine garment and donned the robes of a sage.
And Lakṣmaṇa, right there in the presence of his father, cast off his two beautiful garments and took up the two ascetic robes.
Then Sītā, dressed in silk, seeing the bark garment intended for her own wearing, was terrified like a spotted doe beholding a snare.
Feeling as if she were ashamed, and having accepted him with a heavy heart,
she spoke these words to her husband, who resembled the king of the Gandharvas:
"How indeed do the sages dwelling in the forest fasten their bark garments?"
Having placed the bark garment around her neck and holding one end in her hand,
Janaka’s daughter stood there, ashamed and distressed.
Having arrived there quickly, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
himself fastened the bark garment over Sītā’s silken dress.
While she, who had a protector, was thus clothed in rags like one who is helpless,
all the people cried out, "Fie on you, Daśaratha!"
Sighing hotly, that descendant of Ikṣvāku said this to his wife:
"Kaikeyī, Sītā ought not to go clad in garments of kusha grass."
"O wicked woman, is this exile of Rāma not sufficient for you? Why must you commit these further, miserable sins?"
To his father, who was speaking thus and sitting with his head bowed as he had set out for the forest, Rāma addressed these words:
O you who are censured by the gods, this is my illustrious mother Kausalyā; she is righteous, aged, and of noble character, yet she does not reproach you.

O Giver of Boons, you ought to take pity once more upon me, who am bereft of you, who have sought refuge in you, and who am plunged into an ocean of grief from which no such calamity has been seen before.
You ought to provide for this mother of mine, who bears a child like Mahendra himself,
so that while I am dwelling in the forest, she does not— emaciated by grief— cast off her life and go to the abode of Yama.
Having heard Rāma’s words and beholding him wearing the garb of a sage, the king, together with his wives, lost consciousness. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 34.1)
Tormented by grief, he did not look at Raghava;
and beholding him, he, being dejected in mind, did not address him.
For a moment the lord of the earth remained unconscious, and then, afflicted with grief,
the mighty-armed king lamented, thinking only of Rāma.
"I believe that in the past I must have caused many to be deprived of their offspring, or perhaps I have harmed living beings; it is because of that that this has now come upon me."
But my life shall certainly not depart from this body in the future;
for me, who am being tormented by Kaikeyī, death does not exist.
I see my son standing before me like a blazing fire,
having cast off his fine garments and clothed himself in the raiment of an ascetic.
Indeed, for the sake of this single Kaikeyī— who, striving for her own interest, has resorted to such deceit— this entire people suffers.
Having spoken these words, his senses overwhelmed by tears,
he uttered the name "Rāma" but once, and was unable to speak further.
Having regained consciousness after a moment, that lord of the earth,
with eyes filled with tears, spoke thus to Sumantra:
"Having yoked the royal chariot with the best of horses, come here;
convey this illustrious man from this region to the land beyond."
Thus I consider that this is called the fruit of the virtues of the virtuous:
that a good man, a hero, is sent away to the forest by his father and mother.
Having received the king’s command, Sumantra, swift in his prowess,
harnessed the horses and returned there with the decorated chariot.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the charioteer announced to the prince that the chariot, adorned with gold and yoked with excellent horses, was ready.
The king, who knew the proper time and place and was pure in every respect, quickly summoned his minister in charge of the accumulation of wealth and spoke with certainty.
"And having calculated these years, quickly bring back costly garments and excellent ornaments for Vaidehī."
Thus addressed by the lord of men, he then went to the treasury and,
having brought it all, quickly presented it to Sītā.
The noble Vaidehī, about to depart for the forest,
adorned her limbs with those various and wonderful ornaments.
Adorned with beautiful ornaments, Vaidehī illuminated that palace,
like the radiance of the sun illuminates the sky at the time when the rays have risen.
Embracing her with both arms and smelling the head of Maithilī— who was acting piteously— her mother-in-law spoke these words.
In this entire world, women— who are untruthful yet constantly honored by their loved ones— do not show regard for their husbands when they have fallen into misfortune.
This son of mine, who has been exiled, must not be disregarded by you;
let him be your deity, whether he be without wealth or possessed of wealth.
Having understood her words, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose, Sītā stood facing her mother-in-law and spoke this with palms joined in reverence.
"Noble lady, I shall do everything exactly as you instruct me;
I am well aware of how I must conduct myself toward my husband, and I have heard it all."
Noble lady, you ought not to equate me with the wicked;
I am no more capable of swerving from the Dharma than radiance is from the moon.
A lute without strings cannot be played; a chariot without wheels does not roll;
and even a woman who has a hundred sons does not thrive in happiness if she lacks a husband.
For a father gives in measure, a mother gives in measure, and a son gives in measure;
who would not honor a husband, the giver of what is immeasurable?
Thus situated, I am most excellent, devoted to the higher and lower aspects of the heard Dharma;
Noble Lady, how could I despise women? For a husband is indeed a woman's deity.
Having heard Sītā’s heart-touching words, Kausalyā,
whose nature was pure, suddenly shed tears born of both sorrow and joy.
Approaching her with palms joined in reverence, Rāma, who knows the highest dharma, spoke these words to his mother, who was being treated with great honor in the midst of the other mothers.
"Mother, do not be sorrowful; look upon my father, for the end of our forest dwelling will surely come very soon."
While you are asleep, fourteen years will pass;
then you shall see me returned here in my entirety, surrounded by my friends.
Having spoken these words of well-conveyed meaning to his mother,
he beheld three hundred and fifty mothers as he looked about.
And to those mothers who were likewise distressed, the son of Daśaratha,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words consistent with righteousness:
Whatever harsh thing I have done through living together with you, or even out of ignorance, please forgive me for that; and I bid you all farewell.
Then, as Rāghava was speaking thus, a clamor arose from the wives of the lord of men, like the cry of female cranes.

That palace of Daśaratha, which formerly resounded like the roar of clouds with the music of drums and tabors, became overwhelmed by lamentation and wailing; fallen into calamity, it was filled with profound sorrow.
Then Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined in reverence,
touched the feet of the king and, being dejected, performed a circumambulation around him.
And having also taken leave of him, Rāghava, the knower of dharma, together with Sītā,
prostrated before his mother, being utterly bewildered by grief.
Immediately after his brother, Lakṣmaṇa saluted Kausalyā;
then he again grasped the feet of his mother, Sumitrā.
As he was paying homage, his mother, weeping yet desiring his welfare, smelled the head of the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, and spoke to him.
"You were sent away to dwell in the forest while remaining deeply devoted to your circle of friends;
therefore, my son, do not be negligent toward your brother Rāma as he departs."
Whether in adversity or in prosperity, O sinless one, this is your refuge;
for this is the duty of the virtuous in this world: that one should remain subject to the will of the eldest.
For this is the eternal and appropriate conduct of this lineage:
giving, initiation for sacrifices, and the casting off of the body in battles.
Know Rāma to be Daśaratha; know me to be the daughter of Janaka;
know the forest to be Ayodhyā. Go, my dear, as you please.
Then Sumantra, humble and knowing the rules of propriety, addressed these words to the descendant of Kakutstha with palms joined in reverence, just as Mātali spoke to Vāsava.
"Mount the chariot; may prosperity be yours, O illustrious prince!
I shall quickly convey you, O Rāma, wherever you tell me to go."
"For fourteen years you must dwell in the forest; those years which the Queen has urged upon you must now be undertaken."
Having adorned herself, Sītā, of beautiful limbs, ascended that chariot which resembled the sun with a joyful heart.
In the same manner, having placed the various kinds of weapons, the two brothers' armor,
and that leather-covered quiver upon the seat of the chariot, [they departed].
Seeing that they had ascended with Sītā as the third,
Sumantra boldly urged on the excellent horses, which were equal to the wind in speed.
When Rāghava had departed for the great forest for a long time,
there occurred a fainting in the city, both of the people and of their strength.
That city was filled with confusion and agitation; with its elephants intoxicated and enraged, and the clamor of neighing horses, it resounded with a great noise.
Then that city, including its children and the elderly, being extremely distressed,
rushed toward Rāma alone, just as one afflicted by heat rushes toward water.
Hanging from his sides and from behind, all facing him with faces filled with tears, they spoke to him in great distress.
"O charioteer, restrain the reins of the horses; proceed very slowly.
I wish to behold the face of Rāma, for it will soon become difficult for us to see."
Surely the heart of Rāma’s mother is made of iron, without a doubt,
since it does not break even as her son, who resembles a divine child, departs for the forest.
For Vaidehī has accomplished her purpose; like a shadow following her husband, she, devoted to dharma, does not leave him, just as the radiance of the sun never leaves Mount Meru.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, you have achieved your purpose, for you shall serve your brother, who speaks ever kindly and resembles a god."
"This is indeed a great accomplishment for you, and this is a great exaltation;
this is the path to heaven, that you follow him.
Speaking thus, they were unable to restrain the tears that came to them.
Then the king, surrounded by distressed women and himself dejected in spirit,
went forth from his palace saying, "I shall see my beloved son."
And he heard before him the great sound of weeping women,
like the cry of female elephants when a mighty tusker has been captured.
And his father, the illustrious King of the Kakutsthas, then appeared as if fainting,
like the full moon at the time of being eclipsed by Rahu.
Then, upon seeing the king sinking down, deeply afflicted by grief, a tumultuous cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the men behind Rāma.
"O Rāma! some people cried out, while others wailed, "O Mother of Rāma! Thus they lamented as the opulent inner apartments wailed in grief.
Looking back, Rāma saw on the path his father and mother following him, dejected and bewildered in mind; yet,
bound by the fetters of dharma, he did not look at them openly.
Seeing those two, who were worthy of vehicles, undeserving of suffering, and accustomed to comfort, now traveling on foot, he urged the charioteer, saying, "Drive quickly!"
For that tiger among men was unable to endure the sight of his father and mother in such distress, like an elephant tormented by a goad.
Thus he repeatedly beheld his mother, weeping and running after that chariot, crying out "Rāma! Rāma! and "Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!", appearing as if she were dancing.
"Stay! cried the king; "Go! Go! shouted Rāghava.
Sumantra’s mind was caught between them like a wheel between two spokes.
"Even if you are reproached by the king, you shall say, 'I did not hear it.
This is most sinful and will lead to long-lasting suffering," Rāma said to him.
Carrying out Rāma’s command and taking leave of those people,
the charioteer urged the horses to move swiftly even as they were already proceeding.
The people turned back after circumambulating King Rāma;
yet in their minds and with the flow of their tears, they did not turn back from their devotion to the Manu-descendant.
"One should not follow too far after one whom one wishes to see return," thus the ministers spoke these words to the great king Daśaratha.
Having heard their words, which were endowed with every virtue, the king— his limbs perspiring, his appearance despondent, and feeling wretched along with his wife— stood gazing at that son.
As that tiger among men was departing with palms joined in reverence, a great cry of distress arose from the women in the inner apartments. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 36.1)
Where indeed is that protector going— he who was the refuge and the resort for these people who are now without a lord, weak, and wretched?
Even when accused, he does not become angry, avoiding all causes for provocation; by pacifying everyone who is enraged and sharing equally in their suffering, where does such a person go?
Where indeed is that high-souled one of great splendor going, who conducts himself toward us just as he does toward his mother Kausalyā?
Urged by the king, who was being tormented by Kaikeyī, where indeed is he going— this protector of this people and of the world— to the forest?
Alas! The king is devoid of sense, for he will send Rāma—who is beloved by the world of living beings, who is righteous, and who is devoted to his vow of truth—into exile in the forest.
Thus all those queens, afflicted by grief, wept like cows deprived of their calves; they wailed aloud and cried out piteously.
Hearing that terrible sound of lamentation within the inner apartments, the lord of the earth,
tormented by grief for his son, became deeply distressed.
The Agnihotra sacrifices were no longer offered, and the sun vanished from sight;
the serpents disgorged their mouthfuls of food, and the cows would not suckle their calves.
Triśaṅku, Lohitāṅga, Bṛhaspati, and Budha—
all these planets, being malevolent, have approached Soma and taken their positions.
The stars lost their radiance and the planets were shorn of their luster;
even the Viśākhā constellations appeared in the sky enveloped in smoke.
Suddenly, all the people of the city fell into a state of dejection;
no one set their mind upon either food or recreation.
With faces clouded by tears, not a single person on the royal highway appeared joyful; everyone was utterly overcome with grief.
The cool breeze does not blow, nor does the moon of gentle aspect shine;
the sun does not warm the world, and the entire universe is thrown into turmoil.
The sons who did not seek their own interests, as well as the husbands and brothers of the women,
all abandoned everything and thought only of Rāma.
But all those who were Rāma’s friends, their minds bewildered and overwhelmed by a burden of grief, did not leave their beds at that time.

Then Ayodhyā, bereft of that great-souled one, trembled violently like the earth with its mountains when deprived of Indra, oppressed by a burden of fear; and it roared along with its hosts of elephants, warriors, and horses.
As long as the form of the dust from his departing chariot could still be seen, the best of the Ikṣvākus did not withdraw his eyes. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 37.1)
As long as the king beheld his beloved son, who was exceedingly righteous,
so long did his joy increase upon seeing his son on the earth.
When the lord of the earth no longer saw even the dust raised by Rāma,
he fell to the surface of the ground, afflicted and despondent.
The lady Kausalyā followed at his right arm,
while Kaikeyī, who was fond of Bharata, followed at his left side.
Endowed with policy, righteousness, and discipline,
the king, his senses distressed, looked at Kaikeyī and spoke to her.
"O Kaikeyī, you of wicked conduct, do not touch my limbs!
Indeed, I have no desire to see you; you are neither my wife nor my kinswoman."
And those who depend upon you—neither do they belong to me, nor do I belong to them;
for I abandon you, who are solely intent on wealth and have cast aside dharma.
Whatever I took your hand in marriage and whatever I led you around the sacred fire—
all that I now relinquish, both in this world and in the next.
If Bharata, having obtained this imperishable kingdom,
were to give me that which he has set aside for my father's sake, may it never come to me.
Then, having raised up that lord of men who was covered in dust,
Queen Kausalyā, emaciated by grief, turned back.
Like one who has intentionally killed a Brahmin, or like one who has touched fire with his hand,
that righteous-souled king was filled with remorse upon reflecting on his son, the ascetic.
Turning back again and again, as he sat dejected upon the tracks of his chariot,
the king’s appearance did not shine, like that of the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Afflicted by grief and remembering his beloved son, he lamented;
and having learned that his son had reached the outskirts of the city, he then spoke to him.
The footprints of the principal mounts carrying my son are visible on the path, yet that great-souled one is not seen.
Surely today he will have taken refuge at the foot of some tree, or having placed a piece of wood or perhaps a stone beneath him, he will lie down.
And that wretched man, covered in dust, shall rise from the earth,
sighing like a bull elephant from a mountain stream of female elephants.
Surely the long-armed forest-dwellers will behold Rāma, the lord of the world, rising and departing like one who is helpless.
"Have your desires fulfilled, Kaikeyī; dwell in the kingdom as a widow, for I cannot bear to live without that tiger among men."
Lamenting in this manner, the king, surrounded by a multitude of people,
entered that best of cities like one who has performed an expiatory bath after an ill omen.

Its squares, courtyards, and interiors were empty; its shops and deities were shrouded in dust; it was filled with those exhausted, weak, and afflicted by suffering; and its great highways were no longer crowded.
Beholding that entire city and thinking only of Rāma,
the king entered his palace lamenting, like the sun entering a cloud.
Like a great, unshakeable lake from which the serpents have been carried off by Suparṇa,
the palace was bereft of Rāma, Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa.
"Lead me quickly to the house of Kausalyā, the mother of Rāma. As the king was speaking thus, the doorkeepers led him away.
Then, having entered Kausalyā’s residence and even having ascended the bed, his mind became agitated.
And seeing that, the valiant great king raised his arm and cried out in a loud voice: "Alas, O Raghava, you are abandoning me!"
"Happy indeed will those best of men live at that time,
who shall embrace Rāma and see him returned."
"I do not see you, Kausalyā; please touch me with your hand.
My gaze, following after Rāma, does not turn back even now."
Seeing the king on his bed still brooding only upon Rāma, the queen sat down beside him and, appearing even more distressed, sighed deeply and lamented in her misery.
Then, seeing the king lying dejected upon his bed due to grief, Kausalyā, afflicted by sorrow for her son, spoke to that lord of the earth. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 38.1)
O tiger among men, having sown discord like a double-tongued serpent, Kaikeyī will roam about like a female snake that has cast off its skin, while Rāghava [remains bound].
Having exiled Rāma, that fortunate woman, her desire attained and her mind composed,
will terrify me once more like a wicked serpent within the house.
Then, while wandering for alms in the city, Rāma might dwell in my house;
