it would be better to grant him his wish, even if he were my own son as a slave.
Having caused Rāma to fall from his position at Kaikeyī’s will,
he was assigned as a portion for the Rākṣasas, like an oblation offered by one who maintains the sacred fires on a festival day.
The hero with the gait of a lordly elephant, mighty-armed and wielder of the bow,
has surely entered the forest together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
But what indeed will be the condition of those who, having never experienced suffering in the forest, have been abandoned by you for exile at the command of Kaikeyī?
Deprived of their wealth, these young men have been exiled at the very time for fruition;
how will those miserable ones live, subsisting only on fruits and roots?
Would that this auspicious time for the end of my grief might now arrive,
when I may behold Rāghava here together with his wife and his brother.
Upon hearing that the two heroes had arrived, [the people wondered], "When will Ayodhyā become glorious,
filled with joyful folk, and adorned with rows of uplifted banners?"
When, upon seeing those two tigers among men returned from the forest,
will the city rejoice in its delight, like the ocean on a full-moon day?
When will the mighty-armed hero enter the city of Ayodhyā,
placing Sītā before him on the chariot, like a bull with its mate?
When will thousands of living beings scatter parched grain upon my two sons, those subduers of enemies, as they enter the royal highway?
When will the joyful daughters of the twice-born, bestowing flowers and fruits, perform a circumambulation of the city?
"When will he, who possesses the splendor of an immortal and knows the Dharma, come to me as one matured in both intellect and age, appearing like a youth of three years?"— thus she lamented.
"O hero, I think without a doubt that in the past,
out of greed, I must have cut off the breasts of nursing mothers while their calves were still desiring milk."
O tiger among men, like a cow fond of her calf who has been forcibly separated from it by a lion, I have been rendered childless by Kaikeyī, though I am full of affection for my son.
For I, who have but one son, cannot endure to live without my son— he who is endowed with virtues and proficient in all the scriptures.
Indeed, no capacity whatsoever for life can be conceived by me here,
as long as I do not behold my beloved son, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful one.
For this fire, arisen from grief for my son,
consumes me just as the blessed sun of supreme radiance scorches this earth with its rays during the summer heat.
To Kausalyā, the best of women, who was thus lamenting, Sumitrā, remaining steadfast in dharma, spoke these words consistent with dharma: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 39.1.
"O noble lady, that son of yours is endowed with excellent virtues; he is the best of men.
What is the use of your lamenting thus, or of this piteous weeping?"
O noble lady, that mighty son of yours who has departed, having renounced the kingdom,
was acting rightly by following his high-souled father, who was a speaker of truth.
Rāma, the most excellent, stands firm in that dharma practiced rightly by the learned, which yields eternal fruits after death; he is never to be grieved for.
And the ever-virtuous Lakṣmaṇa maintains the highest conduct toward him; being compassionate toward all beings, that high-souled one has attained his true gain.
Knowing well the suffering that comes from dwelling in the forest, Vaidehī— who is accustomed to comfort— yet follows your son, whose soul is devoted to dharma.
What has your son not attained— he who is a lord who waves the banner of fame throughout the world, and who is devoted to self-restraint and the vow of truth?
Having clearly perceived Rāma’s purity and supreme magnanimity,
the sun ought not to scorch his body with its rays.
At all times, a pleasant breeze, issuing from the forests with a temperate coolness and warmth, shall serve Rāghava, O Śiva.
As he lies sleeping at night, the sinless one, the moon will gladden him by embracing him like a father and touching him with its cool rays.
And he bestowed divine weapons upon that one of great prowess,
having seen the lord of the Dānavas, the son of Timidhvaja, slain in battle by him.
O bull among men, Rāma shall soon be consecrated together with these three: the Earth, Vaidehī, and Śrī.
Beholding him as he departs, they shed tears born of sorrow;
soon you too shall shed from your eyes a flow of tears born of joy.
Seeing your son together with his friends saluting you,
you will soon shed tears of joy, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
Your son, the bestower of boons, having soon returned to Ayodhyā,
will press your feet with his two soft and fleshy hands.
Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa’s mother from Rāma’s mother, the wife of the lord of men,
her grief instantly vanished from her body like an autumn cloud containing but little water.
Devoted to the high-souled Rāma, whose prowess is truth, the people followed him as he departed for his dwelling in the forest. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 40.1)
And although the king and his circle of friends were forcibly turned back,
those who followed Rāma’s chariot did not at all turn back.
For he was dear to the men residing in Ayodhyā, as beloved as the full moon; he was highly illustrious and endowed with every virtue.
Though being entreated by his own subjects at that time, that descendant of Kakutstha,
making his father true to his word, departed for the forest itself.
Gazing with affectionate eyes as if drinking them in,
Rāma spoke with love to those subjects as if they were his own children.
Whatever affection and great respect the residents of Ayodhyā have for me,
let that be bestowed especially upon Bharata for the sake of my pleasure.
For he, of noble conduct and the increaser of Kaikeyī’s joy,
will duly perform what is pleasing and beneficial for you all.
"Though young in years, he is mature in wisdom; though gentle, he is endowed with the quality of heroism.
He will be a worthy husband for you, a dispeller of fear."
"For he, endowed with the qualities of a king, has been designated as the crown prince;
moreover, you must carry out the command of your master as instructed by me."
And so that the Great King does not suffer when I have gone to dwell in the forest, you must act in such a way out of a desire to do what is pleasing to me.
The more the son of Daśaratha remained steadfast in righteousness,
the more the subjects desired Rāma as their lord.
Overwhelmed by tears and dejected, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā,
seemed to draw back the people— who were bound by his virtues— as if to their former state.
Those twice-born ones, who were aged in three ways— by knowledge, by years, and by spiritual power—
shaking their heads from old age, spoke these words from afar.
"O swift and noble horses, carrying Rāma, turn back! You must not go; be well-disposed toward your master. Your master is to be carried *to* the forest from the city, not carried *away* from it."
Beholding those aged twice-born ones thus uttering their piteous lamentations,
Rāma suddenly descended from his chariot.
Then Rāma, intent upon the forest, went on foot together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, his footsteps treading close together.
But Rāma, who was devoted to righteous conduct and possessed eyes of compassion, could not bring himself to leave those twice-born men on foot by means of his chariot.
Seeing Rāma thus departing, their minds filled with agitation and deeply distressed, the twice-born spoke these words to Rāma: *RamS_2,40.18*
This entire Brahmanical order follows you, who are yourself devoted to the Brahman;
even these sacred fires, mounted upon the shoulders of the twice-born, follow after you.
Behold these umbrellas of ours, arising from the Vājapeya sacrifice,
following behind us like swans at the end of the rainy season.
"For you, who have not yet obtained the royal parasol and are scorched by the sun's rays,
we shall provide shade with these parasols of our own, used for the Vājapeya sacrifice."
For that intellect of ours which has always followed the Vedic mantras,
O child, has now been made by you to follow the forest life.
The Vedas, which are our supreme wealth, abide within our hearts;
likewise, wives protected by their own virtuous conduct shall remain even within the home.
No further deliberation is required; your mind is well-settled regarding your course. But if you disregard dharma, what would there be left for me to consider as dharma?
"O you of restrained conduct, we entreat you: turn back with your heads—white-haired like swans—dusty from falling upon the earth."
"The many sacrifices of the twice-born who have gathered here are extensive;
their completion depends upon you, my child, returning."
For all beings, both moving and unmoving, possess devotion;
therefore, show your favor toward those devotees who are now entreating you.
Unable to follow you, their speed uprooted by your roots,
the lofty trees seem to cry out as they are driven along by the force of the wind.
Even the birds, motionless and without seeking food, remaining fixed in one place upon the trees, beg from him who is compassionate toward all beings.
While those twice-born ones were thus crying out to turn him back,
Tamasā appeared there as if to restrain the descendant of Raghu.
Then, having reached the delightful bank of the Tamasā river, Rāghava looked at Sītā and spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 41.1.
"O Saumitri, this first night of our departure for the forest has now arrived;
may you be blessed. You ought not to feel anxious regarding our dwelling in the woods."
Behold the empty forests, which seem to weep on all sides as the deer and birds return to their respective dwellings and settle within them.
Today, the city of Ayodhyā, my father’s capital,
will undoubtedly grieve for us as we depart with our wives and men.
Bharata, who is indeed righteous in soul, will surely console my father and mother with words consistent with virtue, worldly prosperity, and pleasure.
Reflecting again and again upon the benevolence of Bharata,
O Lakṣmaṇa, I do not grieve for my father nor even for my mother.
O tiger among men, you have fulfilled your duty by following me;
for assistance must indeed be sought in order to protect Vaidehī.
"But with water alone, O son of Sumitrā, I shall spend this night;
for this indeed pleases me, even though there are various other forest foods available."
Having spoken thus to the son of Sumitrā, Rāghava also said to Sumantra:
"O gentle one, remain vigilant regarding the horses."
When the sun had set, Sumantra, having tethered the horses and provided them with abundant fodder, remained close at hand.
Having observed the arrival of night and performed the twilight worship of Śivā,
the charioteer prepared a bed for Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā.
Beholding that bed made of tree leaves on the bank of the Tamasā,
Rāma, together with Saumitri and his wife, lay down upon it.
Seeing his brother fast asleep with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to the charioteer about the various virtues of Rāma.
Indeed, while the son of Sumitrā remained awake that night on the bank of the Tamasā as the charioteer recounted the virtues of Rāma, the sun rose.
Not far from the Tamasā river, whose banks were crowded with herds of cows,
Rāma dwelt there that night together with his subjects.
Having risen and observed those subjects, the immensely radiant Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who is endowed with auspicious marks.
O Saumitri, look now at those who, though they have no regard even for their own homes, are sleeping at the roots of trees out of consideration for us, O Lakshmana.
"Just as these citizens are making this vow to turn us back,
they will even give up their lives rather than abandon their resolve."
As long as they remain fast asleep, let us quickly mount the chariot and depart upon a path free from all danger.
Therefore, once again, let not the inhabitants of the city of Ikṣvāku,
who are so devoted to me, now sleep at the roots of trees.
For the citizens are to be liberated from suffering caused by their own actions by the princes;
they are certainly not to be joined with suffering by the princes themselves.
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma, who stood there like Dharma personified: "O highly wise one, it pleases me; let us mount [the chariot] at once."
Then the charioteer, having quickly yoked the chariot with those excellent horses,
reported back to Rāma with palms joined in reverence.
In order to delude the citizens, Rāma spoke these words to Sūta:
"O charioteer, mount the chariot and proceed facing north."
Having gone quickly for a moment, turn the chariot back again;
act with full concentration so that the citizens do not recognize me.
Having heard Rāma’s words, the charioteer did exactly so;
and having returned, he reported to Rāma that the chariot was ready.
Mounting that chariot with his retinue, Rāghava crossed the river Tamasā, which flows swiftly and is filled with turbulent eddies.
Having crossed over, the glorious and mighty-armed one reached the great path that is auspicious and free of thorns— a path of fearlessness even for those who perceive danger.
When the night had turned to dawn, those citizens, being without the descendant of Raghu,
became motionless, their hearts stricken with grief and their minds desolate.
Emaciated by tears born of grief and looking here and there,
the sorrowful ones did not see even a glimpse of Rāma.
Then, having traveled for a short while along the path,
he was once again overwhelmed by great despondency due to the loss of the way.
Due to the loss of the chariot’s path, those high-minded men turned back, saying, "What is this? What shall we do, being thus struck down by fate?"
Then, with weary hearts, they all returned by the very same path they had come, reaching the city of Ayodhyā, where the virtuous were filled with distress.
When the city-dwellers had followed Rāma and turned back, the vital spirits of those dejected people seemed to have departed from them. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 42.1)
Having returned each to his own dwelling, surrounded by their sons and wives,
they all shed tears, their faces veiled by weeping.
The merchants neither rejoiced nor were they merry, nor did they display their wares;
the market goods did not shine, and the householders did not cook.
Seeing what was lost, they did not rejoice; nor did they rejoice at the acquisition of vast wealth.
Having obtained her first-born son, the mother did not rejoice.
And in every house, women, afflicted by grief, reproached their husbands who had returned home with words, as one would strike elephants with goads.
Of what use are houses to them, or wives, or wealth,
or even sons or pleasures, for those who do not behold Rāghava?
Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, is the one true man in the world,
who follows the descendant of Kakutstha, Rāma, attending upon him in the forest.
Fortunate are those rivers, lotus-pools,
and lakes in which the descendant of Kakutstha shall bathe, plunging into their pure waters.
Forests with lovely groves, rivers with vast marshlands, and mountains with their peaks shall all bring glory to the descendant of Kakutstha.
Whether it be a forest or a mountain that Rāma shall approach,
they will not be able to fail to honor him, as if he were a beloved guest who has arrived.
Out of compassion, the mountains will show to the arrived Rāma their crests adorned with various flowers, bearing many clusters of blossoms, and even their principal flowers and fruits out of season.
Displaying various and manifold colorful waterfalls upon the mountain peaks, the trees will delight Rāghava.
Where Rāma is, there is no fear, nor is there any defeat;
for he is a hero with mighty arms, the son of Daśaratha.
Before he goes far from us, let us follow Rāghava;
the shadow of the feet of such a high-souled lord is a source of happiness,
for he is the protector of these people, he is their refuge, and he is their ultimate resort.
"We shall attend upon Sītā, while you attend upon Rāghava," thus the women of the city, afflicted by grief, spoke various words to their husbands.
Rāghava will provide for your security and well-being in the forest; Sītā will likewise attend to the security and well-being of these women.
Who indeed would find delight in this disagreeable dwelling, which is unpleasant, filled with longing people, and has stolen away one's heart?
If the kingdom should fall into the hands of Kaikeyī in an unrighteous manner, like a state without a protector,
we would have no need for life— how much less for sons or wealth?
Since she abandoned both her son and her husband for the sake of power,
whom else would Kaikeyī, that disgrace to her family, not reject?
We swear even by our sons that as long as Kaikeyī lives, we shall never live as dependents in the kingdom while she is still alive.
Who could live happily having encountered that pitiless, unrighteous, and wicked woman who has sent the son of the lord of kings into exile?
For once Rāma has gone forth into exile, the lord of the earth will not survive;
when Daśaratha is dead, it is certain that total ruin will follow immediately thereafter.
"Having stirred up poison and drunk it, you who are of exhausted merit and fallen into a miserable state—
either follow Rāghava or go to the land of the unheard."
Rāma has been falsely exiled along with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa;
we have been surrendered to Bharata like animals to a butcher.
While those women of the city were thus lamenting,
they cried out in extreme distress, as if at the onset of the fear of death.
Likewise, the women were distressed on account of Rāma, just as they would be if a son or a brother had been exiled;
lamenting piteously, they wept with distracted minds, for he was indeed more than a son to them.
Rāma too, that tiger among men, remembering his father’s command, traveled a great distance during the remainder of that very night. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 43.1)
As he was traveling in that very manner, the auspicious night passed away;
having performed his worship of the auspicious twilight, he entered the frontier of the kingdom.
Beholding those villages with their outlying boundaries and the flowering forests, he passed by them swiftly, as if on arrows, with his excellent horses.
Hearing the words of the people living in the village settlement, he said:
"Fie on King Daśaratha, who has fallen under the sway of desire!"
"Alas! Today Kaikeyī, cruel, wicked, and followed by evil, sharp-tongued and having broken all bounds of propriety, persists in this harsh deed."
She who exiles such a son of the king— one who is righteous,
highly wise, compassionate, and unwearied— to dwell in the forest.
Hearing these words of the people living in the villages along his route, the heroic lord of Kosala passed through the Kosala country.
Then, having crossed the river named Vedaśruti, which carries the waters of Śiva,
he set out facing the direction inhabited by Agastya.
Having traveled for a very long time, he then crossed the river Gomatī, which flows toward the ocean, possesses cool waters, and has marshy banks frequented by cattle.
And having crossed the Gomatī as well with his swift-moving horses, Rāghava traversed the Syandikā river, which resounded with the cries of peacocks and swans.
Rāma showed Vaidehī that prosperous land, filled with kingdoms, which had been given long ago by King Manu to Ikṣvāku.
Addressing that charioteer repeatedly with the word "Sūta," the illustrious bull among men, whose voice was like the cry of a rutting swan, spoke.
"When shall I return once more to the blossoming forest by the Sarayū and roam in the hunt, reunited with my mother and father?"
I do not excessively desire hunting in the Sarayū forest;
for this pleasure is incomparable in the world and is esteemed by the hosts of royal sages.
Addressing the charioteer with sweet words and keeping each of those matters in mind, that descendant of Ikṣvāku proceeded along the road, uttering these words.
Having traversed the vast and beautiful Kosalas, the mighty-armed elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa reached Śṛṅgaverapura. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 44.1)
There Rāghava beheld the divine Gaṅgā, which flows through the three worlds, possessing auspicious waters free from moss, holy, and frequented by sages.
Resounding with the cries of swans and cranes, and filled with the warbling of ruddy geese,
it was frequented by porpoises, crocodiles, and serpents.
Having gazed upon that river with its waves, eddies, and whirlpools, the great chariot-warrior said to the charioteer Sumantra, "Let us stay right here today."
"Not far from this river stands a very large ingudī tree, abounding in flowers and young shoots; let us dwell right here, charioteer."
Lakṣmaṇa and Sumantra, having said "So be it" to Rāghava, then approached that iṅgudī tree with their horses.
Having approached that beautiful tree, Rāma, the joy of the Ikṣvākus,
descended from his chariot together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Sumantra also, having dismounted and unyoked the excellent horses,
approached Rāma, who was seated at the foot of a tree, with palms joined in reverence.
There, a king named Guha was a friend of Rāma, equal to his own self;
he was of the Niṣāda caste, powerful, and renowned as a *sthapati*.
Having heard that Rāma, that tiger among men, had arrived in his domain, he approached him,
surrounded by aged ministers and kinsmen.
Then, seeing the lord of the Niṣādas standing at a distance,
Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, approached Guha.
Embracing Rāghava in his distress, Guha said to him:
"O Rāma, this place is just like Ayodhyā to you; what may I do for you?"
Then, having taken various kinds of excellent food and quickly bringing the water for honor (*arghya*), he spoke these words.
Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one! This entire earth is yours;
we are your servants and you are our lord. Rule over our kingdom well.
"Here are presented for you foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk,
and licked, as well as excellent beds and fodder for your horses."
To him who was speaking thus to Guha, Rāghava replied:
"We have been honored and gladdened by you in every way."
Having approached him on foot and showing his affection,
he pressed him with his virtuous arms and spoke these words.
"By good fortune, Guha, I see you healthy along with your kinsmen;
is all well with your kingdom, your friends, and your wealth?"
Whatever has been prepared by you here out of affection, I grant permission for all of it; for I do not engage in the acceptance of gifts.
Know me to be an ascetic dwelling in the forest, devoted to dharma, wearing kusha grass, rags, and deerskin, and subsisting on fruits and roots.
"I have need only of fodder for my horses, and nothing else;
by this much alone, your honor will have honored me well."
For these are dear to my father, King Daśaratha;
by means of these well-prepared horses, I shall be honored.
He commanded Guha to give orders to the men right there: "Let fodder and grain for the horses be provided with all haste."
Then, having performed the evening twilight rites while wearing his upper garment of bark cloth,
he took as his food only water brought by Lakṣmaṇa himself.
Having washed the feet of him who was lying on the ground, along with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa then approached and stood leaning against a tree.
Guha, too, along with his charioteer, conversing with the son of Sumitrā,
then remained watchful over Rāma, vigilant and bearing his bow.
Thus, as that wise and illustrious high-souled son of Daśaratha lay there,
accustomed to happiness and unacquainted with suffering, that night passed for him only after a long time.
To Lakṣmaṇa, who was vigilantly and sincerely attending to his brother’s welfare, Guha, consumed by grief, spoke these words to the descendant of Raghu: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 45.1.
"O dear one, this comfortable bed has been prepared for your sake;
rest well upon it, O prince, as you please."
"All these people are accustomed to hardships, while you are accustomed to comfort;
we shall remain awake through this night for the sake of protecting the descendant of Kakutstha."
"Indeed, there is no one on earth dearer to me than Rāma;
I tell you this truth, and I swear it to you by the truth itself."
Through his grace, I hope for great fame in this world,
as well as the vast attainment of Dharma and the complete attainment of worldly prosperity.
Therefore, with bow in hand and accompanied by my kinsmen, I shall protect my dear friend Rāma from all sides as he lies sleeping together with Sītā.
"Indeed, nothing remains unknown to me as I constantly roam this forest;
for we could withstand even a vast fourfold army."
Then Lakṣmaṇa said to him: "O sinless one, while we are being protected by you who perceives only righteousness, none of us here are afraid."
While the son of Daśaratha lies upon the ground together with Sītā, how can I obtain sleep, or life, or any pleasures?
Behold him, who could not have been overcome in battle by all the gods and asuras together, now lying comfortably upon the grass with Sītā.
This son of Daśaratha, who possesses characteristics similar to his father, was obtained through the power of mantras and asceticism, as well as through various arduous efforts.
Once the king has gone forth into this [religious life], he will not remain for long;
the earth will surely soon become a widow.
Having uttered a great cry, the women have now ceased from their toil;
O dear one, I believe the royal palace has fallen silent.
I do not expect that Kausalyā, the king, and likewise my own mother will all survive this very night.
Indeed, my mother might even live on for the sake of looking after Śatrughna;
but that is the sorrow [I feel] that Kausalyā, the mother of heroes, will perish.
Crowded with devoted people and bringing the joy of pleasant sights,
that city will perish when it is beset by the calamities of its king.
Having failed to attain his desire again and again,
my father will perish without having installed Rāma in the kingdom.
When that time has arrived, all those who have achieved their goals will perform the funeral rites for the deceased king, their father.
It possessed beautiful square courtyards, well-laid-out main thoroughfares,
was replete with mansions and palaces, and was graced by the presence of the finest courtesans.
Crowded with chariots, horses, and elephants, resounding with the noise of musical instruments,
filled with every kind of auspiciousness, and teeming with joyful and well-fed people.
They will roam happily through my father’s capital, which is endowed with parks and gardens and abounds in social gatherings and festivals.
May we, together with him who is true to his promise and remains in good health,
enter Ayodhyā once this forest dwelling has come to an end.
As that high-souled prince stood there lamenting, afflicted by grief, the night passed away.
For as the prince, who seeks the welfare of his subjects, was speaking the truth, Guha, out of deep affection,
shed tears, being oppressed by the calamity like an elephant afflicted by fever and tormented by pain.
When the night had turned to dawn, the highly illustrious Rāma,
whose arms were broad, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
This is the time of the sun’s rising; the blessed night has passed.
O father, that very black bird, the cuckoo, is calling out.
And the cry of peacocks calling out in the forest is heard;
O gentle one, let us cross the swift-flowing Jāhnavī as it journeys toward the ocean.
Having understood Rāma’s words, the son of Sumitrā, who brings joy to his friends,
took leave of Guha and the charioteer and stood before his brother.
Then, having fastened their quivers and girded on their swords,
those two Raghava archers went with Sita toward the Ganges.
But approaching Rāma himself, who knows what is right,
the charioteer spoke with humility and joined palms, saying, "What shall I do?"
"Turn back," he said to him, "for this much has been done for me;
leaving the vehicle, we shall go on foot to the great forest."

Seeing that he himself had been granted permission [to depart], the charioteer Sumantra, distressed, spoke these words to that tiger among men, the descendant of Ikṣvāku: *ātmānaṃ tv abhyanujñātam avekṣyārtaḥ sa sārathiḥ / sumantraḥ puruṣavyāghram aikṣvākam idam abravīt //* RamS_2,46.8 //
No man in this world has ever overstepped this:
that you, along with your brother and wife, should dwell in the forest like common folk.
I do not believe that there is any fruit arising from the practice of celibacy, nor from Vedic study,
nor even from gentleness and uprightness, if such calamity has befallen you.
O hero, Rāghava, dwelling in the forest together with Vaidehī and your brother, you shall attain a state as if conquering the three worlds.
We are indeed ruined, O Rāma, for we have been deceived even by her;
we shall fall under the power of the wicked Kaikeyī and become partakers of sorrow.
Speaking thus, Sumantra the charioteer, seeing that Rāma had gone far away, was as dear to him as his own self; overcome with grief, he wept for a long time.
Then, when his tears had ceased and he had touched water and become pure,
Rāma spoke these sweet words to the charioteer again and again.
"I perceive no friend of the Ikṣvākus equal to you;
act in such a way that King Daśaratha may not grieve for me."
The lord of the earth is old, his mind is stricken by grief, and he is overwhelmed by the burden of desire; therefore, I say this to you.
Whatever that high-souled lord of the earth may command for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī must be carried out without hesitation.
For it is for this purpose that lords of men rule their kingdoms:
so that in all their undertakings, their minds may not encounter obstruction.
Just as that great king does not fall into falsehood and does not languish in sorrow, O Sumantra, act accordingly.

Having saluted the king—who has never known suffering, who is aged, noble, and has conquered his senses—you should speak these words on my behalf: "You should speak these words on my behalf, having first offered salutations to the king—who has never known suffering, who is aged, noble, and has conquered his senses."
I do not grieve at all that Lakṣmaṇa and Maithilī have fallen from Ayodhyā, nor do I grieve that we shall dwell in the forest.
"When fourteen years have passed, you will see Lakṣmaṇa, me, and Sītā, having returned, time and again."
Having spoken thus to the king, O Sumantra, and to my mother,
as well as to the other queens together and to Kaikeyī again and again, [he departed].
"Tell Kausalyā that you are well, and offer salutations at her feet;
also convey my greetings, and those of Sītā, myself, and by the command of the noble Lakṣmaṇa."
And you must say to the great king, "Bring Bharata here quickly";
and once Bharata has arrived, he should be established in the position according to the king's will.
And having embraced Bharata and consecrated him as the crown prince,
the sorrow born of our distress shall no longer overcome you.
And Bharata also should be told: "Just as you behave toward the king, so should you behave toward all your mothers without distinction."
Just as Kaikeyī and Sumitrā are to you without distinction,
so too is Queen Kausalyā, my mother, especially so.

Being turned back by Rāma, Sumantra, emaciated by grief, heard all those words and spoke to the descendant of Kakutstha out of affection: Thus ends the twenty-ninth verse of the forty-sixth sarga of the Ayodhyākāṇḍa in the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa.
Since I speak thus out of affection and without hesitation,
you ought to forgive these words of mine, thinking that I am indeed devoted.
For how indeed, deprived of you, shall I return to that city, which,
through separation from you, O father, will be as if overwhelmed with grief for a son?
Even seeing my chariot without Rāma at that time, the people would have been so overcome that the entire city might well have shattered.
For the city itself would fall into despondency upon seeing this empty chariot,
its own army with only the charioteer remaining, like warriors slain in battle.
Thinking of you today as standing before them in their minds, even though you dwell far away, the subjects have surely been made to fast.
For the cry of distress that was let out by the citizens at my departure would surely increase a hundredfold upon seeing me mounted on the chariot.
"What more shall I say to you, O Queen? I have taken your son to his maternal uncle's house; do not grieve."
I would not speak such words even if they were untrue;
how then could I speak this true word which is so unpleasant?
Furthermore, how will these excellent horses, who are under my command and accustomed to carrying your kinsmen, draw the chariot when it is deprived of you?
If you will indeed reject my request as I entreat you,
I shall enter the fire along with the chariot the very moment I am abandoned by you here.
O Raghava, whatever beings there may be in the forest that create obstacles to your asceticism, I shall repel them with my chariot.
On your account, I have not obtained the pleasure derived from driving the chariot;
yet, on your account, I hope to obtain the pleasure derived from dwelling in the forest.
"Be gracious; I wish to be your close companion in the forest.
"Out of affection, I desire that you be my close companion."
Dwelling in the forest, I shall serve you with my head bowed;
whether it be Ayodhyā or the world of the gods, I shall abandon it in every way.
For without you, I am not able to enter that Ayodhyā,
the capital of Mahendra, just as one of evil deeds cannot enter it.
And these horses as well, O hero, if they serve you while you dwell in the forest,
shall attain the supreme goal.
Indeed, this was my heart's desire when my forest dwelling came to an end:
that I might carry you back to the city once again on this very chariot.
"For fourteen years spent together with you in the forest will pass like a single moment; otherwise, they would last for hundreds of years."
O you who are affectionate toward your dependents, you ought not to abandon me— a devoted servant who stands firm in his duty and follows the path taken by my lord’s son.
To him who was thus piteously entreating in many ways again and again,
Rāma, out of compassion for his servant, spoke these words to Sumantra:
"I know your supreme devotion to me, O you who are devoted to your master;
yet hear also the purpose for which I send you from here to the city."
Seeing that you had gone to the city, my younger mother Kaikeyī would have gained confidence; therefore, Rāma went to the forest.
For that queen, now that I have gone to dwell in the forest, will be well-pleased and will not suspect the righteous king of being a speaker of falsehood.
This is my first wish: that my younger mother may obtain the prosperous kingdom for her son, protected by Bharata.
"For my sake and for the sake of the king, go to the city with the chariot;
and regarding whatever matters you have been instructed upon, speak them exactly as they are."
Having spoken these words and having consoled the charioteer again and again, Rāma spoke these reasoned and resolute words to Guha:
"I shall go after making matted locks; bring me the sap of the banyan tree."
Guha quickly brought that milk to the prince;
with it, Rāma matted the hair of both Lakṣmaṇa and himself.
Then those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, wearing garments of bark and bearing circles of matted hair, shone like sages.
Then, having set out upon the path of the forest-dwellers (vaikhānasa), Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
undertook the vow and spoke to his companion Guha.
O Guha, you must remain vigilant regarding the army, the treasury, the fortresses, and likewise the countryside; for a kingdom is considered to be most difficult to protect.
Then, having granted leave to Guha, the joy of the Ikṣvākus departed quickly and with composure, together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having seen a boat on the riverbank, that joy of the Ikṣvākus,
wishing to cross the swiftly flowing Gaṅgā, spoke this to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Ascend this boat slowly, O tiger among men; and take the high-minded Sītā upon your lap, supporting her yourself."
Having heard his brother's command and complying with it all without opposition,
the self-possessed one first helped Maithilī onto the chariot and then ascended himself.
Then the radiant elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa himself ascended;
thereafter, Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, urged his kinsmen forward.
Having given leave to Sumantra, as well as to Guha and his army,
Rāma boarded the boat and urged the boatmen forward.
Then, impelled by them and steered by the helmsman, that ship,
struck by the force of the auspicious oars, swiftly crossed over the waters.
Having reached the middle of the Bhāgīrathī, the blameless Vaidehī joined her palms in reverence and spoke thus to the river:
O Gaṅgā, protected by you, let this son of the wise Great King Daśaratha fulfill his command.
Having dwelt for a full fourteen years in the forest together with his brother and me, he will indeed return once more.
Then, O blessed Goddess Gaṅgā, having returned safely, I shall worship you with great joy for the fulfillment of all my desires.
For you, O Goddess, are the one who flows through the three paths; you behold the world of Brahmā, and you are seen in this world as the wife of the King of the Ocean.
O Goddess, O beautiful one, I bow to you and praise you now that the tiger among men has returned safely with the kingdom regained.
Out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you, I shall bestow upon the Brahmins hundreds of thousands of cows, garments, and exquisite food.
Thus conversing with Gaṅgā, the blameless Sītā, being herself skillful,
quickly reached the southern bank.
Having reached the shore and left the boat behind, that bull among men,
the scorcher of his foes, set out together with his brother and Vaidehī.
Then the mighty-armed one said to the increaser of Sumitrā’s joy, "Go on ahead, Saumitri; let Sītā follow you."
I shall follow behind you, protecting both you and Sītā;
today, however, Vaidehī will experience the sorrow of dwelling in the forest.
But having watched Rāma continuously as he swiftly reached the far bank of the Gaṅgā, Sumantra,
his vision failing due to the great distance of the road, wept in distress, a wretched man.
Having killed four great deer there— a boar, a rishya, a prishata, and a maharuru—
and taking that sacrificial meat, the two of them, being hungry, went quickly at the proper time to the lord of the forest for their dwelling.
Having reached that tree and performed the evening twilight rites, Rāma, the best among those who give delight, spoke thus to Lakṣmaṇa: (Ramāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 47.1)
Today is the first night that has passed outside the inhabited lands;
since it is spent without Sumantra, you ought not to feel anxious.
"From this day forward, we must remain vigilant during the nights;
for the security and well-being of Sītā now rests upon both Lakṣmaṇa and me."
O Saumitri, let us somehow pass this night by spreading out upon the ground ourselves, using what we have gathered.
Having lain down upon the earth— though accustomed to a costly bed—
Rāma spoke these auspicious words to the son of Sumitrā.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, it is certain that the great king sleeps in sorrow today;
Kaikeyī, having achieved her desire, must surely be satisfied."
For that Queen Kaikeyī, O Great King, for the sake of the kingdom,
might even deprive you of your life upon seeing that Bharata has arrived.
Helpless, old, and separated from me,
what will he do— this man whose soul is consumed by desire, having fallen under the power of Kaikeyī?
Having observed this calamity and the king’s confusion of mind,
it is my conviction that desire alone is more powerful than both dharma and artha.
For what man, even if he were ignorant, would for the sake of a woman abandon a son who follows his will, as my father has abandoned me, O Lakṣmaṇa?
Happy indeed is Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, together with his wife,
who alone shall enjoy the joyful kingdom of Kosala like a sovereign monarch.
For he alone will become the sole head of the entire kingdom,
when our father has passed away in age and I have retired to the forest.
He who abandons both wealth and dharma to pursue desire alone soon meets with such calamity, just as King Daśaratha did.
I believe,
gentle friend, that Kaikeyī has come for the sake of Daśaratha’s end, for my exile, and for the kingdom of Bharata.
"Will Kaikeyī now, deluded by the intoxication of her own good fortune,
perhaps oppress both Kausalyā and Sumitrā on my account?"
"O Lakṣmaṇa, let not Queen Sumitrā dwell in sorrow on my account; you must enter Ayodhyā from here at the proper time."
I alone shall go to the Daṇḍaka forest with Sītā;
for you will become the protector of Kausalyā, who is now without a protector.
For Kaikeyī is of mean character; out of malice she might act unjustly. Indeed, she might hand my mother over to Bharata, who knows what is right.
Surely in some other birth women were separated from their sons;
O Saumitri, that very fate has now befallen my mother.
"For Kausalyā has been separated from me, whom she nurtured for so long and raised with such hardship; yet here I am at the time of the fruit—fie upon me! (Rāmāyaṇa 2.47.20)
O Saumitri, may no woman ever give birth to such a son as I, who brings endless sorrow to my mother.
"O Lak�śmaṇa, I believe that śārikā bird is more distinguished by her affection for me than I am;
for her voice is heard saying, 'O parrot, bite the foot of the enemy!'"
O subduer of enemies, what purpose is served by me, a son who does nothing to help my unfortunate mother as she grieves, being as good as childless?
For my mother Kausalyā is indeed of little fortune, separated from me;
she lies prostrate, afflicted by supreme suffering, fallen into an ocean of grief.
For alone, O Lakṣmaṇa, I could indeed overwhelm Ayodhyā and even the entire earth with my arrows when enraged; yet surely such prowess is not for its own sake.
And because I am afraid of unrighteousness and of the world beyond, O sinless Lakṣmaṇa, I do not have myself consecrated today.
Having lamented thus and in many other ways piteously in that solitary place,
Rāma sat down in silence during the night, his face filled with tears.
To Rāma, who had ceased his lamentation like a fire whose flames have gone out,
or like an ocean that has become motionless, Lakṣmaṇa offered consolation.
"O Rāma, best among warriors, now that you have departed, the city of Ayodhyā is surely shorn of its luster today, like a night when the moon has vanished."
"O Rāma, this for which you are now grieving is not appropriate;
O bull among men, you are causing both Sītā and me alike to despair."
Neither Sītā without you, nor I myself, O Rāghava,
can live for even a moment, like two fish drawn out from the water.
For today, O scorcher of foes, I would not wish to see my father, nor Śatrughna, nor Sumitrā, nor even heaven itself, without you.

Having heard these most excellent and abundant words of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava, the scorcher of his foes, out of reverence for the forest life, undertook the practice of dharma and resolved to dwell there for all those years.
Having spent that auspicious night under that great tree, they set out from that place when the bright sun had risen. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 48.1)
They entered a vast forest and headed toward that place where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā flows into the Yamunā.
Those illustrious ones reached the land and beheld various delightful regions, seeing here and there places never seen before.
Traveling safely and beholding various trees,
Rāma spoke to the son of Sumitrā as soon as the day had turned.
"O son of Sumitrā, behold the rising smoke all around Prayāga;
I believe that the Blessed One’s banner of fire indicates that the sage is nearby."
"Surely we have reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
for the sound of waters clashing against water is being heard."
The logs have been split by forest-dwellers who subsist on them,
and these various trees are seen here in Bharadvāja’s hermitage.
Having traveled comfortably with their bows, the two of them reached the hermitage of the sage at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā as the sun was hanging low, O Sage.
But Rāma, having reached the hermitage and frightening the beasts and birds,
traveled for a short distance and approached Bharadvāja.
Then, having reached the hermitage and desiring a sight of the sage,
the two heroes, followed by Sītā, stood at a distance.
Upon seeing the illustrious one who had performed the agnihotra sacrifice,
Rāma, together with Saumitri and Sītā, saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
And Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother announced himself to him, saying,
"O Blessed One, we two are the sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"This Vaidehī, the auspicious daughter of Janaka and my blameless wife,
has followed me to this desolate forest of asceticism."
As I was being sent away into exile by my father, this beloved younger brother, the son of Sumitrā,
firm in his vows, followed me to the forest.
"O Blessed One, commissioned by our father, we shall enter the forest of asceticism;
there we shall practice only the dharma, subsisting on roots and fruits."
Having heard those words of the wise prince,
the righteous-souled one then brought forward a cow, the guest-offering (arghya), and water.
Seated amidst deer, birds, and sages on all sides,
the sage honored Rāma upon his arrival and addressed him with a welcome.
Having accepted that offering, Bharadvāja then spoke these words, consistent with dharma, to Rāma and his brother who were seated there.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, it has indeed been a long time since I have seen you come here;
I have also heard this account of your exile, which was without cause."
This place at the confluence of the two great rivers is secluded, auspicious, and delightful; may you dwell here in comfort.
Thus addressed by Bharadvāja,
Rāghava Rāma, who is devoted to the welfare of all, replied with these auspicious words.
"O Blessed One, people from the cities and the countryside are near here;
spectators will come to see Vaidehī and me as well.
For this reason, I do not find dwelling here agreeable."
"O Blessed One, behold in a secluded spot this most excellent hermitage site,
where Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka who deserves happiness, finds delight."
Having heard these auspicious words, the great sage Bharadvāja then spoke words full of meaning to Rāghava.
"Ten *krośas* from here, dear father, is a mountain where you shall dwell;
it is frequented by great seers, holy, and pleasant to behold from every side."
Frequented by langurs and inhabited by monkeys and bears,
it is known as Citrakūṭa, resembling Mount Gandhamādana.
As long as a man gazes upon the peaks of Citrakūṭa,
he attains auspicious states and does not set his mind upon evil.
Many sages, having dwelt there for a hundred autumns,
ascended to heaven through their ascetic penance along with Kapālaśiras.
I consider that secluded dwelling of yours to be pleasant;
or else, O Rāma, dwell here with me for the sake of forest life.
Bharadvāja, the knower of dharma, welcomed Rāma— who was dear to him as a guest— along with his wife and his brother, providing for all their desires.
As Rāma approached that great seer at Prayāga,
the holy night arrived while he was recounting various wonderful stories.
When the night had turned to dawn, that tiger among men approached Bharadvāja and spoke to the sage of blazing splendor.
O you whose character is truth, having spent this night here in your hermitage,
may your lordship grant us permission to depart from our dwelling.
When that night had dawned, Bharadvāja said this:
"Go to Citrakūṭa, which is provided with honey, roots, and fruits."
There, O Rāghava, you will see herds of elephants and herds of deer roaming all around on the edges of the forest.

Having reached that auspicious mountain, which resounded with the cries of joyful lapwings and cuckoos and was made most delightful by many wild deer and elephants in rut, he took up residence at the hermitage.
Having spent the night there, the two princes, subduers of their enemies, paid homage to the great seer and then departed toward that mountain. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 49.1)
Seeing them set out, the father followed after his sons like a father follows his sons;
then that great sage proceeded to speak these words.
Then, having reached the Kālindī, a river with swift currents,
you should construct a raft there and cross over the river Aṃśumatī.
Then, having reached a great banyan tree with green foliage,
which was lush, surrounded by many other trees, dark-hued, and frequented by perfected beings (siddhas).
Having gone from there for the distance of one krośa, O Rāma, you will see a dark forest interspersed with *palāśa* and *badarī* trees, as well as bamboo groves along the Yamunā.
"That path to Citrakūṭa has been traveled by me many times;
it is delightful, easy to traverse, and free from forest fires.
Having thus described the way, the great seer turned back.
When that sage had turned back, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"We have performed meritorious deeds, O son of Sumitrā, since the sage shows us such compassion."
Having thus deliberated, those two wise tigers among men,
placing Sītā at their head, proceeded toward the river Kālindī.
Then the two of them constructed a great raft from a collection of logs;
Lakṣmaṇa, having cut it, fashioned a comfortable seat for Sītā.
There, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, helped his beloved— who was like the inconceivable Goddess Śrī herself and was slightly bashful— to ascend the raft.
Then, by means of a raft, they crossed the swift-flowing Yamunā river, which was garlanded with waves and lined with many trees growing upon its banks.
Having crossed over and abandoned the raft, they set out from the forest of the Yamunā and reached a dark banyan tree, cool and with green foliage.
"May I behold Kausalya and the illustrious Sumitra," saying this, Sita joined her palms in reverence and circumambulated the lord of the forest.
Having gone from there for the distance of a *krośa*, the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
killed many sacrificial deer and roamed in the forest of the Yamunā.
Having dwelt in that beautiful forest resounding with flocks of peacocks and filled with elephants and monkeys,
they— whose appearance was undepressed— reached a level riverbank and arrived at their chosen dwelling.
Then, when the night had passed and Lakṣmaṇa was sleeping soundly, the joy of the Raghus gently awakened him. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 50.1)
"O Saumitri, listen to the sweet sounds of the forest creatures as they call out;
let us set forth now, O scorcher of enemies, for it is time to depart."
When he was asleep at that time, Lakṣmaṇa was awakened by his brother;
he then cast off sleep, drowsiness, and the fatigue accumulated on the road.
Then, having risen and touched the auspicious water of the river, they all set out upon the path to Citrakūṭa indicated by the sage.
Then, having set out at the proper time with the son of Sumitrā,
Rāma spoke these words to Sītā, whose eyes were like lotus petals:
O Vaidehī, behold the *kiṃśuka* trees at the end of winter, adorned with their own blossoms like garlands and appearing as if they were ablaze on all sides.
Behold the *bhallātaka* trees in full bloom, untouched by men;
surely I shall be able to live on their fruits and leaves as they hang low.
Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the honeycombs the size of a *droṇa* hanging from tree after tree, filled with honey by the female bees.
This water-fowl cries out, and the peacock calls back to it in this delightful forest region, thickly strewn with carpets of flowers.
Behold this Mount Citrakūṭa, with its towering peaks, frequented by herds of elephants and made resonant by the songs of flocks of birds.
Then, traveling on foot together with Sītā,
the two of them reached the beautiful and enchanting Citrakūṭa mountain.
"Having reached that mountain, which is filled with flocks of various birds, let this be our dwelling for now; O gentle one, let us take our pleasure here."
"Lakṣmaṇa, bring strong and excellent timber;
build a dwelling, O gentle one, for my mind is set upon staying here."
Having heard those words of his, the son of Sumitrā, the subduer of enemies, gathered various trees and then constructed a leaf-hut.
To him who was listening with one-pointed attention, he spoke these words:
"Having procured the meat of a black antelope, we shall perform a sacrifice in the sacrificial hall."
Having slain a sacrificial black antelope, the powerful Lakṣmaṇa,
son of Sumitrā, then cast it into the kindled fire.
Then, perceiving that it was cooked, well-fried, and free of blood,
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāghava, that tiger among men.
"This black antelope has its limbs complete and is roasted like a wild deer;
O god-like deity, perform the sacrifice, for you are indeed skilled."
Having bathed, Rāma— self-restrained, virtuous, and skilled in the recitation of prayers—
performed an excellent bali offering that pacifies all evil.

All of them together entered that delightful dwelling, well-constructed according to the site and sheltered from the wind, its roof covered with tree leaves, just as the hosts of gods enter the Sudharmā assembly hall.

In that most excellent forest, crowded with many various beasts and birds, filled with trees bearing clusters of diverse blossoms, and echoing with the cries of predatory wild animals, those who had conquered their senses sported in great happiness.
Having reached the most delightful Citrakūṭa and that river Mālyavatī with its excellent bathing places,
frequented by deer and birds, he rejoiced with joy and cast off the sorrow born of his exile from the city.
Having conversed for a long time with Sumantra while he was deeply afflicted by grief,
Guha returned to his own home once Rāma had reached the southern bank. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Canto 51, Verse 1)
Then, having been given leave, Sumantra harnessed the excellent horses and set out for the city of Ayodhyā, deeply distressed in mind.
Beholding fragrant forests, rivers, and lakes, as well as villages and cities, he traveled swiftly past them.
Then, at the time of sunset on the third day, the charioteer,
having reached Ayodhyā, beheld it devoid of joy.

Seeing it as if empty and silent, Sumantra, deeply distressed and struck by a surge of grief, reflected: *sa śūnyām iva niḥśabdāṃ dṛṣṭvā paramadurmanāḥ / sumantraś cintayāmāsa śokavegasamāhataḥ //* (Rāmāyaṇa 2.51.5)

"Is the city— with its elephants, its horses, its people, and its king— not being consumed by the fire of grief, scorched by the suffering born of Rāma’s exile? Thus lost in thought, the charioteer entered in haste.
Then, as Sumantra approached, hundreds and thousands of men ran toward the charioteer, asking, "Where is Rāma?"
He told them: "Having taken leave of Rāghava at the Gaṅgā, I have returned, permitted by that righteous, high-souled one."
Perceiving that they had crossed over, the people, their faces filled with tears, sighed "Alas, what a tragedy! and cried out, "O Rāma!"* *RamS_2,51.9*
And he heard the words of those who stood in groups and crowds:
"We are truly lost, we who do not behold Rāghava here."
"At acts of charity, sacrifices, weddings, and great assemblies,
we shall never again behold the righteous Rāma in our midst."
"What is beneficial for these people? What is dear to them? What brings them happiness?
Thinking thus, Rāma protected the city like a father.
And he heard the lamentation of the women standing at the windows along the market streets, who were tormented by grief for Rāma.
With his face veiled, Sumantra proceeded through the middle of the royal highway toward that very palace where King Daśaratha resided.
Having quickly descended from his chariot and entered the royal palace,
he passed through seven courtyards crowded with great throngs of people.
Then, from the palaces here and there, he heard the faint lamentations of Daśaratha’s wives, who were tormented by grief for Rāma.
Having set out with Rāma and now returned here without him,
what indeed will the charioteer say to Kausalyā as she grieves?
And as I think it, life is indeed difficult to sustain; it is certainly not easy for Kausalyā to live on once her son has departed and been torn away from her.
Hearing those words of the king, which were true in form,
the women entered the palace suddenly, as if consumed by a blazing fire of grief.
Having entered the eighth courtyard, he beheld the king in a white chamber, dejected and afflicted, consumed by grief for his son.
Having approached the seated lord of men and saluted him,
Sumantra reported the words of Rāma exactly as they had been spoken.
Having heard that, the king, his mind utterly bewildered and tormented by grief for Rāma, fell to the ground in a swoon, remaining silent.
Then, when the lord of the earth had fainted and fallen to the ground, the inner apartments were thrown into turmoil;
raising their arms, they wailed aloud for the king who lay prostrate upon the earth.

Then Kausalyā, together with Sumitrā, raised up her fallen husband and spoke these words: "Rāma is the refuge of this entire world, including the gods; how then could he, who is so compassionate, have acted otherwise? He is the one who, by his own power, brought about the destruction of Rāvaṇa, who was invincible even to the gods and demons. How could that son of Daśaratha, who is the protector of all living beings, have been overcome by grief? This is surely some great illusion devised by the gods, for it is impossible for him to die."
O illustrious one, why do you not speak to this messenger of that performer of difficult deeds, who has arrived here from his dwelling in the forest?
"O Raghava, having committed this misconduct today, you feel ashamed;
arise, may it be well with you—for there can be no assistance in grief."
"O King, because of fear of whom you do not question the charioteer Rāma—Kaikeyī is not here; speak with confidence."
Having spoken thus to the great king, Kausalyā, overwhelmed by grief and her speech choked with tears, suddenly fell prostrate upon the earth.
Seeing Kausalyā thus lamenting and fallen upon the ground,
and beholding her husband as well, all those women wept aloud.
Then, beholding that cry arising from the inner apartments, the men—both old and young—and all the women wept on every side; the city once again became filled with commotion.
When the king had recovered his breath and returned from his swoon,
he then summoned the charioteer for the sake of news concerning Rāma.
He was aged and deeply distressed like a newly captured elephant,
sighing and lost in thought like an elephant in ill health.

But the king, seeing the charioteer standing before him with his limbs covered in dust, his face filled with tears, and looking dejected, spoke like one deeply afflicted: rājā tu rajasā sūtaṃ dhvastāṅgaṃ samupasthitam / aśrupūrṇamukhaṃ dīnam uvāca paramārtavat // RamS_2,52.3 //
Where indeed will that righteous-souled one dwell, taking refuge at the foot of a tree?
O Sūta, what will Rāghava eat, he who has always been accustomed to great comfort?
How can the son of a protector of the earth sleep upon the ground like one who is helpless?
How will that Rāma live, having taken refuge in the desolate forest, he whom foot-soldiers, chariots, and elephants used to follow as he went?
How did the two princes, together with Vaidehī, enter the forest frequented by wild beasts and inhabited by black cobras?
O Sumantra, how did the two princes, along with the delicate and ascetic Sītā, descend from the chariot on foot?
O charioteer, you have indeed achieved your purpose, since you have seen my two sons entering the depths of the forest like the two Aśvins entering Mount Mandara.
What words did Rāma speak, and what did Lakṣmaṇa say?
O Sumantra, having reached the forest, what did Maithilī say?
O charioteer, tell us of Rāma’s sitting, his sleeping, and his eating.
Thus urged by the lord of men, the charioteer,
with a voice faltering and choked with tears, spoke to the king.
O great king, Rāghava, observing his duty alone, spoke to me after joining his palms in reverence and bowing his head.
O charioteer, in my name, salute with your head the feet of that high-souled father of mine, who has realized the Self and is worthy of worship.
"O Sūta, you must announce my words to everyone in the inner apartments: convey my greetings to each of them according to their rank, wishing them health without exception."
And my mother Kausalyā; may you offer her my greetings of well-being, O Queen, and protect the feet of the King as if they were your own god.
Bharata should be told of my welfare and addressed with these words on my behalf:
"Behave toward all your mothers with due propriety according to the law."
And you must say to the mighty-armed delighter of the Ikṣvāku clan:
"Established in the position of heir apparent, protect your father who remains established in the kingship."
O Great King, even as he spoke thus to me,
the highly illustrious Rāma, whose eyes were as copper-red as lotuses, shed profuse tears.
But Lakṣmaṇa, deeply incensed and sighing, spoke these words: "By what offense has this prince been exiled?"
If Rāma has been exiled whether it was caused by greed,
or for the sake of granting a boon, in every way an evil deed has been committed;
yet, I perceive no just cause for the abandonment of Rāma.
This exile of Rāghava, undertaken without due reflection and contrary to reason through a lack of mental acuity, will produce great remorse.
"O Great King, I do not perceive you as my father;
Rāghava is my brother, my protector, my kinsman, and my father."
Having abandoned that which is dear to all the world and being devoted to the welfare of all the world,
how could the entire world not be won over by you through this deed?
But Janaki, O great king, sighing as an ascetic woman, stood there motionless and bewildered, like one whose mind has been struck by a spirit.
The illustrious princess, who had never before experienced such calamity,
wept from that grief and said nothing at all to me.
Gazing at her husband with a parched face,
she suddenly shed tears upon seeing me departing.
In that very same way, Rāma stood with tears on his face and palms joined in reverence, supported by Lakṣmaṇa’s arm;
and likewise, the ascetic Sītā, weeping, gazed upon the royal chariot and me in that same manner.
But when I turned back, my horses would not move forward on the road; shedding hot tears, they refused to go as Rāma set out for the forest. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 53.1)
Then, having joined my palms in reverence to both princes,
I mounted the chariot and set out, bearing that sorrow within me.
I remained right there for many days together with Guha,
in the hope that Rāma might call for me again.
In your realm, O Great King, even the trees— with their flowers, sprouts, and buds— are withered, emaciated by the calamity that has befallen Rāma.
Living beings did not move about, nor did predatory beasts roam;
overcome by grief for Rāma, that forest became silent.
O lord of men, the lotus ponds have their lotus petals withered, their waters turbid,
their lotuses scorched, and their fish and birds hidden away.
The water-born flowers and the land-born garlands do not shine today with their former fragrance, nor do the fruits, as they did before.
As I enter Ayodhyā, no one greets me;
not seeing Rāma, the people sigh again and again.
Beholding the chariot arrived from the mansions, palaces, and towers, the women, emaciated by the absence of Rāma, raised cries of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
With their long, stainless eyes overflowing with a torrent of tears,
the women, clearly overcome by extreme distress, gaze intently at one another.
I do not perceive any distinction whatsoever in my suffering, whether it concerns enemies, friends, or neutral people.
The people were joyless, and the elephants and horses were dejected;
they were withered by cries of distress and filled with the sound of heavy sighs.
"O Great King, Ayodhyā appears to me joyless and distressed by Rāma’s exile, like Kausalyā deprived of her son."
Having heard the words of the charioteer, with a voice exceedingly piteous and choked with tears, the king spoke this to the charioteer: RamS_2,53.14 //
Urged by Kaikeyī, who possesses a wicked lineage and disposition,
I did not deliberate with the elders who are skilled in counsel.
"Neither after consulting with my friends, nor with my ministers, nor with the merchants,
have I rashly committed this deed out of delusion for the sake of a woman."
"O charioteer, surely this great calamity has arrived by chance through the power of destiny for the destruction of this lineage."
"O charioteer, if I have performed even a small act of merit, let me quickly reach Rāma; my life-breaths urge me on."
Whatever command I may give, let it turn Rāghava back;
I shall not be able to live even for a moment without Rāma.
Or perhaps the mighty-armed one has gone far away;
having placed me upon the chariot, show me to Rāma quickly.
Where is that elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, the great archer with well-formed tusks?
If I am still alive, may I see him together with Sītā.
If I do not see Rāma, who has reddish eyes, mighty arms, and wears jeweled earrings, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
What indeed could be more painful than this: that I, having fallen into such a state, do not see Rāghava here, the joy of the Ikṣvākus?
"Alas Rāma! Alas Lakṣmaṇa! Alas, alas, Vaidehī, you poor ascetic woman!
You do not know that I am dying of grief like one who is helpless. O Queen, this ocean of sorrow is difficult for me to cross while I am still alive."
"It is a misfortune that today, though desiring to see Rāghava here along with Lakṣmaṇa, I do not find them"—
lamenting thus, the highly illustrious king suddenly fell upon his bed in a swoon.
While the king was thus lamenting most piteously— his grief doubled on account of Rāma—
the queen, the mother of Rāma, heard his words and was seized once again by fear.
Then, in the Ayodhyākāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa, verse 54.1:
trembling again and again as if possessed by a spirit,
Kausalyā, lying on the ground as if life had departed from her, spoke to the charioteer.
Lead me, O Kakutstha, to where Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa are; for without them, I cannot endure to live here even for a moment.
"Turn back the chariot quickly; take me as well to Daṇḍaka.
If I do not follow them, I shall go to the abode of Yama."
With a voice faltering and overwhelmed by a surge of tears, the charioteer, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to comfort the queen:
*idam āśvāsayan devīṃ sūtaḥ prāñjalir abravīt //* RamS_2,54.4 *//* "Thus, comforting the queen, the charioteer spoke with his hands folded in salutation."
Abandon grief and delusion, as well as the agitation born of sorrow; having shaken off your torment, Rāghava will dwell in the forest.
And Lakṣmaṇa as well, the knower of dharma who has conquered his senses, attends upon Rāma’s feet in the forest, thereby propitiating the next world.
Even in the lonely forest, having found her dwelling as if in a home, Sītā,
with her mind fully entrusted to Rāma, attains confidence and remains fearless.
I do not perceive even the slightest sign of despondency in her;
Vaidehī appears to me as if she were accustomed to living in exile.
Just as she used to delight in the city groves in the past,
even so does Sītā delight in these solitary forests.
Like a young girl, Sītā, whose face resembles the young moon, finds delight in Rāma; for that virtuous woman has surrendered her very self to Rāma, even in the lonely forest.
For her heart is fixed on him, and her life is dependent upon him;
even Ayodhyā, when bereft of Rāma, would be like a forest to her.
On the road, Vaidehī asks about villages and cities,
observing the courses of rivers and various kinds of trees as well.
Indeed, due to the road, the force of the wind, the agitation, and the heat of the sun,
the moon-like radiance of Vaidehī did not fade away.
The face of that generous Vaidehī, resembling a hundred-petaled lotus and possessing a luster like the full moon, does not waver.
Even now, her feet, which were once as red as liquid lac and yet naturally free from the need for lac-dye, possess a luster equal to the calyx of a lotus.
Like a playful woman whose anklets resound, the beautiful Vaidehī used to walk with a graceful gait; yet even now, she remains devoted to him, having laid aside her ornaments.
Whether she sees an elephant, a lion, or a tiger while dwelling in the forest,
she feels no terror, for she has taken refuge in the arms of Rāma.
They are not to be mourned, nor are you to be mourned, nor even the lord of men;
for this conduct shall be established eternally in the world.
Having shaken off their grief with joyful hearts, firmly established on the path trodden by the great seers,
delighting in the forest and subsisting on wild fruits, they fulfill their father’s auspicious vow.
Nevertheless, though restrained by the charioteer who spoke with great reason, the queen, emaciated by grief for her son, did not cease her lamentation, crying out, "O beloved! O my son! O Raghava!"

When Rāma, the best among those who bring delight and devoted to righteousness, had gone to the forest, Kausalyā, weeping and deeply distressed, spoke these words to her husband: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 55.1).
Although your great fame is celebrated throughout the three worlds,
Rāghava is compassionate, generous, and speaks kindly.
O best among the foremost of men, how will those two sons, along with Sītā—
who have been raised in comfort— endure the suffering of the forest while they are so distressed?
Surely that young, dark-complexioned Maithilī, so delicate and accustomed to comfort, how will she endure both the heat and the cold?
Having eaten auspicious food accompanied by soups and side dishes, how will the large-eyed lady now consume a forest diet of wild grain?
Having heard the auspicious sound of singing and musical instruments,
how will the blameless lady hear the unpleasant sound of flesh-eating lions?
Where indeed does that mighty-armed and immensely powerful one sleep, reclining on his arm which resembles a massive iron bar, looking like the banner of Mahendra?
When shall I behold the face of Rāma— the lotus-colored one with beautiful hair-ends, whose breath is like a lotus, and who possesses supreme, lotus-like eyes?
"Surely my heart is made of the essence of diamond, there is no doubt;
for though it does not see him, it does not indeed shatter into a thousand pieces."
If Rāghava returns again in the fifteenth year,
he will abandon both the kingdom and the treasury, which Bharata shall enjoy.
O lord of the people, why would the eldest and most excellent brother not disregard the kingdom that has been enjoyed in this manner by his younger brother?
A tiger does not wish to eat food brought by another; in the very same way, a tiger among men will not accept what has been tasted by another.
The sacrificial offerings, the clarified butter, the sacrificial cakes, the *kuśa* grass, and the sacrificial posts made of *khadira* wood—
these they do not render stale by using them again in a sacrifice.
For thus has this kingdom been seized by him like wine from which the essence has been extracted; Rāma is unable to accept it, just as one cannot accept a sacrifice from which the Soma has vanished.
Rāghava will not tolerate such an insult,
just as a powerful tiger cannot endure the touching of its tail.
Such was that bull among men, possessing the strength of a lion and the eyes of a bull,
who was slain by his own father, just as a young fish is devoured by its parent.
The eternal duty of the twice-born, as seen in the scriptures,
has been violated by you, since you have sent away your son who is devoted to righteousness.
O King, for a woman, the husband is the first refuge; the son is the second refuge;
kinsmen are the third refuge; a fourth does not exist here in this world.
In this situation, you are no longer mine, and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest;
I have no desire to go to the forest, for I am utterly destroyed by you.
This kingdom, along with the realm, has been destroyed by you; likewise, yourself and your ministers have been slain.
I am destroyed along with my sons, as are the citizens; yet your son and wife are filled with joy.
Hearing these words fraught with such dreadful sounds, the king too fainted in his grief;
then that monarch fell into deep sorrow and once again remembered his own evil deed.
Thus addressed with harsh words by Rāma’s mother, who was both enraged and sorrowful, the king reflected in his grief. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 56.1)
As he was reflecting thus, his past misdeed appeared to him—
that which had been committed previously by him, who was a "shooter by sound," out of ignorance.
Distraught by that grief and by his sorrow for Rāma, the lord,
the king, burning with these two sorrows, spoke to Kausalyā.
I seek to propitiate you, O Kausalyā; here I join my hands in salutation.
For you are always affectionate and compassionate, even toward others.
"O Queen, for women who reflect upon their duty, the husband— whether he be virtuous or devoid of virtue— is indeed a visible deity."
You, who are ever devoted to righteousness and have perceived the higher and lower states of the world,
ought not to speak unpleasant words, even though you are suffering, to one who is already deeply distressed.
Hearing those piteous words spoken by the distressed king,
Kausalyā shed tears like a water-channel discharging fresh rainwater.

Placing her joined palms like a lotus upon her head and weeping, she, terrified and agitated, spoke these words in a hurried voice: *sa mūrdhni baddhvā rudatī rājñaḥ padmam ivāñjalim / sambhramād abravīt trastā tvaramāṇākṣaraṃ vacaḥ //* RamS_2,56.8 //
Be gracious; I entreat you with my head bowed, for I have fallen upon the ground before you.
O Lord, I am but a suppliant; I am ruined, yet I must not be slain by you.
For she is not truly a woman who is propitiated by a praiseworthy and wise husband in both worlds, O hero.
I know the Dharma, O knower of Dharma; I know you to be a speaker of truth.
Yet, afflicted by grief for my son, I have said something quite improper.
Grief destroys fortitude; grief destroys sacred learning;
grief destroys everything—there is no enemy equal to grief.
A blow from an enemy's hand that has fallen upon one can be endured;
however, grief that has fallen upon one cannot be endured, even if it is extremely subtle.
Today is counted as the fifth night of Rāma’s forest exile;
yet for me, whose joy has been destroyed by grief, it feels like five years.
For as she reflects upon him, this grief increases in her heart,
like the great waters of the ocean swelling with force against one who is not dejected.
While Kausalyā was thus speaking these auspicious words,
the sun’s rays grew faint and night drew near.
Then, though comforted by the words of Queen Kausalyā, the king,
overcome by grief, fell under the power of sleep.
Awakening after a moment, his mind overwhelmed by grief, King Daśaratha then fell into deep reflection. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 57.1)
And due to the exile of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, a calamity entered that king who was like Indra, just as the darkness of an asura enters the sun.

On the sixth night after Rāma had departed for the forest, King Daśaratha, at midnight, remembering the evil deed he had committed, spoke these words to Kausalyā, who was afflicted with grief for her son: *(Supplementary Verse 3)*: "O Kausalyā, you have been deprived of your son; O Sumitrā, you have been deprived of your two sons; and I too am deprived of my kingdom and my life. Alas, we have all been utterly ruined!"* *(Supplementary Verse 4)*: "Alas, I am lost! Alas, I am undone! I am ruined by my own wickedness! For I have brought about the destruction of my family through my own hand."* *(Supplementary Verse 5)*: "I am like one who has drunk poison, or like one who has fallen into a pit of fire; I am like one who has been struck down by a thunderbolt, or like one whose heart has been pierced by a poisoned arrow."* *(Supplementary Verse 6)*: "My mind is distracted, my senses are failing, and my limbs are sinking; I am as if dead, yet I do not depart from this world."* *(Supplementary Verse 7)*: "My heart is consumed by the fire of grief, and my body is parched by the heat of sorrow; I am tormented by the pain of separation from my son, as if bitten by a venomous serpent."* *(Supplementary Verse 8)*: "Even though I am overwhelmed by such intense agony, I do not die; surely it is because death itself is waiting for its appointed time."* *(Supplementary Verse 9)*: "I am like a man who has lost his way in a dense forest, or like a blind man who has fallen into a deep abyss; I am like a boat that has foundered upon the great ocean."* *(Supplementary Verse 10)*: "I am like a tree stripped of its fruit in the autumn, or like a dried-up pond in the summer; I am like a cloud that has shed all its water, or like a lamp whose oil is exhausted."* *(Supplementary Verse 11)*: "I am like a man whose wealth has been stolen, or like one whose hopes have been shattered; I am like a bird whose wings have been clipped, or like a fish caught on a hook."* *(Supplementary Verse 12)*: "I am like a man who has been cast into a dark dungeon, or like one who has been abandoned by his friends;
