Whatever one performs, O auspicious lady— whether it be good or evil— the doer, O blessed one, reaps that very result born of his own action.
He who does not understand the relative importance of objectives, the results of actions undertaken,
or the potential faults involved, is called a fool.
Someone who, having cut down a grove of mango trees, waters palāśa trees and,
greedy for fruit upon seeing the flowers, grieves when the time for fruit arrives.
Having cut down the mango grove and watered the *palāśa* trees instead, I,
a fool, have abandoned Rāma at the time of fruiting and now grieve for it.

"O Kausalyā, because of the prince who had acquired the reputation of being a 'prince who shoots by sound' with his bow, I committed this sin. O Queen, that very self-inflicted sorrow has now come upon me."
Just as poison might be consumed here by a fool out of delusion,
so too has this fruit consisting of the piercing of words been swallowed by me unknowingly.
"O Queen, you were unmarried and I was the crown prince;
then the rainy season arrived, which increases intoxication and desire."
For, having drawn up the juices of the earth and having heated the world with his rays,
the sun now enters the formidable quarter frequented by the departed.
The heat vanished instantly, and glossy clouds appeared;
thereupon all the frogs, deer, and peacocks rejoiced.
Covered by water that had fallen and by that which was falling repeatedly,
he shone like a mountain beside a lake filled with intoxicated deer.
During that time of great happiness, I, armed with a bow, arrows, and a chariot,
having resolved to engage in physical exercise, went along the Sarayū river.
At night at a watering place, one whose senses are unsubdued might desire to kill a buffalo, or an elephant that has come to the river, or some other wild beast.
Then, in the darkness, I heard the sound of a water-pot being filled in the water—
a sound beyond the range of sight, like the trumpeting of an elephant.
Then, having drawn my arrow, blazing like a venomous serpent,
I released that sharp shaft which resembled a poisonous snake.
There, at dawn, the voice of a forest-dweller became clearly audible;
and as he fell into the water, a human voice arose there: "Alas! Alas!
How could a weapon fall upon one such as me, a poor ascetic?"
"I have come at night to fetch water at this secluded river;
by whom have I been struck with an arrow, and what have I done to anyone?"
For how indeed can the killing with a weapon be ordained for one like me— an ascetic who has laid down the rod of punishment, living in the forest on forest produce?
Who could have any purpose in killing me, who merely bears a mass of matted hair and wears garments of bark and deerskin? Or what harm have I done to him?
No one would consider such an undertaking to be righteous— being fruitless and consisting solely of harm—
just as they would not consider one who violates the preceptor’s bed.
I do not grieve so much for the loss of my own life;
rather, I grieve for both my mother and father, who are like me.
This aged couple has been supported by me for a long time;
when I have met my death, what means of subsistence will they follow?
"My aged mother and father, and I myself, have been struck down by a single arrow. By what childish and undisciplined person have we all been slain?"
Hearing those piteous words of mine who longed for the Dharma,
the bow together with the arrow fell from my trembling hands to the ground.
Having arrived at that place, dejected and deeply distressed in mind,
I saw an ascetic slain by an arrow on the bank of the Sarayū.
Gazing at me with his eyes, seeing me terrified and distressed in mind,
he spoke these cruel words as if wishing to consume me with his splendor.
"O King, what harm have I done to you while dwelling in the forest, that I,
desiring to fetch water for my preceptor, was struck by you?"
Indeed, when my vital organ was struck by a single arrow,
both my blind parents— my mother and my father— were slain as well.
"Those two, surely weak, blind, and parched with thirst, waiting for me,
will for a long time endure that painful craving born of hope."
Surely there is no connection between the fruits of asceticism or sacred learning,
since my father does not recognize me as I lie fallen upon the ground.
Even though he knows [the danger], what can he do? He is powerless and lacks the means to act, like one mountain unable to protect another mountain that is being split asunder.
O Raghava, go quickly and tell my father this yourself,
so that he does not consume you with his anger like a blazing fire consuming a forest.
"O King, this is the path by which my father's hermitage lies;
go there and propitiate him, lest he, being enraged, should curse you."
"O King, extract the arrow-head from me; a sharp shaft pierces my vital organ, just as a swift current of water erodes a soft, swelling bank."
"I am not a twice-born, O King; let there be no distress in your mind.
I was indeed born of a Śūdra woman by a Vaiśya father, O lord of the realm."
As he was thus speaking with great difficulty, his vital organs pierced by the arrow,
I drew out that shaft from him as he was bending down.
Having lamented with difficulty over him whose limbs were wet with water, who was breathing incessantly from wounds in his vital organs,
and seeing him then lying upon the Sarayū, O blessed lady, I became deeply despondent.
Having committed that great sin through ignorance, my senses were deeply agitated; yet, alone, I reflected with my intellect: "How indeed might this become well-done? (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 58.1)
Then, taking that jar filled with the most excellent water,
I reached that hermitage and proceeded along the path as it had been described.
There I beheld his parents, weak, blind, aged, and without a leader, like two birds whose wings have been clipped.
Engaged in conversations concerning that very cause, we remained seated without moving about;
deprived of her for my sake, we were indifferent and like those who are helpless.
But hearing the sound of my footsteps, the sage spoke these words:
"Why do you delay, my son? Bring water quickly."
"O dear one, because of this playing in the water by you, your mother here is filled with longing; enter the hermitage quickly."
"Whatever offense has been committed against you, my son, either by your mother or by me,
that should not be taken to heart by you, my dear ascetic."
"You are the refuge of those without refuge, and the eye of those with failing sight;
our lives are entirely dependent upon you, yet you say not a word to us."
Beholding that sage with his indistinct voice, faltering and deficient in articulation, I spoke to him as if terrified, overcome by fear.
Having restrained the power of my speech through the mental effort of my actions,
I nevertheless declared to him the fear born from the calamity that had befallen my son.
"I am the Kṣatriya Daśaratha; I am not the son of that great-souled one.
This suffering, despised by the virtuous, has been obtained as the result of my own actions."
"O Blessed One, with bow in hand, I came to the bank of the Sarayū,
desiring to kill some wild beast or an elephant that had come to the watering place."
There, I heard the sound of a water-jar being filled in the water;
thinking, "This is an elephant," I struck him with an arrow.
Then, having gone to the bank of the river, I saw an ascetic lying on the ground, his heart pierced by an arrow, deprived of life.
"O Blessed One, perceiving that sound and desiring to kill the elephant, I discharged an iron arrow into the water; by that, your son was slain."
And with that arrow extracted, he remained right there, established in heaven,
lamenting and grieving for both the venerable ones, crying out, "They are blind!"
"Out of ignorance, I have suddenly struck your son;
since things have come to this, may the sage be gracious to me regarding whatever remains to be done."
Having heard those cruel words, sighing and emaciated by grief,
that one of great splendor spoke to me as I stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
O King, had you not yourself told me of this evil deed, your head would have instantly shattered into a hundred thousand pieces.
O King, the intentional killing of a forest-dweller by a Kṣatriya— especially one committed with full knowledge— could cause even the wielder of the thunderbolt to fall from his station.
Since this was done out of ignorance, you live by that very fact;
otherwise, even today the lineage of the Raghavas would not exist—how then could you?
"O King, lead us to that place," he said to me,
"for today we wish to see our son for the last time."
With his limbs drenched in blood and his deerskin garment scattered about,
he lay unconscious upon the ground, fallen under the power of the King of Dharma.
Then, having led those two, who were deeply distressed, to that place alone,
I allowed the sage to touch his son together with his wife.
Having reached him and touched their own son, those two ascetics fell upon his body, and his father spoke this to him:
"Am I not dear to you, my son? Look upon your mother, O righteous one!
Why do you not embrace me, my son? You are so delicate; speak some words to me."
Or from whom shall I hear, during the latter part of the night, a heart-pleasing and sweet recitation of a scripture, or especially some other work?
Who, having performed the twilight prayers, bathed, and offered oblations into the fire, will sit beside me and comfort me as I am tormented by the fear and grief for my son?
"Having stolen the roots, tubers, and fruits— who will feed me like a dear guest, for I am incapable of work, unrestrained, and without a leader?"
"O son, how shall I support this blind, aged, and ascetic mother of yours— this wretched woman who longs for her son?"
"Stay! Do not go toward the abode of Yama, my son;
tomorrow you shall go together with me and your mother, united once more."
"Both of us, afflicted by grief, helpless, and miserable in the forest,
shall very soon go to the abode of Yama, deprived of you."
Then, having seen Vaivasvata, I shall speak these words to him:
"May the King of Dharma forgive me; may he support my parents."
"O son, you are sinless, though slain by one of evil deeds;
by that truth, go quickly to those worlds reserved for those who fight with weapons."
O son, go to that supreme goal which heroes attain who do not retreat in battles, being slain while facing their enemies.
Go, my son, to that destination which Sagara, Śaibya, Dilīpa, Janamejaya, Nahuṣa, and Dhundhumāra have attained.

That destination which belongs to all the virtuous, and that which is attained through Vedic study and austerity, belongs to the giver of land, to the maintainer of the sacred fires, and to him who observes the vow of fidelity to a single wife.

Go, my son, to that destination reached by those who have given thousands of cows, by those who have supported their teachers, and by those who have surrendered their bodies; for one born into this family never goes to an evil state.
Thus he lamented there piteously again and again;
then, together with his wife, he began to offer water for him.
But that son of a sage, by virtue of his own past deeds, assumed a divine form and,
after consoling his parents for a moment, spoke these words.
"By serving you both, I have attained this great station;
and you two, in turn, shall soon come into my presence."
Having spoken thus, the son of the sage, who had conquered his senses, swiftly ascended to heaven by means of a magnificent, celestial chariot.
Having quickly performed the water-libation rites together with his wife,
that ascetic of great splendor spoke to me as I stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, kill me this very day; I feel no pain in death, since you have rendered me childless by striking my only son with an arrow."
But because my pure son was slain by you through ignorance,
I shall therefore curse you with a most terrible and profound suffering.
"Just as this sorrow born of the loss of a son is mine at present,
so too, O King, will you bring about your own end through grief for your son."
Therefore, O blessed lady, those words of that noble man have come upon me:
that today, out of grief for my son, I shall abandon my life.
O Queen, if Rāma were to touch me even once today, or were to seize me,
that would not befit me, given what I have done to the descendant of Raghu.
I do not see you with my eyes; my memory is failing me.
O Kausalyā, these messengers of Vaivasvata are hurrying me away.
But what could be more painful than this, that at the end of my life I do not see Rāma, the knower of dharma, whose prowess is truth?
Those who shall behold the face of Rāma again in the fifteenth year, adorned with beautiful and auspicious earrings—they are not mere mortals; they are gods.
"Blessed are those who shall behold the face of Rāma, which has eyes like lotus petals, beautiful eyebrows, fine teeth, and a lovely nose, resembling the lord of the stars."
"Blessed are those who shall behold the face of my lord, which is as fragrant as the autumnal moon and like a blossoming lotus."
Happy people shall behold Rāma returned once more to Ayodhyā after his forest exile has ended, like the planet Venus appearing upon its path in the sky.
This grief for my own person is overwhelming me, helpless and senseless,
with such force as the current of a river sweeps away its bank.
"Alas, O Rāghava, O mighty-armed one! Alas, O destroyer of my distress!
King Daśaratha, grieving, has reached the end of his life."
Speaking thus piteously, the lord of men, afflicted by the exile of his beloved son and tormented by intense grief, gave up his life at midnight, he who was of noble appearance.
Then,
when the night had passed, at the very dawn of the following day,
bards gathered around the royal palace.
Then, women and eunuchs, preeminent in number, who were of pure conduct and skilled in attendance, waited upon him as they had done before.
Those skilled in the art of bathing brought water mixed with yellow sandalwood in golden jars at the proper time and according to the prescribed rite.
Likewise, other women, many of whom were young maidens, brought auspicious objects for touching, articles for consumption, and various household utensils.
Then those women who were closest to the bed of the Lord of Kosala gathered together and attempted to awaken their husband.
Overcome with trembling and apprehensive for the king's life,
they quivered like the tips of blades of grass facing the current.
Then, seeing the king while the women were trembling,
that evil which they had suspected became a certainty for them.
Then those beautiful women cried out piteously with loud voices,
like female elephants in the forest whose leader has been driven from his place.
At the sound of their wailing, Kausalyā and Sumitrā suddenly regained consciousness and were awakened from their sleep.
Having seen and touched the king, Kausalyā and Sumitrā cried out, "Alas, our lord! and fell to the surface of the earth.
Rolling upon the surface of the earth, that daughter of the Lord of Kosala,
covered in dust, did not shine, like a star fallen from the sky.
It was filled with people who were terrified, bewildered, and deeply anxious;
it resounded everywhere with tumultuous cries, and its kinsmen were afflicted by intense grief.
The palace of the king, who had met his end, became instantly filled with falling tears and appeared wretched and distressed.
But having learned of the illustrious bull among kings who had passed away, his wives, surrounded by one another,
weeping most piteously and deeply afflicted by grief, threw up their arms and lamented like those who are helpless.

Beholding the lord of the earth dwelling in heaven— like a fire completely extinguished, like an ocean devoid of water, and like the sun whose radiance has been destroyed— (the people were struck with grief). *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Canto 60.1.
Kausalyā, her eyes filled with tears and emaciated by manifold grief,
took hold of the king’s head and addressed Kaikeyī.
"O Kaikeyī, may your desire be fulfilled; enjoy the kingdom free from thorns, having abandoned the king with single-minded devotion, O cruel woman of wicked conduct! (Rāmāyaṇa 2.60.3)
"Rāma has departed, leaving me behind, and my husband has gone to heaven;
like one lost on a desolate path without a caravan, I have no desire to live."
Abandoning that husband who is her own deity, what woman would wish to live, other than Kaikeyī, who has cast aside all righteousness?
A greedy person does not perceive his own faults, just as one eating poison does not perceive its effects;
on account of Kaikeyī and the hunchback, the lineage of the Raghavas has been destroyed.
Having heard that Rāma has been exiled along with his wife by the king, who appointed him to an improper task, Janaka will suffer just as I do.
Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, has gone from here to the end of his life;
likewise, the ascetic Sītā, daughter of the King of Videha,
who is unaccustomed to sorrow, will suffer distress and tremble with fear in the forest.
Having heard the terrifying cries of the beasts and birds roaring through the nights, she will surely take refuge with Rāghava in her fear.
Moreover, he is aged and has few sons; constantly brooding over Vaidehī, he too, overwhelmed by grief, will surely give up his life.
Then the officials removed Kausalyā, who was weeping, wretched, and afflicted by intense grief, after they had embraced her.
Then, having laid the lord of the world upon a trough filled with oil, the ministers,
being commanded, immediately performed all the rites for the king.
But the ministers, though all-knowing, were not able to carry out the calculation of the king's lifespan without his son; therefore, they protected the lord of the earth.
But when the ministers had laid that lord of men in a trough of oil,
the women, perceiving "Alas, he is dead," wailed aloud.
Raising their arms in distress, with faces streaming from their eyes,
they wept, tormented by grief, and lamented piteously.
Deprived of the high-souled king, the city of Ayodhyā did not shine, like a night devoid of stars, or like a woman bereft of her husband.
With people overwhelmed by tears and the women of the household crying out "Alas!
Alas!", the squares and the interiors of the houses became empty and did not shine as they had before.

Deprived of the Great-Souled One, the city shone like the sky robbed of its radiance when bereft of the sun, or like a night when the host of stars has vanished; yet its streets and crossroads were not choked with throats choked by tears.
Men and women gathered together in groups, censuring the mother of Bharata;
at that time, during the passing of the god-like king, they became distressed within the city and found no peace.
When the night had passed and the sun had risen,
the twice-born ministers of the king assembled together and went to the assembly hall.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva, Kāśyapa,
Kātyāyana, Gautama, and the highly illustrious Jābāli.
These twice-born ones, together with the ministers, each uttered their speech,
facing toward Vasiṣṭha alone, the preeminent royal priest.
The past night has passed in misery for us, like a hundred years,
now that the king has met his death through grief for his son.
The great king has gone to heaven, and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest;
the radiant Lakṣmaṇa, too, has gone along with Rāma himself.
Both Bharata and Śatrughna, the subduers of enemies,
remained among the Kekayas in the delightful city of Rājagṛha, at their maternal grandfather’s residence.
"Let some king of the Ikṣvākus be appointed here this very day;
for our kingdom, being without a ruler, might otherwise meet with destruction."
In a kingdom without a king, the rain-god Parjanya, garlanded with lightning and roaring loudly,
does not shower the earth with celestial water.
In a kingless land, not even a handful of seed is sown;
in a kingless land, neither son nor wife remains under the control of their father or husband.
In a kingless state there is no wealth, and in a kingless state there is no wife;
this is another great calamity: how can there be truth in a kingless state?
In a kingless land, people do not joyfully build assembly halls,
delightful gardens, or meritorious dwellings.
In a kingless land, the twice-born who are devoted to sacrifice—
those self-controlled Brahmins of firm vows— do not perform long sacrificial sessions.
In a kingdom without a king, festivals and public assemblies— those which increase the prosperity of the realm— do not flourish, nor do there appear many actors and dancers.
In a kingless land, litigants do not achieve their objectives; those fond of discourse are not delighted by stories when they are told by others who love storytelling.
In a kingdom without a king, men who are full of desire do not go out with their women into the forests on swift-moving vehicles.
In a kingless land, even those wealthy men who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing do not sleep with their doors securely closed, however well-protected they may be.
In a kingdom without a king, even merchants who have accumulated great merit do not travel safely on long journeys.
In a kingless land, the self-controlled sage does not wander alone, cultivating the self by means of the self, wherever he may take up residence for the night.
In a kingdom without a king, security and prosperity do not prevail;
nor can an army, in a kingless state, withstand its enemies in battle.
For as rivers without water, or a forest without grass,
or cows without a cowherd, so is a kingdom without a king.
In a kingdom without a king, no one possesses their own property;
like fish, men constantly devour one another.
For even those who have violated the bounds of propriety, who are nihilists, and whose doubts have been severed,
are brought to a state of rectitude when oppressed by the king's rod of punishment.
Alas, this world would be like darkness and nothing would be discernible,
were there no king in the world to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous.
Even while the great king is still alive, we all do not transgress your word alone, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Having observed that the kingdom has become a wilderness without the king, whose conduct was like that of the best of the twice-born,
you yourself must consecrate the generous prince, the son of Ikṣvāku, as the king here.
Having heard those words of theirs, Vasiṣṭha replied with these words to all the hosts of friends and ministers, and to those brahmins: *Ramāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 62.1.
That Bharata dwells happily in the city of Rājagṛha in the house of his maternal uncle, accompanied by his brother Śatrughna.
Therefore, let swift messengers go quickly on fleet horses to bring back the two heroic brothers; what shall we do while we wait?
"Let us go," they all then said to Vasiṣṭha.
Having heard those words of theirs, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words.
"Come, Siddhārtha, Vijaya, Jayanta, Aśoka, and Nandana!
Listen to what must be done; I shall tell it all to you."

Having gone quickly to the city of Rājagṛha on swift-footed horses, Bharata—freed from grief—must be addressed with these words by my command: “O son of Kaikeyī, you have acted rightly; you have not brought disgrace upon me. Having abandoned the kingdom, I shall dwell in the forest for fourteen years.
