The family priest and all the ministers have inquired after your welfare;
depart with haste, for there is urgent business for you to attend to.
And having gone to this abode of the Raghavas, you must not report to him that Rama has gone into exile, nor that his father is dead.
"Taking silken garments and excellent ornaments for both the King and Bharata, depart at once! Having been thus authorized by Vasiṣṭha, the messengers departed in great haste.
Having crossed the Gaṅgā at Hastināpura, they proceeded westward,
reaching the Pāñcāla country by way of Kurujāṅgala.
They passed with great speed by the divine Śaradaṇḍā river, which had clear waters, was frequented by various birds, and was crowded with people.
Having reached the divine Nikūla tree, which grants boons through truthful prayer,
and having approached and paid homage to it, they entered the city of Kuliṅgā.
Then, having reached Abhikāla, they fell from their celestial splendor due to its overpowering brilliance;
they proceeded through the middle of the Vāhlīka country toward Mount Sudāmā,
beholding the footprint of Viṣṇu, as well as the Vipāśā and the Śālmalī rivers.
Those messengers, their mounts exhausted, traveled by a long and difficult road and reached Girivraja, the preeminent city, swiftly and directly.
For the sake of their master’s pleasure, for the sake of protecting the family, and for the sake of upholding their master’s lineage,
those messengers, free from hesitation, departed in haste for that very city during the night.
On the very night those messengers entered that city,
Bharata also saw this unpleasant dream during that same night.
But when that night had dawned, having seen that unpleasant dream,
the son of the king of kings was deeply distressed.
Perceiving that he was suffering, his sweet-spoken friends, wishing to dispel his distress, began to converse in the assembly hall.
Some played instruments for peace, while others performed dances; others staged plays and various kinds of comedies.
That high-souled descendant of Raghu, Bharata, did not rejoice with those friends who spoke kindly to him while engaging in social conversation and laughter.
Surrounded by his friends and attended by his well-wishers, his dear companion said to Bharata: "Friend, why do you not express your approval?"
To his friend who was speaking thus, Bharata replied:
"Listen to the cause for which this dejection has come upon me."
In a dream, I saw my father, soiled and with disheveled hair,
falling from a mountain peak into a turbid pool of cow dung.
And I saw him floating in that pool of cow dung,
drinking oil with his cupped hands, as if laughing again and again.
Then, having eaten rice mixed with sesame seeds again and again, with his head hanging downward and his entire body anointed with oil, he immersed himself in oil alone.
Even in his dreams, he saw the ocean dried up, the moon fallen to the earth,
and the blazing fire suddenly extinguished.
I see the earth split open and various trees withered;
I see the mountains shattered and enveloped in smoke.
As he sat upon an iron throne, dressed in black garments,
dark-brown women laughed at the king.
Hurrying along, the righteous-souled one, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
set out toward the south in a chariot yoked with donkeys.
Thus was this seen by me this night, which brings such terror:
either I, or Rāma, or King Lakṣmaṇa shall die.

Indeed, that man who travels in a dream by means of a vehicle yoked with donkeys will soon have the crest of smoke from a funeral pyre seen before him. It is because of this omen that I am dejected; therefore, I do not offer you my respects.
My throat seems to parch, my mind is not at ease,
and I feel as though I am loathing myself, yet I do not perceive the cause.
For having observed this course of bad dreams, so manifold in form and never before imagined,
a great fear does not leave my heart as I reflect upon the King, whose appearance is inconceivable.
While Bharata was thus recounting his dream, those messengers, their mounts exhausted,
entered the beautiful city of Rājagṛha, which possessed an unassailable moat.
Having met with the king and the prince, and being honored by them, they grasped the feet of the king and spoke these words to Bharata: ||| RamS_2,64.2 |||
The family priest and all the ministers have inquired after your welfare;
depart with haste, for there is urgent business for you to attend to.
In this matter, O prince, there are twenty crores for your maternal uncle,
the king, and likewise ten full crores for you as well.
Having accepted all of that, Bharata, being deeply devoted to his circle of friends, honored the messengers with gifts according to their desires and spoke to them.
"Is my father, King Daśaratha, in good health? And is there freedom from illness for Rāma and the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa?"
And the noble Kausalyā, the mother of the wise Rāma, is devoted to the Dharma, a knower of the Dharma, a seer of the Dharma, and is also free from illness.
I trust that Sumitrā, the mother of Lakṣmaṇa and of the heroic Śatrughna, who knows the dharma, is also free from disease, she being the middle one.
Ever self-indulgent, fierce, prone to anger, and imagining herself wise,
my mother Kaikeyī— though free from illness— what indeed did she say?
Thus addressed by the high-souled Bharata, those messengers then spoke these humble words to him: "O tiger among men, all is well with those for whose welfare you inquire."
And Bharata, having been addressed thus by those messengers, spoke to them: "I shall take leave of the Great King; the messengers are urging me to haste."
Having spoken thus to those messengers, Bharata, the son of the king,
being urged by the messengers, addressed these words to his maternal grandfather.
"O King, urged by the messenger, I shall go to my father's presence;
I will return again whenever you remember me."
When Bharata had spoken thus, the king, his maternal grandfather,
then smelled the head of the descendant of Raghu and addressed these auspicious words to him.
"Go, my son; I give you my permission. Kaikeyī has been blessed with a worthy son in you. O scorcher of foes, inquire after the welfare of your mother and your father."
And the family priest who is skilled, as well as those other best of the twice-born,
and those two great archers, my dear, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having honored him, the King of Kekaya gave Bharata wealth consisting of excellent elephants, variegated blankets, and skins.
Having honored his son, the King of Kekaya bestowed wealth upon him: two thousand gold neck-ornaments and sixteen hundred horses.
Likewise, Aśvapati quickly gave Bharata trusted ministers who were beloved and endowed with virtuous qualities to accompany him.
His maternal uncle gave him as wealth swift donkeys, well-yoked and of pleasing appearance, as well as Airāvatas and Aindraśiras elephants.
He gave as a gift dogs that had been raised in the inner apartments, possessing the prowess and strength of tigers, with large bodies and fangs for weapons.
Having taken leave of his maternal grandfather and his uncle Yudhājit,
Bharata, accompanied by Śatrughna, mounted his chariot and departed.
Having yoked more than a hundred chariots with wheel-rims adorned with jewels,
the servants followed Bharata as he traveled on camels, oxen, horses, and donkeys.

Protected by his army, the high-souled Bharata, free from enemies, took Śatrughna and ministers equal to himself in devotion to his grandfather, and departed from the palace like a perfected being departing for the realm of Indra.
Having departed from the royal palace facing the east, that valiant one crossed the Hrādinī river,
which has distant shores and waves flowing toward the west.
The illustrious joy of the Ikṣvākus crossed the Śatadrū river.
Having crossed the river at Elādhāna and reached Aparaparpaṭa,
and having crossed the Ākurvatī and Śilā rivers, one reaches Āgneya and Śalyakartana.
True to his promise, pure, and glorious, he gazed upon the Śilāvahā river as he passed over the great mountains toward the Caitraratha forest.
Having reached the Yamunā— which flows swiftly, is known as Kuliṅgā, resounds with noise, and is surrounded by mountains— he crossed over it and then comforted his army.
Having cooled his limbs and comforted the exhausted horses,
he bathed there, drank, and set forth taking water with him.
The noble prince, by means of his noble vehicle, passed through the great forest seldom frequented, as the wind passes through the sky.
Passing through the southern half of Toraṇa, the son of Daśaratha arrived at Jambūprastha and proceeded to the lovely village of Varūtha.
Having made his dwelling there in that lovely forest, he went facing eastward to the garden of Ujjihānā, where the priyaka trees grow.
Having reached the *śāla* and *priyaka* trees and mounted swift horses,
Bharata then took leave of the army and proceeded in haste.
Having stayed at all the sacred fords and having crossed the Uttānikā river and various other rivers with mountain-bred horses, he proceeded.
Having reached Hastipṛṣṭhaka, he passed beyond Kuṭikā;
that tiger among men crossed the Kapīvatī at Lohitya,
the Sthāṇumatī at Ekasāla, and the river Gomatī at Vinata.
Then, having reached the Sāla grove in the city of Kaliṅga,
Bharata quickly arrived with his mounts thoroughly exhausted.
Having quickly traversed the forest at the break of dawn during the night,
he beheld Ayodhyā, which had been founded by King Manu.
Having stayed on the road for seven nights, that tiger among men, seeing Ayodhyā ahead, spoke to his charioteer from the chariot: RamS_2,65.14 //
"O charioteer, this glorious Ayodhyā, with its white soil, is seen from afar; it is the famous Puṇyodyāna, yet it does not appear very familiar to me."
It was densely populated by sacrificial performers, virtuous Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and were mostly wealthy, and it was protected by the best of royal sages.
In the past, a great and tumultuous clamor from men and women was heard all around Ayodhyā; today, I do not hear it.
For at another time, these gardens used to shine with men who, having ceased their play in the evening, were running about in every direction.
"Abandoned today by those who desired them, those [palaces] seem to lament;
O charioteer, that city appears to me as if it were a wilderness."
For here, those foremost of men are no longer seen as they used to be in the past, departing or returning by means of chariots, elephants, or horses.
I see various undesirable and evil omens, as well as unpleasant signs; therefore, my mind is sinking.
With his mounts exhausted, he entered through the Vaijayanta gate;
having been asked for news of victory by the gatekeepers who rose to meet him, he proceeded together with them.
But Rāghava, his heart distracted by many thoughts, having returned the greetings of that person standing at the gate, spoke there to the weary charioteer of Aśvapati.
O charioteer, I see here all those very signs of which we have heard before regarding the destruction of kings.
And I see the people in the city— both men and women— distressed, dejected, lost in thought, emaciated, with eyes filled with tears and faces soiled.

Having spoken thus to the charioteer, Bharata, with a dejected mind, beheld those ominous signs in Ayodhyā and proceeded toward the royal palace; he saw that city with its crossroads, houses, and streets empty, and its door-panels and bolts reddened by dust.
Seeing the city, which shone like the city of Indra, he became even more filled with sorrow as he beheld many things unpleasant to his mind, which had never before existed in that city.
With his head bowed, dejected in spirit, and devoid of joy, the high-souled prince entered his father’s palace.
Not seeing his father there in his father's residence, Bharata then went to see his mother in her own residence. *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 66.1.
But seeing that her son had returned from his journey, Kaikeyī then leaped up in joy, casting aside her golden ornaments.
Having entered his own home, which was now bereft of its splendor,
the righteous Bharata beheld it and grasped the auspicious feet of his mother.
Having smelled the head of that illustrious one and embraced him,
he placed Bharata upon his lap and began to question him.
Only a few nights have passed since you departed from the house of your noble grandfather;
has the fatigue of the journey not yet subsided as you hastened here by chariot?
"Is your grandfather well, O Yudhājit, and your maternal uncle? And have you been happy during your stay abroad, my son? You ought to tell me everything."
Thus questioned by Kaikeyī,
the lotus-eyed Bharata, the joy of the king, related everything to his mother.
Today is the seventh night since I departed from the house of my noble grandfather;
my mother’s father is well, as is my maternal uncle Yudhājit.
"The wealth and jewels that the king, the scorcher of foes, gave me became a burden on the road; therefore, I have come ahead."
Urged on by messengers carrying the king's commands, I have come;
therefore, my mother ought to tell me that which I wish to ask.
"This bed of yours, adorned with gold, is empty;
nor does this people of the Ikṣvākus appear joyful to me."
"The king is most likely in his mother's residence here;
I have come here desiring to see him, yet I do not see him today."
"I shall grasp my father's feet; tell that to me as I ask you, O mother—is he in the residence of my elder mother Kausalyā?"
Deluded by greed for the kingdom, Kaikeyī, though knowing the truth, spoke these terrible and unpleasant words as if they were pleasant to him who did not yet know them:
"Your father has gone to that destination which is the destination of all living beings."
Having heard those words, the pure Bharata, who was noble by birth and devoted to dharma,
suddenly fell to the ground, overwhelmed by the force of grief for his father.
Then, enveloped by grief and pained by the death of his father,
the immensely radiant one lamented, his mind wandering and agitated.
This bed of my father’s, which formerly shone so brilliantly,
does not gleam today, now that it is bereft of that wise man.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, distressed and resembling a god, he raised him up and, afflicted with grief himself, spoke these words: *RamS_2,66.18*
"Arise, arise! Why do you lie there, O prince of great renown?
For virtuous men like you, esteemed in the assembly, do not grieve."
Having wept for a long time and rolled upon the ground, he,
overwhelmed by many sorrows, spoke thus to his mother.
"The king will indeed consecrate Rāma, or perhaps he will perform a sacrifice"—
with this resolve formed, I set out on my journey full of joy.
For this mind of mine is indeed shattered and distressed,
since I do not see my father, who was ever devoted to my pleasure and welfare.
"Mother, by what disease did the king pass away before I had arrived?
Blessed are Rāma and all the others, by whom our father was personally consecrated."
"Surely the illustrious Great King does not know that I have arrived;
for my father would quickly bow down and smell my head."
Where is that hand of my father, whose actions were untiring, with its pleasant touch, which used to constantly wipe me clean when I was covered in dust?
"Tell me quickly of that wise Rāma, whose brother, father, and kinsman I am, and for whom I am a slave— he of unwearied deeds."
"For to one who knows the noble Dharma, the eldest brother is indeed a father;
I shall clasp his feet, for he is now my refuge."
"Noble lady, what did my father, the king of true valor, say?
I wish to hear his final, virtuous message for himself."
Thus questioned, Kaikeyī spoke these words according to the truth:
"Lamenting 'O Rāma! and 'Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!', that high-souled one, the best among those who possess a goal, has gone to the other world."
But your father, overtaken by the law of time, uttered these final words, like a great elephant entangled in snares.
But those men who have accomplished their goals shall behold Rāma returned with Sītā, and the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa returned once more.
Having heard that, he despaired indeed at the announcement of a second unpleasant thing;
with a dejected face, he questioned his mother once more.
And where now is that righteous soul, the increaser of Kausalyā’s joy,
who has gone together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā?
Thus questioned, his mother began to relate the truth exactly as it was; yet, out of a desire for what she thought was pleasant, she spoke words that were simultaneously unpleasant.
For that prince, O son, has gone to the great Daṇḍaka forest clad in bark garments,
accompanied by Vaidehī and followed by Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard that, Bharata was terrified by the suspicion concerning his brother's conduct;
yet, out of pride in the greatness of his own lineage, he proceeded to question him.
I hope that no one’s Brahmanical wealth has been seized by Rāma;
I hope that no innocent person, whether wealthy or poor, has been harmed by him.
I trust that the prince does not covet another man’s wife;
why else would he have been exiled to the Daṇḍaka forest like a killer of an embryo?
Then his fickle mother, out of that very feminine nature, began to recount her own deed exactly as it had happened.
Rāma has not taken any of a Brāhmaṇa’s wealth from anyone;
no one, whether rich or poor, has been harmed by him through sin;
nor does Rāma even look upon the wives of others with his eyes.
But as soon as I heard, O son, of Rāma’s consecration,
I entreated your father for the kingdom and for the exile of Rāma.
Adhering to his own duty, your father did exactly that;
and Rāma, along with Saumitri and Sītā, was sent away.
Not seeing his beloved son, the highly illustrious protector of the earth,
consumed by grief for his son, met his death.
But now, O knower of dharma, you must assume the kingship;
for it was on your account that I have done all this of such a kind.
Therefore, my son, quickly, accompanied by the foremost brahmins led by Vasiṣṭha who are learned in the ritual rules,
perform the cremation of the king of undaunted spirit according to the ordinances, and have yourself consecrated upon the earth.
Having heard that his father had passed away and that his two brothers had been exiled, Bharata, tormented by grief, spoke these words: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 67.1.
"What use indeed is this kingdom to me, who am grieving here, having been struck down and deprived of both my father and my brother, who was like a father to me?"
"You have inflicted sorrow upon me who was already in sorrow, like applying caustic to a wound,
by making the king a departed spirit and turning Rāma into an ascetic."
"You have come like the Night of Doom for the destruction of the lineage;
my father did not realize that he was embracing a burning coal."
Kausalyā and Sumitrā, tormented by grief for their son,
would find it difficult to remain alive even if they were to obtain you, my mother.
Surely the noble one, whose very soul is dharma and who knows how to behave toward elders, maintains toward you the highest conduct, just as he behaves toward his mother.
For likewise my eldest mother, Kausalyā, who is far-sighted,
abides in righteousness toward you as if you were her own sister.
Having sent her son, who had perfected his soul and was clad in garments of bark and rags,
away to dwell in the forest, how is it that you do not grieve, O sinful woman?
Having sent away into exile that hero who perceives no evil, who has disciplined his soul and is illustrious, now clothed in bark garments— what indeed do you see as the reason for this?
I believe that I have not been understood by you, who are greedy, regarding Rāghava;
for thus you have brought about this great misfortune for the sake of the kingdom.
For, not seeing those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
by what power of my own might could I venture to protect the kingdom?
For that righteous-souled great king, possessing great strength, constantly relied upon him who was powerful, just as Mount Meru relies upon the forest of Meru.
How then shall I bear this burden, which is like the yoke raised by a great draft-animal; with what strength, like a young ox encountering the pole, shall I endure it?
Or else, if I should possess the power through yogic means or by the strength of my intellect,
I will not fulfill the desire of you who are so greedy for your son;
I shall bring back from the forest my brother, who is dear to his own people.
Having spoken thus, the high-souled Bharata, piercing her with a multitude of most unpleasant words,
cried out again in his affliction of grief like a lion dwelling in a mountain cave.
Having thus reproached his mother, Bharata,
overcome by great anger, then spoke these words once more.
Fall from your kingdom, Kaikeyī, you cruel woman of wicked conduct!
Abandoned by righteousness, do not weep for me when I am dead.
What indeed did the king or the exceedingly righteous Rāma do wrong to you,
that death and exile have come upon both of them equally because of you?
"O Kaikeyī, you have incurred the sin of foeticide by destroying this lineage; go to hell and never attain the same world as your husband."
"Since you have committed such an evil deed through this terrible act—
having abandoned one who is beloved by all the world— you have brought fear upon me as well."
On your account my father has passed away and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest;
you have brought infamy upon me in the world of the living.
"O you who have the form of a mother, yet are my enemy, cruel, and lustful for the kingdom— I am not to be addressed by you, O woman of wicked conduct, who have slain your husband!"
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and my other mothers,
overcome with great sorrow because of you, the defiler of the family— ||| RamS_2,68.8 |||
"You are not the daughter of the wise Dharmarāja Aśvapati;
you are a Rākṣasī born there, the destroyer of your father's lineage."
That you have sent the righteous Rāma, who is ever devoted to truth, away to the forest, and that our father has gone to the third heaven out of grief; [all this is because of you].
Whatever sin you hold as primary, let that fall upon me— me who am deprived of my father,
abandoned by my two brothers, and disliked by the whole world.
Having separated Kausalyā, who is devoted to dharma, from you— a man of evil resolve— to what world will you go today, you who are destined for hell?
O cruel woman, do you not realize that Rāma, born of Kausalyā, is the eldest son, equal to his father, and the very refuge of his kinsmen?
A son is born from the major and minor limbs and is even born from the heart;
therefore, because of his dearness, he is more beloved to a mother than any other kinsman.
Once, it is said, Surabhi, who knows the Dharma and is honored by the gods,
saw her two sons on the earth while they were carrying [her], deprived of their senses.
Seeing her two sons on the ground, exhausted at midday,
she wept out of grief for her children, her eyes overwhelmed with tears.
As that high-souled king of the gods was passing below,
subtle drops of fragrant scent fell upon his body.
Seeing that illustrious lady tormented by grief, Indra, the king of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt, spoke these words with joined palms and an anxious heart.
"Is there perhaps no great danger for us from any quarter?
O you who desire the welfare of all, tell me: what is the cause of your grief?"
Thus addressed by the wise king of the gods, the steadfast Surabhi,
skilled in speech, then replied with these words.
"O Lord of the Immortals, may no evil whatsoever come upon you from any source;
however, I grieve for my two sons who have fallen into misfortune."
O Lord of the Gods, having seen these two oxen— emaciated, miserable, scorched by the rays of the sun, and being tormented by the farmer— [he felt compassion].
For these two, born from my own body, are indeed suffering and oppressed by their burden;
seeing them, I am consumed with grief, for there is nothing as dear as a son.
Even she, the wish-fulfilling cow who has thousands of sons, grieves;
how much more so will Kausalyā fare without Rāma?
"She is a virtuous woman who has but one son, yet she has been made childless by you;
therefore, you shall experience constant suffering both here and after death."
For I shall undoubtedly perform this entire act of honoring my brother and my father, as well as increasing his fame.
Having caused my son of great splendor, born of Kausalyā, to be brought here,
I myself shall enter the forest frequented by sages.
Thus, like an elephant in the forest urged on by lances and goads,
he fell to the ground in a rage, hissing like a serpent.
With bloodshot eyes, his garments disheveled, and all his ornaments cast aside, that scorcher of foes,
the prince, fell upon the ground like the banner of Indra at the conclusion of a festival.
While the high-souled Bharata was thus crying out,
Kausalyā, having recognized his voice, spoke these words to Sumitrā: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 69.1)
"Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, who performs cruel deeds, has arrived;
I wish to see that far-sighted Bharata."
Having spoken thus to Sumitrā, she— pale and clad in soiled garments—
set out trembling and distraught toward where Bharata was.
Then Rāmānuja, accompanied by Śatrughna, set out for where Bharata’s residence was, that of Kausalyā.
Then Śatrughna and Bharata, seeing Kausalyā in her grief,
embraced her as she lay fallen, afflicted by sorrow and deprived of her senses.
Kausalyā, deeply afflicted by grief, replied thus to Bharata:
"Alas, this kingdom which you desired has now been obtained by you without any thorns;
yet it was swiftly secured by Kaikeyī through her cruel deed."
Having sent my son away to dwell in the forest clad in bark garments,
what benefit does that cruel-looking Kaikeyī perceive in this?
Kaikeyī ought to dispatch me quickly as well,
to where my highly illustrious son Hiraṇyanābha resides.
Or rather, I myself, accompanied by Sumitrā, shall set out happily,
placing the sacred fire before me, to where Rāghava has gone.
Or rather, you ought to take me yourself today to that place where my son, that tiger among men, is performing his austerities.
For this vast kingdom of yours, filled with wealth and grain and abounding in elephants, horses, and chariots, has been bestowed upon you by her.
To Kausalyā, who was thus lamenting and overwhelmed by many sorrows, Bharata then replied with palms joined in reverence: ||| RamS_2,69.12 |||
"Noble lady, why do you reproach me, who am innocent and unaware?
You know well my vast and steadfast affection for Rāghava."
May his intellect never at any time follow the teachings of the scriptures—
he who is true to his word, the best among the virtuous, and in whose approval the noble one has departed.
May he go into the service of the most wicked, may he urinate facing the sun;
may he strike a sleeping cow with his foot—he whose approval the noble one has sought.
"Having caused his master to perform great labor while he himself was rendered useless,
let that very unrighteousness belong to him with whose consent the noble one has gone."
While the king protected all beings like his own children,
let the sin of those who act with hostility toward him fall upon him by whose consent the noble one has gone into exile.
"Let that unrighteousness which belongs to a king who fails to protect his subjects— having extracted the sixth part as tribute— be his, with whose approval the noble one has departed."
And having promised the sacrificial fee to the ascetics for the rite, may that sin belong to him by whose consent the noble one has gone away, while they were thus deceiving them.
In this battle crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and thick with weapons,
let him not commit the deed that the noble one has gone to perform with your approval.
May that evil-minded man, with whose consent the noble one has departed, lose the fruit of this scripture of extremely subtle meaning which was taught with great effort by the wise one.
May that pitiless man, with whose approval the noble one has departed, eat milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, and goat’s meat in vain, and may he show contempt for his elders.
Surrounded in his own home by sons, wives, and servants,
may he alone eat delicacies, for whose sake the Noble One has gone away with his consent.
May he incur that sin which is said to arise from the killing of a king, a woman, a child, or an elder,
and may he incur that sin which arises from the abandonment of one’s dependents.
Whatever sin is attributed to one who sleeps during both twilights,
that same sin shall belong to him with whose consent the noble one has departed.
May he incur that sin which belongs to one who sets fire to a dwelling, that sin which belongs to one who violates the bed of his guru,
and that sin which belongs to one who betrays a friend.
May he never perform service to the gods, the ancestors, or likewise to his mother and father— he by whose consent the noble one has gone away.
May he from whose consent the noble one has departed fall this very day from the world of the virtuous, from the fame of the virtuous, and likewise from the deeds cherished by the virtuous.
While thus consoling Kausalyā, who was deprived of both husband and son, the prince, himself afflicted by grief, fell down.
To Bharata, who was thus cursing himself with painful oaths in his unconscious state and was tormented by grief, Kausalyā spoke these words.
O son, this sorrow of mine arises even more intensely,
for by swearing these oaths you are indeed threatening my very life.
"By good fortune, your soul, along with Lakṣmaṇa, has not wavered from dharma.
My child, being true to your promise, you shall attain the worlds of the virtuous."
As that great-souled one was thus lamenting, afflicted by grief,
his mind became agitated due to delusion and the suppression of his sorrow.
As he lamented, unconscious, his intellect lost, fallen upon the ground,
and sighing long and repeatedly, that night passed for him in grief.
To Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, who was thus tormented by grief, Vasiṣṭha— the best of speakers, the seer of excellent speech— spoke. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, Canto 70, Verse 1)
Enough with grieving; may prosperity be yours, O illustrious prince! Perform the final funeral rites for the lord of men, for the time has come.
Having heard Vasiṣṭha’s words, Bharata regained his composure;
knowing what was right, he caused all the funeral rites for the deceased to be performed.
Lifted from the soaking of the oil and placed upon the ground,
the lord of the earth lay there with a face of yellowish hue, as if fast asleep.
Having laid Daśaratha upon an excellent bed adorned with various jewels, his son, deeply distressed, then lamented.
"O King, what have you resolved while I am away and have not yet returned,
having exiled Rāma, who knows the dharma, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa?"
Where will you go, O Great King, abandoning these grieving people who are now bereft of Rāma, that lion among men of untiring deeds?
But who, O King, will provide for your security and well-being in this city now that you have departed for your own home,
dear father, and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest?
"O King, the earth, widowed by being deprived of you, does not shine;
to me, the city appears like a night bereft of the moon."
To Bharata, who was thus lamenting with a dejected mind,
the great seer Vasiṣṭha spoke these words once more.
O mighty-armed one, let those funeral rites which must be performed for this lord of the people be carried out without distraction and without hesitation.
"So be it," Bharata replied, honoring those words of Vasiṣṭha;
he then urged on all the officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers in every way.
But those who were outside the fire-sanctuary in front of the lord of men were carried away according to the prescribed rite by the officiating priests and the sacrificers.
Then, having placed the lifeless king upon a palanquin,
the attendants, their throats choked with tears and their minds despondent, carried him away.
Scattering gold, fine gold, and various garments,
the people went before the king along the path.
Others, having brought sandalwood, aloe-wood resin, sarala, padmaka, and devadāru wood, likewise prepared the funeral pyre.
Then, having offered various other fragrances there to the lord of the earth,
the officiating priests laid him down in the midst of the funeral pyre.
Then, having offered oblations into the fire, his officiating priests muttered prayers; and there the chanters of the Sāman sang the Sāman hymns according to the scriptures.
Then, accompanied by their elders, his women departed from the city in palanquins and carriages according to their rank.
Then the officiating priests and the women, led by Kausalyā and consumed by grief, circumambulated the king who had maintained the sacred fires in a counter-clockwise direction.
There, the piteous cry of thousands of distressed women was heard, sounding like the cries of female cranes at that hour.
Then, weeping and wailing helplessly again and again,
those beautiful women descended from their vehicles onto the bank of the Sarayū.
Having performed the water-libation rites together with Bharata, the king’s wives, the ministers,
and the family priests entered the city with eyes clouded by tears and spent ten days in sorrow upon the ground.
Then, when ten days had passed and he had performed his purificatory rites, the prince,
having reached the twelfth day, caused the funeral rites (śrāddha) to be performed.
He gave to the Brahmins jewels, wealth, and abundant food,
as well as many white goats and cows by the hundreds.
The son gave female and male servants, vehicles, and very large dwellings to the Brahmins as funeral offerings for that king.
Then, at the time of dawn on the thirteenth day,
the mighty-armed Bharata, overwhelmed by grief, lamented.
With his throat choked with sobs, having approached the base of the funeral pyre for the sake of purification,
he spoke these words to his father, deeply distressed.
Father, now that Raghava— the brother for whom I was entrusted by you—
has departed for the forest, I have been abandoned by you in this desolate place.
O Father, O King, where have you gone, abandoning that mother Kausalyā, leaving her like an orphan whose son has been sent away into the forest?
Having seen that circle of burnt bones, ruddy with ashes,
and the extinction of his father's body, he groaned and despaired.
But seeing him, he fell to the surface of the earth, weeping and dejected,
like the mechanical banner of Śakra when it has fallen and is being raised up again.
Then all his ministers rushed toward him, who was observing pure vows,
just as sages rush to Yayaati when he has fallen at the time of his end.
And Śatrughna, seeing Bharata overwhelmed with grief,
fell unconscious upon the ground as he remembered the protector of the earth.
Like one insane and devoid of sense, he lamented in great sorrow,
repeatedly recollecting those various qualities and limbs of his father.
The fierce ocean of grief, originating from Mantharā, teeming with the crocodile that is Kaikeyī, and consisting of the granting of boons— though seemingly unshakeable— submerged him.
O father, where have you gone, leaving behind Bharata, who is so delicate, young, and constantly cherished by you, and who now lies there lamenting?
"Indeed, you used to invite us all to feasts, drinks, garments, and ornaments; who will do that for us today?"
Yet at the time of its rending, the earth did not split apart—
even though it was deprived of you, the high-souled king who knew the dharma.
Since my father has ascended to heaven and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest, what purpose is there in my life? I shall enter the fire.
Deserted by both my brother and my father, I shall not enter the empty Ayodhyā protected by the Ikṣvākus; I shall enter the forest of asceticism.
Having heard their lamentation and observed that calamity,
all the followers became even more deeply distressed.
Then both Śatrughna and Bharata, despondent and exhausted,
writhed upon the ground like two bulls with broken horns.
Then Vasiṣṭha, their father’s priest and a man of sound character, raised Bharata up and spoke these words to him.
Three pairs of opposites prevail among all beings without distinction; since these are unavoidable, one ought not to behave in this manner.
And Sumantra, the knower of reality, having raised Śatrughna up and comforted him, caused him to hear about the birth and passing away of all living beings.
Having risen, those two illustrious tigers among men shone like two separate banners of Indra, weathered by rain and sun.
Wiping away their tears, with bloodshot eyes and speaking piteously,
the ministers urged the two sons to hasten toward other duties.
*Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 72.1:
Here, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, spoke these words to Bharata, who was tormented by grief as he desired to set out on his journey.
Rāma, who is endowed with such goodness that he is the refuge of all beings in times of distress— how much more so his own kin— has been exiled to the forest by a woman.
Why does this one named Lakṣmaṇa, who is powerful and endowed with valor,
not release Rāma even by means of defying his father?
But a king who has fallen under the sway of a woman and has mounted upon a wrong path must be restrained beforehand, after having carefully considered what is right and what is wrong.
While Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, was speaking thus,
the hunchback woman, adorned with all her ornaments, appeared at the eastern gate.
Anointed with the essence of sandalwood and wearing royal garments,
she appeared like a female monkey bound by ropes, though adorned with variegated girdles.
Then, having observed that merciless hunchback who had committed such a wicked deed,
the gatekeeper seized her and presented her to Śatrughna.
She for whose sake Rāma has gone to the forest and your father has cast off his body—this very woman is wicked and cruel; deal with her according to your judgment.
And Śatrughna, having understood those words, being deeply distressed and firm in his vows, spoke thus to all those who dwelt in the inner apartments:
"Intense suffering was produced for my brothers as well as for my father,
so that they might experience this very fruit of their cruel deed."
Thus addressed by him, the hunchback woman, quickly surrounded by her circle of female companions,
was seized with force and made that house resound with her cries.
Then all her friends, becoming deeply distressed and perceiving that Śatrughna was enraged, fled in every direction.
And her entire circle of female friends addressed her, saying:
"Since he has approached us in this manner, he will leave nothing of ours remaining."
"Let us seek refuge with Kausalyā—she who is compassionate, generous, knower of dharma, and illustrious; for she shall be our certain refuge."
And then Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies, his eyes copper-red with rage,
dragged the wailing hunchback across the surface of the earth.
As Mantharā was being dragged here and there,
her various and manifold colorful ornaments were shattered upon the ground.
Then the royal palace, filled with those treasures,
shone forth even more brilliantly, like the autumnal sky.
Seizing Kaikeyī with powerful rage, that bull among men rebuked her and spoke these harsh words.
By those harsh and painful words, Kaikeyī was deeply distressed;
terrified by the fear of Śatrughna, she sought refuge with her son.
Seeing him enraged, Bharata spoke this to Śatrughna:
"Women are not to be slain by any living beings; let her be forgiven."
I would kill this wicked Kaikeyī, who acts with such evil intent,
if the righteous Rāma did not despise me as a matricide.
If the righteous Rāghava learns that even this hunchback has been killed,
he will certainly no longer speak to you or me.
Having heard Bharata’s words, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
then turned back from his wrath and released Mantharā.
Mantharā fell down at the feet of Kaikeyī,
sighing and afflicted by great sorrow, and she lamented piteously.
Seeing Kubjā’s consciousness clouded by Śatrughna’s assault, Bharata’s mother,
herself appearing distressed, slowly comforted her as she gazed on like a trapped female curlew.
Then, at the time of dawn on the fourteenth day, the king-makers assembled and addressed these words to Bharata: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 73.1.
Daśaratha, who was our most venerable elder, has gone to heaven after having sent away his eldest son Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa into exile.
O illustrious prince, become our king this very day;
by good fortune, this leaderless kingdom does not fall into ruin.
"O Raghava, O prince, having taken all these items for the consecration, your kinsmen and the guilds await you."
"Accept this great kingdom, O Bharata, inherited from your father and grandfather;
have yourself consecrated and protect us, O bull among men."
Having circumambulated all the vessels for the consecration ceremony,
Bharata, firm in his vows, replied to all those people.
"Indeed, the sovereignty of the eldest is always appropriate for our lineage;
you, who are wise men, ought not to speak to me in this manner."
"For our elder brother Rāma shall indeed become the lord of the earth,
while I shall dwell in the forest for fourteen years."
"Let a great army, possessing the mighty force of four divisions, be prepared;
I shall bring my eldest brother, the descendant of Raghu, back from the forest."
Having placed all these preparations for the consecration before me, I shall go toward the forest for the sake of Rāma.
Having consecrated that tiger among men right there and placed him at the forefront,
I shall indeed bring back Rāma, like the sacrificial fire from the altar.
I shall not fulfill the desires of this woman who merely bears the name of mother;
I will dwell in the difficult forest, and Rāma shall become king.
"Let the craftsmen prepare the road, leveling the uneven places; let guards who are experts in navigating difficult terrain follow along the path."
To that prince who was speaking thus for the sake of Rāma,
all the people replied with these most excellent and glorious words:
May the lotus-glorious Śrī attend you as you speak thus,
you who desire to give the earth to the eldest son of the king.
O Prince, having heard that unsurpassed speech which had been uttered,
tears born of intense joy fell toward him, originating from the eyes of the noble lady’s face.
Having heard these words, they, along with their ministers and their assemblies, were joyful and their grief departed;
and by your command, the people devoted to the best of men, as well as the class of artisans, were instructed regarding the road.
Then there were those who knew the terrain, experts in the work of measurement lines,
brave men devoted to their own crafts, as well as diggers and engineers.
The laborers, the master builders, the men skilled in machinery, as well as the carpenters, the road-makers, and the wood-cutters.
Well-sinkers, plasterers, bamboo-workers,
and those who were capable and observers, set out before him.
But that vast multitude of people, proceeding toward that place with joy and great speed,
shone like the ocean during a full-moon tide.
Having mounted their respective vehicles, those experts in the art of driving set out ahead with various kinds of equipment.
Cutting down various trees, as well as creepers, climbing plants, shrubs, stumps, and even rocks, those people cleared a path.
In regions where there were no trees, some planted trees; in various places, others cut them down with axes, hatchets, and sickles.
Other powerful men, even more powerful than the rest, cleared away the thickets of vīraṇa grass and the difficult terrain here and there.
Others filled wells with dust, while some filled long chasms; likewise, others made the low-lying areas level on all sides.
Then those men bound those who were to be bound, crushed those who were to be crushed, and likewise broke apart those various regions that were to be broken.
In no long time at all, they constructed many canals carrying abundant water, numerous in their various forms and resembling the ocean;
they also made many kinds of wells adorned with circular platforms.
It had floors paved with plaster, trees in full bloom,
flocks of birds crying out in intoxication, and was adorned with banners.
Sprinkled with sandalwood water and adorned with various flowers,
the road for the army shone greatly, resembling the path to heaven.
Then, having been commanded, those authorized men, acting according to the command,
[set out] for delightful regions abounding in many sweet fruits.
Furthermore, they adorned with ornaments that very residence which was intended for the high-souled Bharata, making it resemble a person already decorated with jewelry.
Under auspicious constellations and at favorable moments, those skilled in such matters established the residence for the high-souled Bharata.
Furthermore, they were heaped with much dust and surrounded by moats;
there, they resembled the Indrakīla pillars and were adorned with excellent gateways.
All were joined with rows of palaces, enclosed by white-washed walls, adorned with banners, and possessed well-constructed great highways.
With their lofty mansions and gabled pavilions appearing as if gliding through the sky, those dwellings shone like the city of Śakra.
Having reached the Ganges, which was filled with groves of various trees,
possessed cool and pure water, and teeming with large fish;
Just as the stainless sky at night shines forth adorned by the host of the moon and stars,
so did that royal road, constructed in due order by skillful artisans, appear beautiful and resplendent.
Then, on that night of auspicious beginnings, the bards and genealogists, skilled in the nuances of speech, praised Bharata with hymns filled with blessings. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 75.1)
Struck by golden mallets, the drum that announces the watches resounded;
hundreds of conchs were blown, and musical instruments of high and low pitches were played.
That great sound of musical instruments, as if filling the very heavens,
further overwhelmed Bharata, who was already tormented by grief, with even greater sorrows.
Then, having woken up and silenced that clamor, Bharata declared,
"I am not the king," and spoke thus to Śatrughna:
Behold, Śatrughna, the great harm done to the world by Kaikeyī;
King Daśaratha has departed, leaving his sorrows upon me.
The royal fortune of that high-souled King of Dharma, rooted in righteousness,
wanders about like a boat without a helmsman upon the water.
Thus, seeing Bharata lamenting in this way, unconscious and miserable,
all those women then wept aloud.
While he was thus lamenting, the highly illustrious Vasiṣṭha, who was well-versed in the duties of kings, entered the assembly hall of the lord of the Ikṣvākus.
The righteous-souled one, together with his retinue, entered that beautiful hall made of gold and filled with jewels and gems, which resembled the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods.
He, the knower of all the Vedas, sat upon a golden throne covered with a most excellent carpet and gave instructions to his messengers.
"Bring the brahmins, kṣatriyas, warriors, ministers,
and the leaders of the guilds here quickly and without distraction, for we have an urgent matter to attend to."
Then a great tumultuous roar arose from the people approaching on chariots, horses, and elephants.
Then the subjects greeted the approaching Bharata with the same joy they had greeted Daśaratha, just as the immortals greet Śatakratu.
Like a lake filled with calm waters, teeming with whales and serpents, and containing gems, shells, and pebbles,
the assembly hall, graced by the son of Daśaratha, shone just as it did in the past when Daśaratha himself was present.
The wise Bharata beheld that assembly hall, filled with a multitude of noble men and held in high esteem, like a night graced by the full moon.
Then, as the noble ones entered their seats according to custom,
she appeared like a night with a full moon at the end of the rainy season.
But having observed all the subjects of the king assembled together, the priest, who knew the dharma, spoke these words softly to Bharata: *ramS_2,76.3*
"Father, King Daśaratha, practicing righteousness, has departed for heaven after bestowing upon you this prosperous earth, abounding in wealth and grain."
Thus Rāma, whose steadfastness was rooted in truth, remembering the dharma of the virtuous,
did not abandon his father’s command, just as the risen moon does not forsake its radiance.
The kingdom, with its thorns removed, has been granted to you by your father and your brother;
enjoy it with your ministers rejoicing, and have yourself consecrated immediately.
May those from the north, the west, and the south alone,
as well as the inhabitants of Aparānta and those by the sea, bring jewels to you by the millions.
Having heard those words, Bharata, who knows the dharma and desires to follow it, was overwhelmed with grief; he went in his mind to Rāma.
With a voice choked with tears, that youth, whose tone was like the call of a swan,
lamented in the midst of the assembly and rebuked the domestic priest.
Who like me would seize the kingdom from one who has lived the life of celibacy, who is wise, purified by sacred knowledge, and striving in righteousness?
"How could one born of Daśaratha become a usurper of the kingdom?
You ought to speak here of the righteousness regarding both the kingdom and me, as well as Rāma."
The eldest, most excellent, and righteous-souled descendant of Kakutstha, who is equal to Dilīpa and Nahuṣa, deserves to obtain the kingdom just as Daśaratha did.
If I were to commit a sin favored by the ignoble and leading away from heaven,
I would become a disgrace to the lineage of the Ikṣvākus in this world.
Whatever sin has been committed by my mother, I do not approve of it;
staying here, with palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to you who dwell in the forest fastness.
I shall follow Rāma alone; he, the descendant of Raghu, is the king and the best among bipeds, and he is worthy of sovereignty over even the three worlds.
Having heard those words consistent with righteousness, all the members of the assembly,
their minds fixed upon Rāma, shed tears out of joy.
But if I am unable to turn my noble brother back from the forest,
I shall dwell right there in the forest, just as the noble Lakṣmaṇa does.
I shall employ every means to forcibly turn him back,
even before the eyes of you noble sirs, who are virtuous and established in excellence.
Having spoken thus, the righteous Bharata, who was devoted to his brother,
addressed Sumantra, the expert in counsel, who was standing nearby.
"Rise quickly and go, Sumantra, by my command;
swiftly order the expedition and assemble the army."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Bharata, Sumantra was delighted and gave all instructions exactly as he had been commanded, with joyful devotion.
Having heard that the expedition had been ordered for the return of Rāghava, those subjects, the army commanders, and the troops were filled with joy.
Then all the wives of the warriors, having learned of their husbands' departure on the expedition, joyfully urged them on in every house.
Accompanied by warriors, the army commanders urged forth the entire force with swift horses, ox-carts, and chariots that were as fast as thought.
Seeing that army ready, Bharata, in the presence of his elder brother,
said to Sumantra at his side, "Hurry my chariot!"
Having received Bharata’s command, he was filled with joy;
taking the chariot yoked with excellent horses, he set forth.
Then that descendant of Raghu, firm in truth, powerful, and possessed of steadfast truth and valor, speaking most appropriately,
Bharata addressed his illustrious elder who had gone to the great forest, seeking to appease him.
"Rise quickly, Sumantra, and go to those foremost of men who are skilled in military affairs;
for I wish to bring that Rāma, dwelling in the forest, back by means of conciliation for the welfare of the world."
Having been duly commanded by Bharata, that son of the charioteer, his desires fully satisfied,
gave orders to all the leading ministers, the chief officers of the army, and his circle of friends.
Then, rising up in every household, those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras,
and Brahmins yoked camel-carts, donkeys, elephants, and well-bred horses.
Then,
having risen at dawn and mounted his excellent chariot,
Bharata set out swiftly, longing for a sight of Rāma. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 77.1)
All the ministers and family priests went before him,
having mounted chariots yoked with horses that resembled the chariot of the sun.
Nine thousand elephants, duly equipped,
followed Bharata as he departed, the delight of the Ikṣvāku dynasty.
Sixty thousand chariot-warriors, armed with various weapons,
followed the illustrious prince Bharata as he departed.
A hundred thousand horses, fully mounted, followed the illustrious prince Bharata, the descendant of Raghu, as he proceeded on his way.
Kaikeyī, Sumitrā, and the illustrious Kausalyā,
delighted at the sight of Rāma, departed in a radiant vehicle.
And groups of noble people set out to see Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa,
their minds filled with joy as they recounted various wonderful stories about him.
When shall we behold Rāma— the dark as a rain cloud, mighty-armed, of steadfast being, firm in his vows, and the destroyer of the world’s sorrow?
For as soon as he is seen, Raghava will dispel our grief,
just as the rising sun dispels the darkness of the entire world.
Speaking such auspicious words with great joy and embracing one another, those citizens then departed.
And all the others there who were highly esteemed, as well as the merchants and all the subjects, then went toward Rāma with joyful hearts.
And whoever are jewel-workers, as well as excellent potters, those who perform the work of weaving, and those who live by the sword; ||| RamS_2,77.12 |||
Peacock-feather workers, sawyers, polishers, and likewise drillers; ivory-workers, plasterers, and those who live by perfumes.
Goldsmiths, as well as woolen-cloth washers, bath-attendants, dressers, physicians, incense-makers, and vintners; RamS_2,77.14 //
Washermen, weavers, the village headmen and leaders of the cowherd settlements,
actors with their wives, and likewise fishermen— these all departed.
Thousands of Brahmins, who were self-composed, learned in the Vedas, and esteemed for their conduct, followed Bharata as he traveled in ox-carts.
Well-dressed, wearing clean garments, and anointed with polished red ointments,
they all followed Bharata slowly in various kinds of vehicles.
Exultant and joyful, that army followed the son of Kaikeyī;
that host accompanying Bharata came to a halt.
Having observed that army following him and the Ganges with its auspicious waters,
Bharata, skilled in speech, addressed all his ministers.
"Encamp my army according to your judgment in every respect;
having rested, we shall cross the great river tomorrow."
Moreover, I wish to descend to the river and offer water for the sake of the funeral rites of the king who has gone to heaven.
When he had spoken thus, the ministers, saying "So be it," composed themselves and settled them each separately according to their own respective preferences.
Having encamped that army, resplendent with its equipment, along the great river Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rules,
Bharata then remained there, contemplating the return of the high-souled Rāma.
Then, seeing the army with its banners encamped along the river Gaṅgā, the King of the Niṣādas hurriedly spoke to his kinsmen: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 78.1)
Therefore, this great army appears like the ocean;
even reflecting upon it with my mind, I do not perceive its end.
For this very one, with his massive body and the Kovidāra tree as his banner upon the chariot,
will either bind the fishermen or else slay us.
Then Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, approached to slay Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, who had been exiled from the kingdom by his father.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is both my lord and my friend;
desiring his welfare, remain here on the bank of the Gaṅgā, fully prepared for battle.
Let all the Dāśas who dwell along the river Gaṅgā remain there,
guarding the river with their forces, subsisting on meat, roots, and fruits.
He commanded that five hundred boats, each manned by a hundred fishermen and likewise by a hundred young men clad in armor, should remain stationed there.
But when Bharata becomes satisfied with Rāma here,
then this auspicious army shall cross the Gaṅgā today.
Having spoken thus, Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, took up offerings consisting of fish, meat, and honey, and approached Bharata.
Seeing him approaching, the powerful son of the charioteer,
who was well-versed in etiquette, then addressed Bharata with humility.
This master-craftsman, surrounded by a thousand kinsmen, is skilled in the Daṇḍaka forest; he is an elder and a friend of your brother.
Therefore, O descendant of Kakutstha, let Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, see you;
he will undoubtedly know where Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are.
Having heard these auspicious words from Sumantra, Bharata quickly spoke these words: "Let Guha see me."
Having received permission, Guha, filled with joy and surrounded by his kinsmen, approached Bharata and, bowing low, spoke these words.
"This region is indeed our private pleasure garden, and we have been deceived by you;
therefore, we all inform you: dwell within your own family of fishermen."
There was roots and fruit brought by the Niṣādas, as well as fresh meat and dried meat, and a great variety of forest produce, both high and low.
I hope that your army, having been well-fed, will spend this night here;
honored with various desired objects, you shall depart tomorrow morning together with your troops.
Thus addressed by Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, the highly wise Bharata replied with words consistent with reason and purpose: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 79.1)
"O friend of my preceptor, your desire is indeed formidable,
since you wish to challenge such an army as mine all alone."
Having spoken these excellent words to Guha, the illustrious and highly energetic Bharata addressed the lord of the Niṣādas once again.
"By which way shall I go to Bharadvāja’s hermitage, O Guha? This region along the banks of the Gaṅgā is extremely dense and difficult to traverse."
Having heard those words of the wise prince,
Guha, whose domain was the forest depths, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
The fishermen, armed with bows and well-composed, will follow you;
and I too, O prince of great renown, shall follow.
I hope you do not go with ill intent toward Rāma, whose actions are untiring;
this great army of yours creates a kind of suspicion within me.
To him who was speaking thus, Bharata— stainless as the sky— addressed Guha with these words in a gentle voice.
May that time never come when such suffering occurs; you ought not to suspect me, for that Rāghava is my eldest brother, equal to a father to me.
"I am going to bring back that descendant of Kakutstha who is dwelling in the forest;
you must not entertain any other thought, Guha—I tell you this truly."
But he, his face beaming with joy upon hearing what Bharata had said,
spoke these words once more to Bharata in his delight:
Blessed are you; I see no one equal to you upon the surface of the earth, you who desire to renounce here a kingdom that has come to you without effort.
Truly, your eternal fame shall traverse the worlds,
you who desire to bring back Rāma even though he has fallen into distress.
While Guha was thus conversing with Bharata at that time,
the sun shone with diminished luster and the night drew near.
Having settled that army and being gratified by Guha,
the illustrious one returned once more to his bed together with Śatrughna.
For such grief, consisting of anxiety for Rāma, has come upon the high-souled Bharata, who, though undeserving of it, is ever observant of dharma.
Burning with an internal fire, he torments Rāghava,
just as a hidden fire within a tree consumes it when scorched by a forest conflagration.
Sweat born from the fire of grief flowed from all his limbs,
just as the Himalayas, heated by the rays of the sun, exude snow.
With meditation as its rocky cavern, with sighs as its mineral veins,
with the multitude of trees that are dejection, and with grief and fatigue as its towering peaks;
The son of Kaikeyī was overwhelmed by a great mountain of suffering, which possessed the infinite being of delusion and the bamboo-stalks of the medicinal herbs of his torments.

The high-souled Bharata, accompanied by Guha and his kinsmen, arrived there composed in mind; then Guha, perceiving that Bharata was deeply distressed, once again consoled him regarding his elder brother.
Then Guha, whose domain was the forest, related the true nature of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa to the immeasurable Bharata.
To that Lakṣmaṇa, who was awake, endowed with virtues, and bearing an excellent bow and quiver, I spoke at length for the sake of protecting his brother.
"O dear one, this comfortable bed has been prepared for your sake;
take heart and rest upon it at ease, O delight of the Raghus."
"All these people here are accustomed to hardships, while you are accustomed to comfort;
O righteous-souled one, we shall remain awake for the sake of guarding you."
For there is no one on earth dearer to me than Rāma;
do not be anxious, nor shall I speak an untruth before you.
Through his grace, I hope for very great fame in this world,

For nothing remains unknown to me as I constantly roam this forest;

Thus addressed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,

While the son of Daśaratha lies upon the ground together with Sītā, how can I find sleep, or life, or any pleasures?

This son of Daśaratha, endowed with auspicious marks, was obtained through great asceticism and various arduous efforts; he is his only son.

It possessed beautiful square courtyards, well-laid-out main roads,

The Great Being was delicate, with the shoulders of a lion and long arms;

"My son, I hope no illness afflicts your body?
For today the life of this royal house depends entirely upon you."
"O son, having seen you, I live on now that Rāma has departed with his brother and King Daśaratha has passed away; today you alone are our protector."
"O son Lakṣmaṇa, I hope you have not heard any unpleasant news regarding me,

Having recovered his breath for a moment, the highly illustrious one, while still weeping,

Various kinds of food, edibles, and diverse fruits have been brought by me in great abundance for Rāma’s consumption.
Rāma, whose prowess is truth, consented to all of that;

"O friend, we must not accept gifts; rather, we should always give.

Then, for the sake of Rāghava, the son of Sumitrā quickly brought sacrificial grass himself and prepared an auspicious bed behind him.
Rāma entered that bed together with Sītā;
and having washed their feet, Lakṣmaṇa withdrew.
This is that very root of the *iṅgudī* tree, and this is that very blade of grass,

Having fastened to his back two quivers, well-filled with arrows and equipped with leather guards for his fingers and palms, the scorcher of foes,

He said to all his mothers: "That high-souled one slept here on the ground during the night; this was the place where he lay."
Born on this earth to Daśaratha, who was of noble lineage, highly fortunate, and wise, Rāma ought not to sleep [in such a place].
Having previously slept upon a heap of excellent coverlets spread over a deerskin, how does that tiger among men now lie upon the bare ground?
Always in the upper chambers of palaces and in the turrets,

Variegated with heaps of flowers, fragrant with sandalwood and agallochum,

He was constantly awakened by the sounds of singing and instrumental music, by the tinkling of exquisite ornaments, and by the resonant beats of excellent drums.
At the proper time, that scorcher of enemies was praised by many bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists with suitable verses and hymns of praise.
"This seems unbelievable in this world; it does not appear true to me. Indeed, my mind is bewildered, for it is my thought that this is a dream."
Surely there is no deity whatsoever more powerful than Time,
since that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, must lie thus upon the bare ground.
And Sītā, the daughter of the King of Videha, lovely to behold and beloved,
the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, lay upon the ground.
"This is my brother's bed;
indeed, it has been turned over, and all the grass upon the hard ground has been crushed by his limbs."
I believe that Sītā slept upon this bed at that time with her ornaments on,
for here and there are seen adhering gold droplets.
It is very clear that Sītā’s upper garment was caught here at that time;
for thus do these silk threads appear clinging [to the tree].
I believe my husband’s bed is comfortable, since the young Maithilī, though she is ascetic and delicate, does not perceive any suffering.
Born into a lineage of universal sovereigns, bringing happiness to all the world and beloved by all the world, he has renounced his dear and unsurpassed kingdom.
How is it that Rāghava—who is dark as a blue lotus, with red eyes, and lovely to behold; who was worthy of happiness and undeserving of suffering—now lies upon the bare ground?
"Vaidehī has indeed achieved her purpose, she who has followed her husband to the forest;
we, however, are all rendered uncertain, being deprived of that great-souled one."
With Daśaratha having gone to heaven and Rāma having taken refuge in the forest, the earth appears to me as if it were empty and without a helmsman.
And no one, even in his mind, aspired to the earth protected by the prowess of his arms, even while he was dwelling in the forest.
The royal capital was left unprotected, its defenses empty and unguarded, its horses and elephants unrestrained, and the gates of the city left wide open.
Enemies do not set their hearts upon an army that is dispirited, depleted, in a precarious position, and unprotected, just as they avoid food mixed with poison.
From this day forward, I shall sleep upon the ground or on blades of grass,
constantly subsisting on fruits and roots, and wearing matted hair and bark garments.
For the sake of that promise, I shall dwell happily in the forest for the remainder of his life;
having undertaken that vow, it shall not prove false.
Śatrughna will dwell with his brother for his sake,
while the noble one, together with Lakṣmaṇa, shall protect Ayodhyā.
"The twice-born shall consecrate the descendant of Kakutstha in Ayodhyā;
may even the gods make this desire of mine come true."

If, even when being propitiated by me in person with my head bowed and in many ways, he does not comply, then I shall dwell for a long time with Rāghava; living in the forest, he ought not to disregard me.
Having spent that night right there on the bank of the Gaṅgā, that descendant of Raghu,
Bharata, rose at dawn and spoke thus to Śatrughna: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 83.1)
"Śatrughna, arise! Why do you lie there? Bring Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, quickly—blessings be upon you—he will ferry the army across."
"I am awake; I do not sleep, for I am likewise reflecting upon my noble brother," thus spoke Śatrughna when urged by his brother.
While those two lions among men were thus conversing with one another,
Guha approached at the proper time and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Bharata.
O Kakutstha, did you spend the night happily on the riverbank? And is all well with you and your army?
Having heard those words of Guha, spoken out of affection,
Bharata, who was entirely devoted to Rāma, spoke these words as well.
"O King, may our night be pleasant, and may we be honored by you;
let the ferrymen ferry us across the Gaṅgā with many boats."
Then Guha, having heard Bharata’s command,
hurriedly entered the city and spoke to those kinsmen.
Arise, awake, and may it ever be well with you!
Pull together the boats; we shall ferry the army across.
Thus addressed, they rose up in haste at the king’s command and brought together five hundred boats from all sides.
Others, recognizable by their svastikas, were excellent bearers of great bells;
they were resplendent, adorned with banners, well-yoked, and firmly harnessed.
Then Guha brought forward an auspicious boat, recognizable by its swastika markings, covered with white woolen blankets, and filled with joyful sounds.
Bharata and the mighty Śatrughna ascended it,
as did Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and the other royal women.
First, the family priest and those brahmins [were to depart] to their preceptor;
immediately after them followed the king’s wives, as well as the wagons and market stalls.
The clamor of those setting fire to their dwellings, plunging into the sacred waters, and gathering up their belongings reached even unto heaven.
Those boats, adorned with banners and manned by the fishermen themselves, then sped swiftly along, carrying the people who had boarded them.
Some were filled with women, some with horses,
and some there carried vehicles, draft animals, and great wealth.
Having gone to the opposite shore and disembarked those people,
they returned while the fishermen’s kinsmen prepared their variegated nets.
The elephants, adorned with banners and urged on by their riders,
shone as they crossed the water like mountains bearing their flags.
Some ascended onto boats, while others crossed by means of rafts;
some crossed using jars and pots, and others crossed with their own arms.
That auspicious army, having been ferried across the Gaṅgā by fishermen themselves,
set out at the hour of Maitra for the supreme forest of Prayāga.
Having comforted the army and settled it according to their pleasure,
the high-souled Bharata, surrounded by his officiating priests, set out to see Bharadvāja, the foremost of sages.
Having seen Bharadvāja’s hermitage from a distance of just one *krośa*,
that bull among men halted his entire army and proceeded on foot with his ministers.
For, knowing the dharma, having laid aside his weapons and equipment and wearing two linen garments, he proceeded on foot, placing the domestic priest at the head.
Then, upon seeing Bharadvāja, Rāghava halted those ministers and proceeded behind his family priest.
Then, upon seeing Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, the great ascetic, quickly rose from his seat, saying to his disciples, "The guest-offering! (arghyam).
Having come together with Vasiṣṭha and being saluted by Bharata,
the one of great splendor recognized him as the son of Daśaratha.
Having offered them water for their hands and feet, as well as fruits,
the knower of dharma then inquired after the welfare of their family in due order.
Knowing that Daśaratha had passed away, he did not mention the king, even though he was aware of Ayodhyā’s military strength, treasury, allies, and ministers.
Vasiṣṭha and Bharata asked him about his well-being regarding his body,
his sacred fires, his trees, his disciples, and the deer and birds.
Having agreed by saying "So be it," Bharadvāja, the great ascetic,
spoke these words to Bharata out of the bonds of affection for Rāghava.
"What is the purpose of your coming here while you rule your kingdom?
Tell me all of this, for my mind finds no peace."
Kausalyā gave birth to him who was the slayer of enemies and the increaser of her joy;
he, together with his brother and his wife, was long exiled to the forest.
That highly illustrious one, who was commissioned by his father who had been commissioned by a woman,
was indeed destined to dwell in the forest here for fourteen years.
I hope you do not wish to commit an evil act against that sinless one,
desiring to enjoy the kingdom free from thorns along with his younger brother.
Thus addressed, Bharata replied to Bharadvāja with eyes clouded by tears, his voice faltering from grief.
"I am ruined if even the Blessed One regards me in this way;
do not suspect any fault in me, for do not instruct me thus."
And this was not what my mother intended when she spoke on my behalf;
I am not pleased by this, nor did I accept those words.
I, however, have come as a supplicant to that tiger among men,
in order to lead him back to Ayodhyā and to bow at his feet.
Considering that I have come to you in this state, you ought to show me favor.
Tell me, O Blessed One, where King Rāma is now.
Out of favor, Bharadvāja spoke these words to Bharata:
"O tiger among men, born of the lineage of Rāghava, this is worthy of you:
your conduct toward your elders, your self-restraint, and your devotion to the virtuous."
Knowing that this was already established in your mind, I questioned you in order to strengthen it and to greatly increase your fame.
"That brother of yours dwells on the great mountain Citrakūṭa;
tomorrow you shall go to that region, so dwell here today with your ministers.
O wise one, skilled in the aims of desire, fulfill this wish of mine."
Then, with his noble vision thus confirmed, Bharata, the son of the lord of men, spoke these words: "So be it. And he then resolved to spend the night in that great hermitage.
Then,
having resolved to stay there, the sage likewise invited Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, to accept hospitality.
But Bharata said to him, "Surely this has already been done by you:
the water for the feet, the guest-offering, and whatever hospitality is available in the forest."
Then Bharadvāja spoke to Bharata, as if smiling:
"I know you to be full of affection; you would be pleased with anything whatsoever."
"O bull among men, I desire to provide a meal for this army of yours; such is my pleasure, and you are worthy of it."
And for what purpose have you come here after leaving your army far behind?
O bull among men, why did you not arrive here with your forces?
Bharata, with palms joined in reverence, replied to that ascetic:
"O Blessed One, I have not approached you with my army out of fear of the Blessed One."
O Blessed One, excellent horses, men, and rutting, choice elephants follow me, covering the vast earth.
Thinking that they might not harm the trees, the water, the ground, or the huts and leaf-sheds in the hermitages, I have come here alone.
"Let the army be brought here from this place," was the command given by the supreme seer;
and Bharata acted accordingly, bringing the army together.
Then, having entered the fire-sanctuary, drunk water, and wiped his mouth,
he summoned Viśvakarman for the purpose of performing the rites of hospitality.
"I summon Viśvakarman and Tvaṣṭṛ as well;
I wish to perform a hospitable reception, so let the necessary arrangements be made for that."
May all the rivers that flow toward the east and those that flow toward the west,
both upon the earth and in the atmosphere, come together from every direction this very day.
Let some flow with maireya wine, others with well-prepared surā liquor,
and still others with cool water resembling the juice of sugarcane stalks.
I summon the gods and Gandharvas— Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū—
as well as the divine Apsarases and all the Gandharvīs from every quarter.
Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Miśrakeśī, and Alambuṣā—
those beautiful women who attend upon Śakra and those who attend upon Brahmā— I summon them all, together with Tumburu and their retinues.
That divine forest among the Kurus, which possesses garments like its foliage and ornaments as its blossoms,

"May the Blessed Lord Soma ordain for me here excellent food—
