And there were various garlands fallen from the trees,
as well as drinks such as wine and various kinds of meat.
Thus endowed with meditative concentration and incomparable splendor,
the sage spoke, being perfectly attuned to the essence of the training and disciplined by austerity.
As he meditated with his mind, facing the east with palms joined in reverence,
all those deities arrived there one by one.
Then, after touching Malaya and Dardura, the wind that dispels sweat blew with propriety—
pleasing to the soul, comfortable, and auspicious.
Then divine showers of flowers fell from the sky,
and the sound of celestial drums was heard in all directions.
Excellent winds blew, and throngs of Apsarases danced;
the gods and Gandharvas sang, and lutes emitted their melodies.
That sound, uttered softly, evenly, and endowed with the quality of rhythm (*laya*), entered the heavens, the earth, and the ears of all living beings.
When that divine sound, so pleasing to the ears of men, had ceased,
the Bharata army beheld the architectural masterpiece of Viśvakarman.
For the ground became level for five yojanas on all sides,
covered with many patches of grass resembling blue lapis lazuli.
In that place there were *bilva*, *kapittha*, *panasa*, and *bījapūraka* trees,
as well as *āmalaka* and mango trees, all adorned with fruit.
And from the Northern Kurus, a forest possessing divine enjoyments arrived, as did a celestial river surrounded by many trees growing upon its banks.
There were bright four-winged mansions, stables for elephants and horses,
clusters of palaces and lofty towers, and auspicious arched gateways.
The royal palace, with its beautiful gateways, resembled a white cloud;
it was adorned with white garlands and sprinkled with divine perfumes.
It was quadrangular and spacious, provided with couches, seats, and vehicles;
it was endowed with all divine flavors and possessed celestial food and clothing.
All food had been prepared, the vessels were washed until they were spotlessly clean,
all the seats were arranged, and there was a magnificent, excellent bed with a well-spread coverlet.
Permitted by the great seer, the mighty-armed Bharata, son of Kaikeyī, entered that residence filled with jewels.
All the ministers, together with the family priests, followed him;
and they were filled with joy upon seeing the preparations for his residence.
There, Bharata, together with his ministers, approached the divine royal throne, the fan, and the parasol, as one would a king.
Having bowed down before Rāma, he honored the seat;
then, taking up a yak-tail fan, he sat down upon the minister’s seat.
Then all the ministers and the family priest sat down in order of precedence;
after them, the commander-in-chief and the counselor took their seats.
Then, in that very moment, by the command of Bharadvāja, rivers with mud of milk-rice appeared there before Bharata.
On both banks of those rivers are delightful and divine dwellings, plastered with white clay, which have arisen through the grace of Brahmā.
And at that very moment, twenty thousand women, adorned with divine ornaments and sent by Brahmā, arrived.
Adorned with gold, jewels, pearls, and coral,
twenty thousand women sent by Kubera arrived.
Seized by those [apsarases], a man appears as if mad;
twenty thousand hosts of apsarases have come from the Nandana grove.
Nārada, Tumburu, Gopa, Parvata, and Sūryavarcas—
these kings of the Gandharvas sang before Bharata.
Alambusā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā,
and Vāmanā danced before Bharata at the command of Bharadvāja.
By the command of Bharadvāja, those garlands which exist among the gods and those found in the Caitraratha grove were seen at Prayāga.
By the power of Bharadvāja, the bilva trees became drummers, the vibhītaka trees became holders of the sacrificial wooden pins (śamyā),
and the aśvattha trees became dancers.
Then the *sarala*, *tāla*, *tilaka*, and *naktamālaka* trees,
filled with joy, rushed there, having assumed the forms of hunchbacks and dwarfs.
The *śiṃśapā*, *āmalakī*, and *jambū* trees, as well as other creepers in the forest,
assumed the forms of young women and dwelt in Bharadvāja’s hermitage.
"O drinkers of liquor, drink the liquor; and you who are hungry, eat the milk-rice; and let pure meats be eaten as much as you desire."
On the lovely banks of rivers, the women would bathe each man individually, seven or eight women attending to him alone.
Carrying [the wine], women with beautiful eyes gathered together;
having wiped [the vessels] according to the proper rule, those excellent women made him drink.
The mighty warriors urged on the excellent Ikṣvāku combatants, feeding the mounts— horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, and likewise the offspring of Surabhi— as well as sugarcane and honeycombs.
The horse-keeper did not recognize his horse, nor did the elephant-seizer recognize his elephant;
that army, intoxicated, heedless, and exultant, appeared there in full splendor.
Satisfied by all their desires, anointed with red sandalwood paste,
and accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, the soldiers raised their voices.
"We shall not go to Ayodhyā, nor shall we go to the Daṇḍaka forest;
may it be well with Bharata, and likewise may there be happiness for Rāma."

Thus the foot soldiers, the elephant-riders, the horsemen, and the attendants—being without a protector and having received that decree—raised this cry: iti pādātayodhāś ca hastyaśvārohabandhakāḥ / anāthās taṃ vidhiṃ labdhvā vācam etām udairayan // RamS_2,85.56 //
Those thousands of men following Bharata there shouted with great joy and said, "This is heaven!"
Then, as they were eating that food which was like nectar,
they beheld those divine delicacies and their minds turned toward consuming them.
The servants, maidservants, daughters-in-law, and even the soldiers—
all became exceedingly satisfied and were all dressed in new, unwashed garments.
Elephants, donkeys, camels, cattle, horses, deer, and birds were well-fed there;
indeed, no one had to provide for another.
No man was seen there who was not dressed in white garments, nor anyone who was hungry, nor even anyone who was soiled, nor any man whose hair was covered in dust.
And also with soups prepared from āja and vārāha meats, consisting of excellent collections of seasoned condiments, perfected with fruit extracts, and endowed with fragrance and flavor.
There, the people, filled with wonder, beheld thousands of iron vessels, adorned with flower-flags and brimming on all sides with white rice.
Along the edges of the forest, there appeared wells whose mud was like milk-porridge;
those cows were yielders of every desire, and the trees dripped with honey.
There were ponds filled with *maireya* liquor, surrounded by heaps of savory meat,
as well as heated cauldrons containing the flesh of antelopes, peacocks, and chickens.
And there were thousands of vessels made of gold, as well as cooking pots,
jars, and bowls filled with well-prepared curds,
along with fragrant, ripe, and pale wood-apples in the prime of their youth.
There were lakes filled with mango juice, and others with white curd;
at their edges were pools of milk-rice and heaps of sugar.
At the riverbanks, the men saw pastes, powders, decoctions, and various kinds of bathing preparations placed in vessels.
He also saw collections of white, fibrous tooth-sticks,
and white sandalwood pastes kept in small boxes.
There were polished mirrors, heaps of garments,
and thousands of pairs of wooden sandals and leather shoes.
Eyebrow-pencils, combs, brushes, umbrellas, and bows; variegated armor for protecting the vital organs, as well as beds and seats.
They plunged into ponds full of water for the drinking of donkeys, camels, elephants, and horses, and into lakes with excellent landing-stairs that were filled with blue and white lotuses.
And they saw there, on all sides, soft heaps of grass with the color of blue lapis lazuli, intended as fodder for the animals.
Those men were filled with wonder upon seeing that marvelous hospitality, which was like a dream, provided by the great seer for Bharata.
Thus, as they were enjoying themselves like the gods in the Nandana grove,
that night passed away in the lovely hermitage of Bharadvāja.
And those rivers and the Gandharvas departed as they had come,
after taking leave of Bharadvāja and all those beautiful women.
In the same way, men intoxicated and wild with liquor were there; likewise, divine aloe-wood and sandalwood were scattered about;
and likewise, various divine and excellent garlands were strewn here and there, crushed by the people.
Then,
having spent that night there and being hospitably entertained, Bharata, together with his retinue, went at his own will to visit Bharadvāja.
Having seen that tiger among men, Bharata, approaching with palms joined in reverence after he had offered his fire-oblation, the seer Bharadvāja addressed him.
"O sinless one, was your night spent happily here in our domain? Is all your company well? Tell me, have you been honored with hospitality?"
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed down, Bharata spoke to that seer of supreme splendor as he was departing from the hermitage.
"O Blessed One, I have been well-rested along with my entire army and mounts;
together with my ministers, I have been powerfully gratified by you with all my desires."
Free from fatigue and distress, well-supplied with food and provided with excellent shelter—
even including our servants— we have all lived in great happiness.
"I address you, O Blessed One, O best of sages, as I am about to set out for my brother's side; look upon me with a friendly eye."
O knower of dharma, tell me of the hermitage of that righteous, high-souled one; tell me which path leads there and how far it is.
Thus questioned by Bharata, who was longing for the sight of his brother,
the highly effulgent Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism, replied.
Two and a half yojanas from Bharata, in a desolate forest,
stands Mount Citrakūṭa, with its lovely caves and groves.
Reaching its northern flank, there is the river Mandākinī,
covered with trees in full bloom and possessing lovely flowering groves.
Immediately thereafter, O dear one, there is the river and Mount Citrakūṭa;
their leaf-hut is there, and it is certain that the two of them dwell there.

O lord of armies, O highly fortunate one, lead your host— crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots— along the southern path itself, keeping it to your left and right; then you shall behold Rāghava.
And hearing that the king of kings was departing, the women,
though worthy of carriages, abandoned their vehicles and surrounded the Brahmin.
Trembling, emaciated, and dejected, Kausalyā, together with Queen Sumitrā, grasped the feet of the sage there with both her hands.
Her desire not having been fulfilled, Kaikeyī, reproached by all the world and overcome with shame, grasped his two feet.
Having circumambulated the Blessed One, the Great Sage,
he then stood not far from Bharata with a dejected mind.
Then Bharadvāja, firm in his vows, questioned Bharata:
"O Rāghava, I wish to know the specific distinction among your mothers."
Thus addressed by Bharadvāja, the righteous Bharata,
skilled in speech, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
O Blessed One, behold this queen, the consort of my father, who is now so wretched, emaciated by grief and fasting, and who resembles a goddess.
Kausalyā gave birth to that tiger among men, Rāma, who strides with the prowess of a lion, just as Aditi gave birth to Dhātṛ.
She who stands here dejected, clinging to his left arm,
is like a branch of the Karṇikāra tree in the middle of a forest with its flowers withered.
The two sons of this goddess are both princes with the complexions of gods;
they are the heroes Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, whose prowess is truth.
On whose account those two tigers among men have gone from here to their destruction,
and King Daśaratha, deprived of his sons, has gone to heaven.
Know this Kaikeyī— desirous of power, ignoble yet appearing noble, cruel, and fixed in evil intent— to be my mother;
for I see her as the very root of my own great calamity.
Having spoken thus with a voice faltering with tears, that tiger among men,
his eyes copper-red, sighed repeatedly like an enraged serpent.
Then the great seer Bharadvāja, possessed of vast intelligence, replied with these meaningful words to Bharata as he was speaking.
O Bharata, Kaikeyī should not be viewed with ill-will by you;
for this exile of Rāma will result in future happiness.
Having saluted him and performed a circumambulation, Bharata, being fully accomplished in his purpose, took leave of him and urged his army, saying, "Let the troops be readied!"
Then, having yoked many divine chariots drawn by horses and adorned with gold, various kinds of people, desiring to depart, mounted them.
And the elephant-maidens and the elephants themselves, adorned with golden girths and banners,
set forth with a roar like clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Various vehicles, both large and small, and even those of great value, proceeded; while the foot soldiers went on foot alone.
Then, in the finest of vehicles, the women headed by Kausalyā,
longing for the sight of Rāma, set forth at that time with joyful hearts.
And that illustrious Bharata, having mounted a splendid palanquin that shone like the young sun and was well-prepared, set forth accompanied by his retinue.
That great army, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, set forth,
covering the southern direction like a rising great cloud;
it passed through forests inhabited by beasts and birds.
With its elephants, horses, and warriors filled with joy, that army of Bharata shone there as it plunged into the great forest, terrifying the multitudes of beasts and birds.
Afflicted by that great marching army with its banners, the intoxicated leaders of the forest-dwelling herds fled together with their troops. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 87.1)
Bears, herds of spotted deer, and ruru deer were seen on all sides, amidst the forest groves, upon the mountains, and by the rivers.
That righteous son of Daśaratha set forth, joyful,
surrounded by a vast and resounding fourfold army.
The army of the high-souled Bharata, resembling the surge of the ocean,
covered the earth just as a cloud covers the sky during the rainy season.
Covered by floods of horses and elephants of great speed,
the earth became invisible for a long time at that moment.
Having traveled a long distance, his mounts being utterly exhausted,
the illustrious Bharata spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of ministers.
"Since the form of the place appears exactly as I have heard it described,
we have clearly reached that region of which Bharadvāja spoke."
This is Mount Citrakūṭa, as well as the river Mandākinī;
and there in the distance shines this forest, resembling a dark blue cloud.
At present, the delightful plateaus of Mount Citrakūṭa are being trampled by my elephants, which resemble mountains themselves.
These trees on the mountain ridges are shedding their blossoms,
like thick clouds releasing water at the end of the summer heat.
"Behold, Śatrughna, this mountain region frequented by kinnaras,
covered on all sides by horses like the ocean by sea-monsters."
These herds of deer, driven on with great speed,
appear like rows of clouds in the autumn sky scattered by the wind.
These men place fragrant garlands of flowers upon their heads,
just like the people of the South with their cloud-like dark complexions.
This forest, which was once silent and terrifying to behold,
now appears to me as if it were Ayodhyā itself, teeming with people.
The dust raised by his hooves stands covering the heavens;
the wind swiftly carries it away, as if doing me a kindness.
O Śatrughna, behold these chariots yoked with horses and driven by master charioteers as they swiftly rush through the forest.
Behold these beautiful peacocks, now terrified;
they are entering this mountain, the dwelling place of winged creatures.
This region appears exceedingly delightful to me;
this dwelling of ascetics is clearly like the path to heaven itself.
In the forest, many spotted deer accompanied by their mates appear beautiful to behold, as if variegated with flowers.
"Excellent! Let the troops set out and search the forest so that those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, may be seen."
Having heard Bharata’s words, the brave men, weapons in hand,
entered that forest and then beheld smoke.
Having observed the column of smoke, they returned and said to Bharata:
"Fire does not exist in a place devoid of humans; clearly, the two Raghavas are right here."
Now, these two princes, tigers among men and subduers of foes, are not here;
clearly there are other ascetics here who resemble Rāma.
Having heard those words of theirs, which were esteemed by the virtuous, Bharata,
the crusher of enemy forces, spoke to all his soldiers.
"Be alert, sirs; stay here. You must not go further ahead.
I alone shall go, along with Sumantra and my preceptor."
Having been addressed thus, they all then stood there on every side; Bharata fixed his gaze upon the column of smoke.
That army, which had been stationed by Bharata, became joyful even as it beheld the smoke ahead,
for it soon realized then that it would be reunited with its beloved Rāma.
Having dwelt for a long time on that mountain, he who was fond of mountains and forests desired the welfare of Vaidehī and sought to delight his own heart. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 88.1)
Then the son of Daśaratha, resembling an immortal, showed the wonderful Citrakūṭa to his wife, just as Purandara showed [Amarāvatī] to Śacī.
"Neither the fall from my kingdom, O blessed lady, nor separation from my friends troubles my mind as much as seeing this beautiful mountain does."
"Behold this mountain, O blessed lady, filled with various flocks of birds and adorned with mineral-rich peaks that seem to pierce the sky."
Some resembled silver, some were like blood;
some were yellow or madder-red in color, and some possessed the luster of excellent jewels.
Some regions of that lord of mountains, adorned with minerals, shine like the *puṣpārka* and *ketaka* flowers, while others possess the luster of *jyotīrasa*.
Surrounded by various herds of deer and groups of leopards, bears, and wolves,
and teeming with many birds, this mountain shines forth, inhabited by creatures that are not malevolent.
With mangoes, rose-apples, *asanā*, *lodhra*, *priyāla*, jackfruit, *dhava*,
*aṅkola*, *bhavya*, *tiniśa*, *bilva*, *tinduka*, and bamboos;
With *kāśmarya*, *ariṣṭa*, and *varaṇa* trees, as well as *madhūka*, *tilaka*, *badarī*, *āmalaka*, *nīpa*, *vetra*, *dhanvana*, and *bījaka* trees.
Abounding with such trees as are flowering, laden with fruit, shady, and delightful, this mountain nourishes its own splendor.
O blessed lady, behold these high-minded kinnaras on the delightful mountain plateaus, sporting in pairs and inciting the passion of desire.
Behold the swords hung upon the branches and the exquisite garments, as well as the delightful pleasure-grounds of the Vidyādhara women.
With waterfalls, springs, and streams flowing here and there,
this mountain shines like an elephant shedding rutting ichor.
Carrying the fragrances born of various flowers, the cave-breeze approaches and gratifies the sense of smell; what man would it not gladden?
O blameless one, if I were to dwell here for many autumns together with you and Lakṣmaṇa, grief would not consume me.
"O beautiful lady, I am indeed delighted by this mountain, which is lovely with many flowers and fruits, filled with various flocks of birds, and possesses wonderful peaks."
By this dwelling in the forest, I have obtained a twofold fruit:
freedom from debt to my father, and likewise the pleasure of Bharata in the dharma.
O Vaidehī, are you perhaps finding delight on Citrakūṭa with me,
beholding various sights that are disciplined in mind, speech, and body?

"This very thing, dwelling in the forest for the sake of spiritual liberation after death, the supreme royal sages have declared to be the nectar of immortality for kings— this was said to me by my great-grandfathers."
Hundreds of vast rocks belonging to the mountain shine on all sides,
abundant and possessing many colors— blue, yellow, white, and crimson.
At night, thousands of medicinal herbs on the lord of mountains shine with their own radiant splendor, like crests of fire blazing with their own beauty.
O beautiful lady, some regions of this mountain resemble deserts, some resemble gardens, and others shine as single massive rocks.
As if having pierced through the earth, Citrakūṭa shines forth as it rises up;
that auspicious peak of Citrakūṭa is visible from every side.
Behold the excellent beds of those filled with desire, covered with kuṣṭha, puṃnāga, tagara, and birch leaves, and spread with ten thousand lotus petals.
O lady, look! Lotus garlands are seen crushed and cast aside by lovers, as are various kinds of fruits.
That mountain Citrakūṭa, abounding in roots, fruits, and water, surpasses even the Vasvaukasārā lotus-lake and the Northern Kurus.
But during this time, O Sītā, while dwelling in the forest together with you and Lakṣmaṇa,
I shall find delight that increases the dharma of my lineage, remaining on the path of the virtuous through my own supreme restraints.
Then,
having emerged from the mountain, the Lord of Kosala showed Maithilī the beautiful river Mandākinī with its auspicious waters.
And the lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the daughter of the King of Videha, that woman of noble form whose face resembled the beautiful moon.
Behold the river Mandākinī, delightful with its variegated sandbanks, frequented by swans and cranes, and endowed with blossoming flowers.
It was surrounded on all sides by various kinds of trees growing on its banks, laden with flowers and fruit, shining like the lotus-pond of Kubera, the king of kings.
Now, these delightful bathing places, their waters turbid from being drunk by herds of deer, produce a sense of delight in me.
Wearing matted hair and deerskins, and clad in upper garments of bark, the sages bathe in the river Mandākinī at the proper time, my dear.
With their arms raised high according to the rule,
these other sages of firm vows worship the sun, O large-eyed lady.
With its peaks shaken by the wind, the mountain seemed to dance along the river, as the trees on all sides shed their leaves and flowers.
Behold the river Mandākinī, which resembles a necklace of jewels, which is graced with sandy banks, and which is crowded with perfected beings (siddhas).
Behold the heaps of flowers shaken down by the wind and spread abroad;
behold others as well, floating about in the midst of the water.
And those birds called rathāṅgas,
O auspicious lady, whose speech is exceedingly sweet, are alighting upon them while uttering beautiful notes.
O beautiful one, I consider the sight of Citrakūṭa and the Mandākinī, as well as your own presence, to be far superior to dwelling in the city.
Bathe with me in this river whose waters are perpetually stirred by the Siddhas, who have shaken off all impurities and are endowed with austerity, self-restraint, and tranquility.
"O Sītā, O beautiful lady, plunge into this Mandākinī like a female friend, submerging the lotuses and water-lilies."
O lady, always regard these wild beasts as the citizens [regard Ayodhyā], this mountain as Ayodhyā, and this river as the Sarayū.
The righteous Lakṣmaṇa remains steadfast in my command, and you, O Vaidehī, are so well-disposed; together you both bring me great joy.
Bathing at the three daily libations and subsisting on honey, roots, and fruits,
I have no longing now for Ayodhyā nor for the kingdom, being with you.
For indeed, in this delightful river, agitated by herds of elephants, its waters drunk by elephants, lions, and monkeys,
and adorned with trees bearing flowers in full bloom— who would not find happiness once they have crossed over it?
Thus speaking these many affectionate words regarding the river in the company of his beloved, Rāma,
the enhancer of the Raghu dynasty, wandered through the lovely Citrakūṭa, which shone with the luster of collyrium for the eyes.
As Bharata sat there,
the dust and the clamor of the approaching army appeared, reaching up to the very heavens.
In the meantime, terrified by that great noise and afflicted by it,
the intoxicated leaders of the herds fled in all directions along with their followers.
Rāghava heard that sound arising from the army and beheld all those troop-leaders fleeing in every direction.
Seeing them fleeing and hearing that sound,
Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was possessed of radiant splendor.
"Come, Lakṣmaṇa, look here; Sumitrā is truly blessed with a noble son in you.
A tumultuous sound, deep as a terrifying thunderclap, is being heard."
O Saumitri, you ought to find out whether it is a king or a royal official who is wandering in the forest for the hunt, or some other wild beast;
you must ascertain all of this according to the truth without delay.
Hurrying, Lakṣmaṇa climbed a flowering *sāla* tree and,
surveying all the directions, gazed toward the eastern quarter.
Looking toward the north, he beheld a vast army,
crowded with chariots, horses, and elephants, and joined by disciplined foot soldiers.

"Let the noble one extinguish the fire, and let Sītā take refuge in the cave;
meanwhile, string your bow and prepare your arrows as well as your armor."
Rāma, that tiger among men, replied to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O son of Sumitrā, look closely; whose army do you think this is?"
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words,
as if wishing to incinerate that army like an enraged fire.
Desiring a fully established kingdom and having clearly obtained the consecration,
Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, is coming here to kill us both.
Truly, this most magnificent and glorious tree shines forth;
it stands resplendent upon the chariot as the raised trunk of the Kovidāra banner.
These men mount swift-moving horses and roam about according to their pleasure;
these riders, mounted upon elephants, shine forth with great joy.
O hero, having taken up our bows, let us take refuge on the mountain;
perhaps that one whose banner bears the Kovidāra tree may come under our power in battle.
Shall I ever see Bharata, for whose sake you, O Rāghava, as well as Sītā and I, have encountered such great calamity?
O Raghava, for whose sake you have been cast from your eternal kingdom—this enemy Bharata has arrived, O hero; he must surely be slain by me.
O Raghava, I see no fault in the killing of Bharata;
for no unrighteousness is ordained in the abandonment of those who have previously committed offenses.
Once he is slain, rule over the entire earth.
Today, let Kaikeyī, who craves the kingdom, behold her son slain in battle by me— afflicted with extreme grief like a tree broken by an elephant.
And I shall slay Kaikeyī, along with her attendants and her kinsmen;
let the earth today be liberated from this great defilement.
O giver of honor, today I shall release this restrained anger and resentment upon the enemy armies, like a fire set loose among dry thickets.
Today, piercing the bodies of my enemies with sharp arrows, I shall drench this forest of Citrakūṭa with blood.
Let beasts of prey drag away the elephants, the horses, and the men slain by me, their hearts pierced through by my arrows.
In this great forest, I shall become free from my debt to my arrows and my bow by slaying Bharata along with his army; of this there is no doubt.
But Rāma, having pacified the son of Sumitrā, Lakṣmaṇa, who was highly agitated and overwhelmed with anger, then spoke these words: *Ramāyaṇa*, *Ayodhyākāṇḍa*, 91.1.
What need is there here for a bow, or a sword with its scabbard,
now that the great archer and highly wise Bharata has come in person?
Since it is the right time that this Bharata desires to see us,
he would not do anything harmful toward us even in his mind.
Has Bharata ever done anything unpleasant to you before,
or why do you now fear Bharata so much that you suspect him in this matter?
For Bharata must not be addressed with harsh words nor with unpleasant speech;
indeed, it is I who would be spoken to unpleasantly if anything disagreeable were done to Bharata.
How indeed could sons ever kill their father in any calamity,
or a brother kill his brother, O Saumitri, who is as dear as his own life?
If you speak these words for the sake of the kingdom, then upon seeing Bharata, I shall say: "Let the kingdom be given to him."
For if Bharata is addressed by me in truth, Lakṣmaṇa, saying,
"Give the kingdom to him," he will surely say, "So be it."
Thus addressed by his brother Dharmaśīla, who was devoted to his welfare,
Lakṣmaṇa seemed to enter his own limbs out of shame.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa feeling ashamed, Rāghava replied:
"I believe this mighty-armed one has come here to see us."
Reflecting upon his dwelling in the forest, he will either take her back home,
or he will take this Vaidehī, who has been accustomed to the utmost luxury.
O hero, these two excellent horses, possessing noble lineage and captivating beauty, shine forth; they are as swift as the force of the wind and endowed with great speed.
This very elephant of immense body, named Śatruñjaya, the aged mount of my wise father, trembles at the head of the army.
Having descended from that sālā tree, Lakṣmaṇa, the conqueror in assembly, stood by Rāma's side with his palms joined in reverence.
Then, commanded by Bharata so that there might be no crowding,
he had the army encampment established all around that mountain.
That army of the Ikṣvākus, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, encamped along the side of the mountain, covering an area of one and a half yojanas.
At Citrakūṭa, that army, led by the wise Bharata who placed righteousness foremost and cast off all pride,
shone brightly as it was deployed for the purpose of propitiating the joy of the Raghus.
Having encamped his army, the lordly Sugrīva, the best among those who go on foot,
desired to approach that descendant of Kakutstha, who was himself following the path of his elders.
As soon as the army had been stationed according to its assigned quarters in a disciplined manner,
Bharata spoke these words to his brother Śatrughna:
O gentle one, you ought to search this forest quickly on all sides with these groups of men, accompanied by these hunters.
"As long as I do not see Rāma, or the mighty Lakṣmaṇa,
or the highly fortunate Vaidehī, there shall be no peace for me."
"As long as I do not behold my brother’s auspicious face, which resembles the moon and has eyes like lotus petals, there shall be no peace for me."
"As long as I do not bear upon my head the feet of my brother, which are endowed with the marks of royalty, there shall be no peace for me."
"As long as he who is worthy of the kingdom does not stand established in his ancestral realm,
and until he is moistened by the waters of consecration, there shall be no peace for me."
The highly fortunate Vaidehī, daughter of Janaka, has accomplished her purpose,
for she follows her husband across the earth bounded by the oceans.
That mountain Citrakūṭa is truly fortunate, resembling the king of mountains,
for upon it dwells the descendant of Kakutstha like Kubera in the Nandana grove.
This difficult forest, inhabited by predatory beasts, has achieved its purpose now that Rāma, the one of great splendor and the best among wielders of weapons, dwells within it.
Having spoken thus, the immensely energetic Bharata, that bull among men,
entered the great forest on foot.
That best of speakers passed through the midst of those groves of trees that had grown on the mountain ridges, their tops covered in blossoms.
Having reached a flowering *sāla* tree on Mount Citrakūṭa,
he saw the raised banner of the fire that had been brought to Rāma’s hermitage.
Seeing him, the illustrious Bharata rejoiced along with his kinsmen,
knowing that Rāma was there, like one who has reached the further shore of the ocean.
Having observed Rāma’s hermitage on Mount Citrakūṭa, which was frequented by holy people,
that high-souled one quickly departed with Guha, having first re-established his army there.
When the army had encamped, Bharata, filled with longing, then went to see his brother Śatrughna, pointing out the way. *Rāmāyaṇa*, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 93.1.
"Having instructed the seer Vasiṣṭha, 'Bring my mothers here quickly,' he,
who was devoted to his guru, went forward in haste."
Sumantra, moreover, followed close behind Śatrughna,
for his thirst to behold Rāma was as great as that of Bharata.
Then, as he was proceeding, the illustrious Bharata beheld his brother’s leaf-hut situated within the hermitage of the ascetics, as well as the cottage.
Then, in front of that hall, Bharata saw logs of wood broken apart and flowers gathered together.
And in that forest, he saw large heaps prepared from the dried dung of deer and buffaloes for the sake of warding off the cold.
Then, as he was walking along, the mighty-armed and radiant Bharata, being joyful,
spoke to Śatrughna and all those ministers.
"I believe we have reached that place of which Bharadvāja spoke;
for I think the Mandākinī River is not far from here."
"These bark garments must have been tied high by Lakṣmaṇa;
this is a path marked for recognition by one wishing to travel at an improper hour."
And this was the roaming about on the side of the mountain by those swift elephants with uplifted tusks, as they roared at one another.
The smoke of that very sacrificial fire which the ascetics constantly desire in the forest is seen here, thick and black-pathed.
"Here, filled with joy, I shall behold the noble Raghava, that tiger among men who honors his elders, like a great seer."
Then, after traveling for a short while toward Citrakūṭa, that descendant of Raghu reached the Mandākinī river and spoke these words to his people:
O tiger among men, that lord of people sits upon the earth in the vīrāsana posture;
having reached this desolate place, he says, "Fie on my birth and my life!"
On my account, the Lord of the World, the highly effulgent Raghava, has met with calamity; having renounced all desires, he dwells in the forest.
Thus reviled by the world, I shall today fall again and again at the feet of Rāma and Sītā to seek their favor.
While lamenting thus in that forest, the son of Daśaratha beheld a great, holy, and delightful leaf-hut.
It was covered with many leaves of *sāla*, *tāla*, and *aśvakarṇa* trees;
it was spacious and strewn with soft *kuśa* grass, like a sacrificial altar at a ritual.
It was adorned with bows resembling Indra’s weapon, capable of bearing great strain,
backed with gold, of immense strength, and destructive to enemies.
It was adorned with terrible arrows, resembling the rays of the sun, resting within their quivers,
like the city of Bhogavatī graced by serpents with blazing hoods.
She was resplendent with two great silver garments and two swords,
and she was also adorned with two shields variegated with golden spots.
With their variegated finger-guards made of iguana-skin fastened on, adorned with gold,
they were unassailable by hosts of enemies, like a lion’s cave by deer.
There, in Rāma’s dwelling, Bharata beheld a large and holy sacrificial altar, sloping toward the northeast and glowing with a blazing fire.
After gazing for a moment, Bharata beheld his elder brother,
Rāma, seated in the hut, wearing a mass of matted locks.
He beheld Rāma seated there, wearing a black antelope skin and garments of bark and rags, resembling a blazing fire on all sides.
He who has the shoulders of a lion, mighty arms, and eyes like lotuses;
the protector of the earth as far as the ocean's edge, a practitioner of righteousness.
The mighty-armed one sat upon the sacrificial ground strewn with darbha grass, like the eternal Brahmā, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him, the illustrious and righteous Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, overwhelmed by sorrow and delusion, ran toward him.
And having seen him, he lamented in distress with a voice choked with tears;
unable to maintain his composure, he spoke these words.
"He who would have been attended by the subjects in an assembly now sits here before me, attended only by wild animals."
That great-souled one, who was formerly honored with many thousands of garments,
now wears this deer skin here while practicing dharma.
He who formerly wore various and colorful garlands now,
O Rāghava, endures this burden of matted hair— how can he bear it?
He whose accumulation of merit has been perfected through sacrifices performed according to the injunctions seeks that dharma which arises from the affliction of the body.
How can this body of yours, which was once attended with highly precious sandalwood paste,
now be attended by me with filth?
"Because of me, this suffering has befallen Rāma, who is accustomed to happiness. Fie upon my life, which is cruel and despised by the world!"
Lamenting thus in his distress, his lotus-like face covered in sweat,
Bharata fell weeping, unable even to reach Rama's feet.
Afflicted by grief, the mighty prince Bharata,
having once piteously cried out "O Noble One!", said nothing further.
With his throat choked with tears, he looked at the illustrious Rāma; crying out "Noble brother! he was then unable to say anything more.
And Śatrughna also, weeping, paid homage at the feet of Rāma;
embracing them both, Rāma likewise shed tears.
Then the two princes met with Sumantra and Guha in the forest,
just as the sun and the moon meet with Venus and Jupiter in the sky.
Seeing those kings, who resembled leaders of elephant herds, assembled there in that great forest,
all those forest-dwellers too shed tears, casting aside their joy.
Having smelled the crown of his head and embraced him, Rāma, the descendant of Raghu,
placed Bharata upon his lap and, with a composed mind, questioned him.
"Where indeed was your father, my dear, when you came to the forest?
For while he was still alive, it was not fitting for you to come to the wilderness."
"Ah, after a long time I see Bharata come from afar! But he has a dejected appearance; my son, why have you come to this forest?"
Is King Daśaratha well— he who is true to his promise, the performer of Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and firm in his commitment to dharma?
O dear one, is that learned Brahmin, who is constant in dharma and of great luster,
being duly honored as the preceptor of the Ikṣvākus?
"Father, I hope Kausalya and Sumitra, the mother of progeny, are well;
and I hope the noble Queen Kaikeyi is happy and rejoicing."
Is your family priest— a son of noble birth, endowed with discipline, learned, free from envy, and observant— honored by you?

Is your wise and upright priest devoted to the sacred fires, knowledgeable in the ritual procedures, and always informing you at the proper time regarding what has been offered and what is yet to be offered?
"My son, do you hold in high regard the preceptor Sudhanvan, who is perfected in the excellence of archery and weaponry and is a master of the science of statecraft?"

My dear son, have you appointed as ministers those who are equal to yourself in character, heroic, learned, masters of their senses, of noble birth, and capable of discerning intentions from gestures?
For the counsel of kings, O Raghava, is indeed the root of victory,
provided it is well-guarded by ministers who are keepers of counsel and experts in the treatises.
I hope you do not fall under the power of sleep, that you wake at the proper time,
and that during the latter part of the night you contemplate the skillful means for achieving your goals.
I hope you do not deliberate on counsel alone, nor with too many people; I hope that the counsel you have deliberated upon does not leak out and spread throughout the kingdom.
O Raghava, having determined a purpose that requires little effort but yields great results, do you begin to carry it out quickly and not procrastinate?
Do those kings know all their undertakings— whether already well-performed, or those whose form has been completed— as things that ought not to be done again?
I hope, my dear father, that your secret counsel is not discovered through logical reasoning, nor by those who have not been informed, whether by you yourself or by your ministers.
"Would you prefer a single wise man over a thousand fools?
For a wise man can bring about great ultimate welfare in times of difficult circumstances."
Even if a lord of the earth attends upon thousands or even tens of thousands of fools, there is no assistance to be found among them.
Even a single minister who is wise, brave, skillful,
and discerning can bring a king or a royal official to great prosperity.
I trust that the principal servants have been appointed to great tasks, the middling to middling ones, and the lowly to inferior duties.
I trust you appoint as ministers those who have passed the tests of integrity, who are hereditary, pure,
and eminent, and that you assign them to the most important tasks.
I hope that the sacrificial priests do not despise you, as one might despise a fallen man, or as women despise a lover who accepts gifts from a fierce man.
He who does not slay a physician skilled in means, one devoted to corrupting his servants, or a hero desiring power, is himself destroyed.
I trust you have appointed as your commander-in-chief one who is bold, brave, steadfast, wise, pure, of noble birth, loyal, and skillful?
And have your principal men, who are powerful, skilled in battle, proven in their valor, and courageous, been honored and respected by you?
Do you provide the food and wages for the army as is appropriate,
giving them at the proper time and not delaying?
For when there is a delay in the payment of food and wages, the hired servants become resentful and turn hostile toward their master; that is remembered as a very great calamity.
I trust that all these noble sons are devoted to you above all else; I trust that, with focused minds, they would even sacrifice their lives for your sake.
O Bharata, has a messenger been appointed by you who is a native of the land, learned, capable, eloquent, a speaker of what he is told, and wise?
Do you keep watch over these eighteen [offices]— ten in your own faction and five in each of the three others—
by means of three spies for each, who remain unknown to one another?
O destroyer of enemies, do you always treat with no contempt those who have been expelled, those who have returned, and those who are weak?
I hope, my dear, that you do not serve those Lokāyatika brahmins;
for these fools, who imagine themselves to be wise, are skilled only in what is useless.
While the principal treatises on Dharma exist, those of dull intellect,
having acquired mere speculative knowledge, proclaim it to be useless.
O dear one, it was formerly inhabited by our ancestors, those heroes;
its name is true to its meaning, its gates are firm, and it is crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
It was filled with thousands of noble men— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— who were always devoted to their own duties, had conquered their senses, and possessed great energy.
Do you protect Ayodhyā, which is prosperous and flourishing, filled with people skilled in the medical arts and surrounded by palaces of various forms?
Is it graced with hundreds of shrines, crowded with well-settled people,
and adorned with temples, water-stations, and ponds?
Filled with joyful men and women, adorned with social gatherings and festivals,
its boundaries well-cultivated, abounding in cattle, and entirely free from violence.
O Rāghava, does the prosperous countryside— free from dependence on rain for its waters, delightful, and devoid of wild beasts— dwell in happiness?

I hope all those who depend on agriculture and cattle-rearing for their livelihood are dear to you; for, my son, the world prospers in happiness when it is supported by the economic way of life (vārttā).
I trust you have provided for their maintenance through protection and care;
for all those who dwell within his realm must be protected by the king in accordance with dharma.
Do you console the women, and are they well-protected? Do you not place undue trust in them, and do you not disclose secrets to them?
I hope the elephant grove is well-guarded and that you take pleasure in the elephants;
I hope you regularly show them, adorned with ornaments, to the people on the great highway, rising again and again in the forenoon, O Prince.
I trust that all the fortresses are fully supplied with wealth, grain, weapons, and water, as well as with engines, artisans, and archers.
Is your income vast, O Raghava, and is your expenditure indeed small? I hope that your treasury does not flow away to unworthy recipients.
I trust your expenditures are directed toward the gods, the ancestors, the Brahmins, guests,
warriors, and your circle of friends.
I trust that the noble one, pure of soul and innocent, has not been accused of theft; and that this pure man, though unasked by those skilled in the treatises, is not being bound out of greed?
O bull among men, is a thief who has been seized, interrogated at the proper time, and seen with the evidence of his crime, ever released out of greed for wealth?
O Raghava, do your ministers, who are deeply learned, remain free from favoritism when they consider the affairs of both the wealthy and the destitute during times of adversity?
O Raghava, those tears which fall from those who have been falsely accused,
they destroy the children and cattle of one who governs for the sake of his own pleasure.
O Raghava, do you seek to sustain the elderly, the young, and the foremost physicians through these three: with gifts, with thought, and with speech?
I trust that you pay homage to your gurus, the elderly, ascetics, deities, guests,
all sacred shrines, those who have attained their goals, and the brahmins.
I hope that you do not obstruct dharma for the sake of wealth, nor wealth for the sake of dharma,
nor both of them for the sake of pleasure, greed, or desire.
O best among victors, O knower of time, do you attend to wealth, virtue, and pleasure, dividing them all appropriately according to their proper seasons, O Bharata?
O highly wise one, do those brahmins, who are experts in the meaning of all the scriptures, along with the people of the city and the countryside, wish you well?
Atheism, falsehood, anger, negligence, procrastination, not seeing those possessed of knowledge, laziness, and the fivefold sensory indulgence.
Deliberating on matters alone, consulting with those who do not understand the purpose, failing to initiate what has been decided, and failing to protect the secrecy of counsel.
And do you avoid these fourteen faults of kings: the failure to perform auspicious rites, and rising [from one's seat] in every instance?
I hope, O Rāghava, that you do not eat delicious food all alone;
and I hope that you bestow it upon your friends who look forward to receiving it.
Having heard Rāma’s words, Bharata replied:
"What will the duty of a king avail me, who am devoid of righteousness?"
"O bull among men, this eternal law has always been established among us:
O King, while the eldest son remains, a younger son cannot become the monarch."
O Raghava, go with me to the prosperous Ayodhya and have yourself consecrated for the welfare of this lineage of ours.
They say a king is merely human, yet in my view he is regarded as a god, for his conduct, which is consistent with righteousness and purpose, they call superhuman.
While I remained in Kekaya and you had taken refuge in the forest,
the noble King, a performer of sacrifices esteemed by the virtuous, ascended to heaven.
"Arise, O tiger among men! Let the water-offering be made for our father;
I and this Śatrughna have already performed the water-rite."
"O Raghava, it is said that what is given by a beloved son indeed becomes inexhaustible in the worlds of the ancestors; and you, truly, were your father's beloved."
Hearing those piteous words concerning his father’s death spoken by Bharata, Rāghava became unconscious.
Having uttered those most unpleasant words, O scorcher of enemies, Bharata spoke;
then Rāma, stretching out his arms like a tree with flowering branches,
fell indeed to the ground as if cut down by an axe in the forest.
For thus lay Rāma, the lord of the earth,
fallen upon the ground like an elephant, exhausted by the collapse of its bank, fast asleep.
Your brothers, weeping together with Vaidehī, sprinkled water upon that great archer who was emaciated by grief on every side.
But he, having regained consciousness and shedding tears from his eyes,
the descendant of Kakutstha began to speak piteously at great length.
What indeed can I do for that high-souled one, born so ill-fated,
who died out of grief for me and was not even consecrated by me?
O sinless Bharata, oh, you have achieved your purpose, since by you and Śatrughna the king has been honored with all the funeral rites!
Deprived of its sovereign, distracted, and bereft of the lord of men,
I have no desire to go to Ayodhyā even though my forest exile has come to an end.
O scorcher of enemies, now that my father has gone to the other world, who indeed will instruct me once I have completed my forest exile in Ayodhyā?
Where shall I ever again hear those words, so pleasing to the ear, which my father used to speak to me in consolation when he saw that I was conducting myself with virtuous conduct?
Having spoken thus to Bharata, Rāghava, tormented by grief, approached his wife whose face resembled the full moon and said:
"Sītā, your father-in-law is dead; Lakṣmaṇa, you are deprived of your father.
Bharata announces that the lord of the earth has gone to heaven."
Having consoled the weeping daughter of Janaka, Rāma,
himself distressed, spoke these sorrowful words there to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Bring me ingudi oil-cake and a bark garment as an upper cloth;
I shall go to perform the water-libation for my high-souled father."
Let Sītā go in front, and you follow beside her;
I shall go behind, for this path is indeed most dreadful.
Then, his constant companion, who knew the Self, possessed great intelligence,
was gentle, self-controlled, tranquil, and firm in his devotion to Rāma.
Sumantra, together with those princes, having comforted Rāghava,
supported him and helped him descend into the auspicious Mandākinī river.
Then those illustrious ones, having reached with great difficulty the beautiful river Mandākinī, which possesses excellent landing places and forests that are always in bloom.
Having reached a swift-flowing, auspicious, and mud-free bathing place,
they sprinkled water upon the king, saying, "May this come to pass."
And raising his joined palms filled with water, the protector of the earth, facing the southern direction, spoke these words while weeping: RamS_2,95.27 //
"O tiger among kings, may this pure and inexhaustible water,
given by me today, attend upon you who have gone to the world of the ancestors."
Then, having ascended from the banks of the Mandākinī, that radiant Rāghava,
together with his brothers, performed the funeral libations for his father.

Having placed oil-cake mixed with *iṅguda* and jujube fruits upon a bed of *darbha* grass, Rāma, afflicted by great sorrow and weeping, spoke these words: aiṅgudaṃ badarīmiśraṃ piṇyākaṃ darbhasaṃstare / nyasya rāmaḥ suduḥkhārto rudan vacanam abravīt // RamS_2,95.30 //
"O Great King, eat this with pleasure, for we are those who eat what you eat;
whatever food a man has, his deities have that same food."
Then, having crossed back from the riverbank by that very same path,
that tiger among men ascended the mountain with its lovely peaks.
Then, having reached the door of the leaf-hut, the lord of the world took both Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa by their hands.
From the sound of those brothers weeping together with Vaidehī, an echo arose in the mountain, like the roar of lions.
Hearing that tumultuous noise, the Bharata soldiers were terrified and said,
"Bharata has surely met with Rāma";
yet it was the great sound of those very men mourning their deceased father.
Then, abandoning their garments, they all, with one mind, rushed toward that sound and fled to their respective places.
Some went on horses, others on elephants, and others on well-adorned chariots; likewise, other men who were very delicate went on foot alone.
Desiring to see Rāma, who had been away for but a short time as if he had been gone for a long time, all the people went suddenly to the hermitage.
Eager to witness the reunion with their brothers, they departed quickly on various kinds of vehicles crowded with hooves and wheel-rims.
That ground, struck by many vehicles with their hooves and wheel-rims,
emitted a tumultuous sound like the sky at the gathering of clouds.
Terrified by him, the elephants, surrounded by their female mates,
fled from that forest to another wood, seeking refuge in its fragrance.
Boars, deer, lions, buffaloes, bears, monkeys,
tigers, gokarṇas, and gavayas, along with spotted deer, were struck with terror.
Chakravākas, natyūhas, swans, kāraṇḍavas, and plavas,
as well as male cuckoos and krauñcas, fled in all directions, deprived of their senses.
Terrified by that sound, the sky was filled with birds and the earth was covered with men; both then shone forth.
Then, seeing those men with eyes filled with tears and deeply distressed,
he who knew the dharma embraced them like a father and like a mother.
There, the prince embraced some men, while others saluted him;
having approached them all, he then greeted his friends and kinsmen according to their rank.
Then, as those great-souled ones were weeping, their sound was heard continuously, resonating through the earth and the sky,
filling the mountain caves and all directions like the deep rumble of a drum.
Placing the wives of Daśaratha before him, Vasiṣṭha, thirsting for the sight of Rāma, proceeded toward that place. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 96.1)
And the king’s wives, proceeding slowly toward the Mandākinī,
beheld there that sacred bathing place frequented by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
With her face parched and filled with tears, the dejected Kausalyā spoke to Sumitrā and the other royal women.
This is the defiled [lamentation] of those protectorless ones whose actions were once undefiled; it is the very first instance in the forest of those who have been deprived of their realm.
"O Sumitrā, from here your son Saumitri always fetches water himself, unweariedly, for the sake of my son."
Upon the ground, upon darbha grass with its tips pointing southward, that large-eyed woman saw her father’s offering of *iṅgudī* seed-cake placed there.
Seeing that [ring] placed on the ground by Rāma, who was distressed for his father,
Queen Kausalyā spoke to all the wives of Daśaratha.
Behold this [offering] given by Rāghava to his father, the high-souled Rāghava, the lord of the Ikṣvākus, according to the prescribed rites.
For that high-souled king, who is equal to a god and has already enjoyed all pleasures, I do not consider this food to be appropriate.
Having enjoyed the earth bounded by its four oceans, that powerful lord of the world, who was like Mahendra himself, how is it that he now eats a mash of *iṅgudī* seeds?
Therefore, nothing appears to me in this world to be more painful than that at which the prosperous Rāma might offer ground iṅgudī seeds to his father.
Seeing that my father was given a cake of inguda seeds by Rāma,
why does my heart not shatter into a thousand pieces from grief?
Having thus consoled their distressed co-wife,
those women then went to the hermitage and beheld Rāma, who appeared like an immortal fallen from heaven.
Beholding Rāma abandoned with all his possessions, his mothers,
afflicted and emaciated by grief, wept aloud.
Rising up, Rāma, that tiger among men who is true to his promise, grasped the auspicious feet of all those mothers.
With their auspicious hands, pleasant to the touch and with soft fingers and palms,
those large-eyed women wiped the dust from Rāma’s back.
The son of Sumitrā, too, beholding all those mothers, was filled with sorrow; he greeted them without delay, slowly, immediately after Rāma.
All the women behaved toward Lakṣmaṇa, who was born of Daśaratha and possessed auspicious marks, in the same manner as they did toward Rāma.
Sītā also, having touched their feet in salutation,
stood before her mothers-in-law in her distress, her eyes filled with tears.
Embracing her— who was afflicted by grief, emaciated by dwelling in the forest, and miserable— Kausalyā spoke these words, as a mother would to her daughter.
How has the daughter of the King of Videha, the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha,
and the wife of Rāma, come to suffer such misery in the desolate forest?
Like a lotus scorched by the sun, like a water-lily withered, like gold obscured by dust, or like the moon defiled by clouds; ||| RamS_2,96.22 |||
O Vaidehī, beholding your face, the grief born from the friction-sticks of calamity burns intensely in my mind, like fire consuming its own source.
While his mother was thus speaking in her distress, that descendant of Raghu, the elder brother of Bharata, approached and took hold of Vasiṣṭha’s feet.
Like Indra, the lord of the immortals, before Bṛhaspati, Rāghava grasped the feet of that family priest who was like fire itself and possessed of abundant splendor, and sat down together with him.
Then, together with his ministers, the city notables, and the soldiers, as well as with the people most deeply conversant in dharma, the righteous Bharata sat down near his elder brother.
Then, having sat down and beheld Rāghava in the guise of an ascetic,
the heroic Bharata, blazing with splendor, joined his palms in reverence like the self-controlled Mahendra before Prajāpati.
"What words will Bharata speak today to Raghava after bowing and honoring him?"—
such was the supreme curiosity that truly arose among those noble people at that time.
That descendant of Raghu, Lakṣmaṇa of steadfast truthfulness and great majesty, and the righteous Bharata,
surrounded by their friends, shone like the three sacrificial fires accompanied by the members of the assembly at a ritual.
Having consoled his brother, who was so devoted to his elders, Rāma, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, began to question him. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 97.1)
"I wish to hear what has been spoken by you: why have you come to this region, O wearer of rags, matted hair, and deerskin?"
"For what reason have you entered this region, wearing a black antelope skin and matted hair, having abandoned your kingdom? You ought to tell me all of that."
Thus addressed by the high-souled descendant of Kakutstha, the son of Kaikeyī,
having firmly grasped [his feet] once more with joined palms, spoke these words.
Having performed a most difficult deed and abandoned his noble son, my father,
the mighty-armed one, afflicted by grief for his son, has gone to heaven.
O scorcher of enemies, urged by the woman Kaikeyī, my mother,
he committed this very great sin that destroys his own fame.
Without having obtained the fruit of sovereignty, my mother, a widow emaciated by grief,
will fall into a most terrible hell.
It behoves you to show favor to me, who have become your slave;
consecrate me this very day in the kingship, even as Maghavan.
All these subjects and those who are widowed mothers have come into your presence; you ought to show them favor.
O giver of honor, having attained the kingdom through righteousness in accordance with the proper sequence and in a manner consistent with your own nature, fulfill the desires of your friends.
Let the earth, together with you as her husband, be no longer widowed,
just as an autumn night is not widowed by the stainless moon.
And together with these ministers, I have entreated you with my head bowed low; it behooves you to show favor to me, who am your brother, your disciple, and your servant.
Therefore, O tiger among men, I do not venture to transgress this entire circle of ministers, which is eternal, ancestral, and honored.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Bharata, son of Kaikeyī, with tears in his eyes, again grasped Rāma’s feet with his head.
Embracing his brother Bharata, who was sighing again and again like an elephant in rut, Rāma spoke these words.
How could a person such as you— of noble birth, endowed with courage, radiant, and firm in his vows— commit a sin for the sake of a kingdom?
I see no fault in you, O destroyer of enemies, not even the slightest;
nor should you, out of childishness, reproach your mother.
O knower of dharma, as much reverence as there is for one’s father, who is honored by the world, so much reverence, O best of those who uphold dharma, is there for one’s mother as well.
"O Raghava, having been told by my mother and father, who are both virtuous in character, 'Go to the forest,' how could I act otherwise?"
"You must receive the kingdom of Ayodhyā, honored by the world;
I, however, must dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, clothed in bark garments."
Having thus made this distribution in the presence of the world and having given his commands, the great king Daśaratha, endowed with immense splendor, departed for heaven.
And that righteous king, the authority and teacher of the world, has granted you your rightful share; it is fitting for you to enjoy it.
"O gentle one, having resorted to the Daṇḍaka forest for fourteen years,
I shall enjoy the portion granted to me by my high-souled father."
"What my high-souled father— who is honored by the world of men and resembles the lord of the gods— said to me,
that alone I consider to be for the supreme self's welfare, and not the imperishable status of sovereignty over all the worlds."
Then, as those lions among men remained surrounded by their circles of friends,
the night passed away in sorrow while they were still lamenting.
When the night had turned into a beautiful dawn, those brothers, surrounded by their friends,
performed their oblations and recitations at the Mandākinī and approached Rāma.
As they sat together in silence, no one said anything;
but Bharata, in the midst of his friends, spoke these words to Rāma.
"My mother has been consoled and this kingdom has been granted to me;
therefore, I give it to you alone—enjoy the kingdom free from all thorns."
Like a dam breached by a great torrent of water at the onset of the rains,
this vast fragment of a kingdom is difficult for anyone other than you to hold together.
O lord of the earth, I have no power to follow your course, which is like the gait of a swift horse or the flight of the bird Tārkṣya.
O Rāma, life is always well-lived for him by whom others are supported; but life is ill-lived by him who lives off others.
Just as a tree that has been planted and nurtured by a man becomes a great tree with a thick trunk, difficult to climb because it has grown tall; ||| RamS_2,98.8 |||
When he has blossomed but does not display fruit,
he shall not experience that joy for the sake of which he was brought forth.
This is the analogy, O mighty-armed one; you ought to understand its meaning:
if you, our bull-like lord, do not indeed govern us who are your servants.
O Great King, let the guilds and the foremost men from all sides behold you,
the subduer of enemies, established in your kingdom like the scorching sun.
O descendant of Kakutstha, let the intoxicated elephants trumpet in your procession;
let the women of the inner apartments rejoice with composed minds.
Upon hearing these words of Bharata as he entreated Rama, the various people of the city thought, "Well said! (sādhu).
Seeing the illustrious Bharata thus afflicted and lamenting, the self-possessed and disciplined Rāma consoled him.
There is no exercise of free will for the self; this person is not its own master.
From here and there, destiny drags him along.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
Just as ripe fruits have no fear other than falling,
so for a man who is born, there is no fear other than death.
Just as a house with sturdy pillars sinks down once it has become dilapidated,
so too do men sink down when they have fallen under the power of old age and death.
The days and nights pass for all living beings here,
swiftly exhausting their lifespans, just as the rays of the sun dry up water in the summer heat.
Grieve for yourself; why do you grieve for another?
For your life is wasting away, whether you are standing still or moving about.
Death goes along with him; death sits down with him.
Having traveled a very long path, he returns accompanied by death.
Wrinkles have appeared on his limbs and his hair has turned white;
when a man is worn out by old age, what indeed can he do to exert power?
They rejoice when the sun has risen, and they rejoice when the sun has set;
human beings do not perceive the wasting away of their own life.
Living beings rejoice upon seeing the beginning of a season as it arrives anew;
yet, through the revolution of the seasons, there occurs the exhaustion of the life-force of all creatures.
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart after some time has passed; ||| RamS_2,98.25 |||
In this way, wives, sons, kinsmen, and wealth, having come together, quickly disperse; for their separation is certain.
No living being here returns according to its own will;
therefore, the deceased has no power over that which he laments.
For just as someone standing on the road might say to a caravan that is traveling,
"I too shall come along behind you."
Thus has the eternal path been trodden by our ancestors, fathers and grandfathers;
having entered it, how could one grieve, since there is no deviation from it?
As one's life falls away like a stream that never turns back, one must apply the self to happiness; for it is taught that all living beings are destined for happiness.
Our father, the lord of the earth, being righteous in soul, having shaken off all sin through auspicious sacrifices accompanied by full sacrificial fees, has gone to heaven.
By properly supporting his dependents, by protecting his subjects,
and by acquiring wealth in accordance with dharma, our father has gone to the third heaven.
Having performed various kinds of sacrifices and obtained abundant enjoyments,
and having attained an excellent lifespan, the lord of the earth went to heaven.
Having cast off this worn-out human body, our father has indeed attained divine prosperity that dwells in the world of Brahmā.
But no wise person such as you, nor one like him, who is learned and highly intelligent, ought to grieve in this manner.
These various kinds of grief, as well as lamentation and weeping,
must indeed be avoided by a wise and steadfast person in all circumstances.
"Be at peace and do not grieve; go and dwell in that city.
You have been thus commanded by your father, who is self-controlled, O best among the eloquent."
Wherever I have been appointed by that very man of meritorious deeds,
there indeed shall I carry out the command of my noble father.
"O subduer of enemies, it is not right for me to abandon his teaching;
therefore, you too must always honor it, for he is indeed our kinsman and our father."
When Rāma had thus spoken these meaningful words and ceased,
the righteous Bharata addressed him with these wonderful and righteous words.
For who indeed in this world could be such as you, O subduer of enemies— one whom sorrow does not distress, nor whom joy does not cause to exult?
You are esteemed by the elders, and you consult them regarding your doubts;
as one who is dead is to one who lives, so is that which is non-existent to that which exists.
Whoever should possess such an attainment of wisdom—by what means could he be tormented?
Having encountered such a calamity, he ought not to despair.
O Raghava, you are a great-souled being equal to the immortals, true to your promise,
all-knowing, all-seeing, and possessed of supreme intelligence.
One endowed with such virtues as yours, who is skilled in understanding both the origin and the passing away of things,
ought not to encounter suffering that is most difficult to bear.
Whatever evil was committed by my lowly mother out of affection for me while I was away,
and whatever unpleasantness she caused, may you be gracious toward me.
"I am bound by the bond of dharma; therefore, I do not strike this mother here with a severe punishment, even though she is a wrongdoer deserving of such punishment."
How could I, born of Daśaratha— who was of pure lineage and conduct—
knowing what is dharma, perform such a despicable act that is contrary to dharma?
"My teacher, my active elder, my deceased father, and my father—let me not revile him in the assembly, for he is a deity. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.98.49)
For who that knows the Dharma and understands righteousness, O knower of dharma, would perform such a base and sinful deed as this, desiring merely to please a woman?
"For there is an ancient Vedic revelation that 'at the time of death, living beings become deluded';

"O Lord, protect Kaikeyī, myself, our father, our friends, and our kinsmen, as well as all the people of the city and the countryside; you must save us all."
Where is the forest, and where is the duty of a Kṣatriya? Where are matted locks, and where is the protection [of subjects]?

such is the nature of mortals, yet you are needlessly distressed.

"This common folk has spread the notion that the Aṣṭakā rites have the ancestors as their deity;

"Sacrifice, give, be initiated, perform austerities, and renounce."
"O Mahāmati, form the conviction that there is nothing beyond this;
abide in what is perceptible and turn your back on what is imperceptible."
Placing before you the wisdom of the virtuous, which serves as a guide for all the world,
accept the kingdom, having been entreated by Bharata.

Whether one is of noble birth or of low birth, whether a hero or merely a man who fancies himself such,

abandoning what is auspicious and devoid of the prescribed rules of action— [then I would be lost].

would think much of me in this world as one of evil conduct and a defiler of the world?"

while I abide by this way of life that fails my solemn vow?

for whatever the conduct of kings is, such indeed is the conduct of their subjects.

therefore, a kingdom has truth as its essence, for the world is established upon truth.

for in this world, the speaker of truth attains the supreme state.

everything was indeed water, wherein the earth was fashioned;
from that, Brahmā, the self-existent, came into being together with the gods.

he lifted up the earth and created the entire world together with his self-realized sons.

He was formerly the Prajāpati, and Ikṣvāku was the son of Manu.

from Kukṣi, moreover, the heroic Vikukṣi was born.

and the son of Bāṇa was the mighty-armed and illustrious Anaraṇya.

from that Pṛthu, O great king, Triśaṅku was born.
By virtue of his truthful speech, that hero ascended to heaven in his physical body.
Triśaṅku had a son, the highly illustrious Dhundhumāra;
from Dhundhumāra was born the most radiant Yuvanāśva.
The illustrious Māndhātṛ became the son of Yuvanāśva;
and from Māndhātṛ was born the highly resplendent Susaṃdhi.
Susandhi also had two sons, Dhruvasandhi and Prasenajit;
and from Dhruvasandhi was born the illustrious Bharata, the slayer of enemies.
From the mighty-armed Bharata was born one named Asita,
against whom these rival kings arose as enemies:
the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, and the heroic Śaśabindus.
Having arrayed all those [enemies] against him in battle, the king was driven into exile;
he became a sage, finding delight on that beautiful, excellent mountain.
And it is heard that his two wives had become pregnant.
A descendant of Bhṛgu named Cyavana had taken refuge on the Himavat;
having approached that ṛṣi, Kālindī paid her respects to him.
The Brahmin addressed her, who desired a boon for the birth of a son;
then, having returned home, the queen gave birth to a son.
But his co-wife, desiring to destroy the fetus, gave him poison;
because he was born together with that very poison, he became known as Sagara.
That king named Sagara, who caused the ocean to be dug,
having performed a sacrifice on the auspicious day, [acted] with such impetuosity that he terrified these subjects.
We have heard that Asamañja was the son of Sagara;
though still alive, he was cast out by his father for performing evil deeds.
Aṃśumān was the powerful son of Asamañja;
Dilīpa was the son of Aṃśumān, and Bhagīratha was the son of Dilīpa.
From Bhagīratha came Kakutstha, from whom the Kākutsthas are said to derive their name;
Kakutstha’s son was Raghu, from whom the Rāghavas are named.
But the son of Raghu was the radiant Kalmāṣapāda, who grew up as a man-eater; he became renowned on earth by the name Saudāsa.
The son of Kalmāṣapāda was known as Śaṅkhaṇa, who,
having encountered his prowess, perished along with his army.
Śaṅkhaṇa’s son was the brave and illustrious Sudarśana;
Sudarśana’s son was Agnivarṇa, and Agnivarṇa’s son was Śīghraga.
Maru was the son of Śīghraga, and Maru’s son was Praśuśruka.
The son of Praśuśruka was Ambarīṣa, who was possessed of great luster.
Ambarīṣa’s son was Nahuṣa, whose valor was truth;
and Nahuṣa’s son was Nābhāga, who was supremely righteous.
Aja and Suvrata were both the sons of Nābhāga;
and the son of Aja was the righteous King Daśaratha.
"You are his eldest heir, renowned as Rāma;
therefore, accept your own kingdom and look after the world, O King."
