for these shall provide for the welfare and security of the entire world."
Having ascended and then descended from the sandals, that tiger among men,
possessed of great splendor, presented them to the high-souled Bharata.
Taking those well-adorned sandals, the powerful Bharata, who knows the dharma,
circumambulated Rāghava and placed them upon the head of the noble elephant.
Then, having honored that assembly of people, his elders, the ministers, the subjects, and likewise his two younger brothers in due order,
the enhancer of the Raghava lineage dismissed them, remaining steadfast in his own duty like the immovable Himalaya.
With their throats choked by tears, his mothers were indeed unable to address him out of grief;
but Rāma, having saluted all his mothers while weeping, entered his own cottage.
Then, having placed the two sandals upon his head, Bharata,
filled with joy and accompanied by Śatrughna, ascended the chariot.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and Jābāli of firm vows—
all the ministers, honored for their counsel— went forth at the front.
Then, keeping the great mountain Citrakūṭa on their right, they proceeded eastward toward the beautiful river Mandākinī.
Beholding thousands of delightful and diverse realms,
Bharata then proceeded along his side with his army.
Then, not far from Citrakūṭa, Bharata beheld the hermitage where that sage Bharadvāja had made his dwelling.
Having arrived at that hermitage of Bharadvāja, the wise delighter of his lineage descended from the chariot and paid homage at his feet.
Then Bharadvāja, filled with joy, spoke these words to Bharata:
"My son, has your purpose been accomplished by meeting with Rāma?"
Thus addressed by the wise Bharadvāja, Bharata,
who is devoted to righteousness, replied to Bharadvāja.
Being thus entreated by his preceptor and by me, Rāghava, firm in his prowess and supremely delighted, spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha.
"I shall truly fulfill that very promise of my father;
for fourteen years is the duration of the vow made by my father."
Thus addressed, the immensely wise Vasiṣṭha, skilled in speech, replied with these great words to Rāghava, who was himself proficient in discourse.
"O highly wise one, joyfully bestow these gold-adorned sandals upon Ayodhyā, which shall ensure your security and well-being."
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava stood facing the east and gave those sandals, wrought of gold, to him for the sake of his kingdom.
Having been dismissed by the great-souled Rāma, I am now returning;
taking these auspicious sandals, I shall go back to Ayodhyā itself.
Having heard these auspicious words of the high-souled Bharata,
the sage Bharadvāja uttered even more auspicious words.
"O tiger among men, best of those endowed with virtue and conduct, this is not surprising that noble qualities should abide in you, just as rainwater flows into a low-lying place."
That mighty-armed Daśaratha, your father, was truly immortal—
he who had such a son as you, whose soul is righteous and who is devoted to dharma.
Having spoken these words to that high-souled seer, he joined his palms in reverence,
grasped the seer’s feet, and began to take his leave.
Then, having circumambulated Bharadvāja again and again,
the illustrious Bharata departed for Ayodhyā together with his ministers.
With chariots, carts, horses, and elephants,
that vast army followed Bharata as it turned back once more.
Then, having crossed the divine river Yamunā, which was garlanded with waves,
they all beheld once again that river Gaṅgā, whose waters are auspicious.
Having crossed that river filled with beautiful water, he, together with his kinsmen and his army,
entered the lovely city of Śṛṅgaverapura.
From Śṛṅgaverapura, Bharata, tormented by grief, beheld Ayodhyā once more and spoke thus to his charioteer: ||| RamS_2,105.23 |||
"Charioteer, look! Ayodhyā is devastated and does not shine;
it is formless, joyless, wretched, and its sounds have been silenced."
Arriving in a chariot with a smooth and deep resonance, the illustrious lord Bharata quickly entered Ayodhyā. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 106.1)
It was like a dark, unilluminated night, frequented by cats and owls, where men and elephants lay hidden, and which was struck by deep gloom.
She was the beloved wife of Rāhu’s enemy, blazing with a splendor like Śrī herself,
yet she was tormented by that risen planet like Rohiṇī alone.

She was like a mountain river with its waters scant, warm, and agitated, where the birds were scorched by the heat, and where the fish, large and small, and the crocodiles lay dormant; she was utterly wasted away.
Like a smokeless flame, golden-hued, rising from the sacrificial fire, sprinkled with oblation, yet subsequently reduced to extinction; such was she.
With its armor shattered, its elephants, horses, chariots, and banners broken,
and its foremost heroes slain, it was like an army in great battle that has fallen into calamity.
Having been full of foam and sound as it rose from the ocean,
it became silent like a wave of water when the wind that had stirred it has subsided.
It was like a sacrificial altar that had become silent when the time for the Soma-pressing had ended, abandoned by all the ritual implements and the handsome officiating priests.
She stood in the middle of the cow-pen, distressed and not grazing on the fresh grass,
like the neglected consort of the bulls, longing for her husband.
She was like a brand-new string of pearls deprived of its finest gems— gems that were radiant, exceedingly lustrous, and seemed as if they were still blazing.
Suddenly shaken from her place as her merit was exhausted,
she was like a star fallen from the sky, its vast radiance withdrawn.
Like a forest creeper at the end of spring, adorned with flowers and graced by intoxicated bees,
now withered and scorched by the sparks of a swift-moving forest fire.
With all its thoroughfares bewildered and its markets and shops closed up,
it was like the sky shrouded by clouds, wherein the moon and stars are hidden from view.
It was strewn with broken, excellent drinking bowls overturned,
like an unadorned drinking hall in the sky where the drinkers have been slain.
With its ground torn up and low-lying, strewn with broken vessels,
its water used up, it was like a ruined water-station that had collapsed.
It was broad and wide, with its nooses still attached,
fallen upon the ground like the string of a swift bow severed by arrows.
She was driven suddenly by a horseman skilled in war,
like a weak young mare that has dropped its load and been abandoned.
When the rainy season had fully set in, he entered the circle of clouds,
like the radiance of the sun obscured by dark-blue storm clouds.
But the illustrious Bharata, the son of Daśaratha, standing upon his chariot,
spoke these words to the charioteer who was driving that excellent vehicle.
Why indeed is the deep sound of singing and instrumental music not heard today in Ayodhyā as it was before? It seems to have been silenced.
The fragrance of the intoxication of wine, the scent of garlands,
and the aroma of incensed aloe-wood no longer wafted everywhere.
The sound of the most excellent vehicles, the gentle neighing of horses,
the trumpeting of elephants in rut, and the great roar of chariots are no longer heard in this city now that Rāma has been exiled.
With young men of handsome appearance and noble gait rushing together through Ayodhyā, the great highways no longer shine.
Speaking thus in many ways, he entered his father’s residence,
which was bereft of that lord of men, like a cave devoid of its lion.
Then, having settled his mothers in Ayodhyā, Bharata, firm in his vows and tormented by grief, spoke these words to his elders: (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 107.1)
"I shall go to Nandigrāma; I bid you all farewell today.
There, without Rāghava, I shall endure all this sorrow."
For the king has gone to heaven and my elder has retired to the forest;
I await Rāma for the sake of the kingdom, for he is the illustrious king.
Having heard these auspicious words of the high-souled Bharata,
all the ministers and the family priest Vasiṣṭha spoke.
O Bharata, these words which you have spoken out of affection for your brother are worthy of praise; they are indeed consistent with your own character.
Who among men would not approve of you, who are ever devoted to your kinsmen, who abide in brotherly affection, and who have entered upon the noble path?
Having heard the pleasing words of his ministers, exactly as they had desired, he spoke these words to the charioteer: "Let my chariot be harnessed."
With a joyful countenance, having paid homage to all his mothers,
that illustrious one ascended the chariot accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having swiftly ascended the chariot, both Śatrughna and Bharata,
filled with supreme joy and surrounded by their ministers and family priests, set forth.
In front of them, the venerable twice-born ones, headed by Vasiṣṭha,
all proceeded facing the east toward where Nandigrāma was located.
And that army, unsummoned and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
set forth once Bharata had departed, as did all the city-dwellers.
But that righteous Bharata, devoted to his brother,
standing upon his chariot and placing the sandals upon his head, went quickly to Nandigrāma.
Then Bharata, having quickly entered Nandigrāma,
swiftly alighted from his chariot and spoke these words to his elders.
"This kingdom has been given to me by my brother himself as a formal entrustment;
and here are these gold-adorned sandals that ensure its security and prosperity.
I shall protect this until the return of Rāghava."
Having quickly joined them together myself once more, I shall behold those two feet of Rāma together with the sandals.
Then, having laid down my burden and met with Rāghava,
I shall hand over the kingdom to my elder and devote myself to the service of my guru.
Having bestowed these excellent sandals and the renunciation of the kingdom upon Rāghava,
I shall have both this kingdom and Ayodhyā, and I shall become cleansed of sin.
When the descendant of Kakutstha has been consecrated and the people are joyful and delighted,
my pleasure and my fame shall be four times greater than from the kingdom itself.
Lamenting thus in distress, the highly illustrious Bharata,
filled with sorrow, governed the kingdom from Nandigrāma together with his ministers.
Then that heroic lord Bharata, wearing bark garments and matted locks and assuming the garb of an ascetic, dwelt in Nandigrāma together with his army.
Then Bharata, who was devoted to his brother, eager for Rāma’s arrival,
obedient to his brother’s word, and faithful to his promise, remained there.
Then, having consecrated the sandals, Bharata dwelt in Nandigrāma at that time,
reporting all his governance to the two sandals.
When Bharata had departed, as Rāma was dwelling in the forest of asceticism, he observed that the practitioners of austerity were filled with agitation and anxiety. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 108.1)
He observed those ascetics who, having taken refuge in Rāma at the hermitage in front of Citrakūṭa, were devoted to him and now appeared anxious.
Pointing at Rāma with their eyes and knitted brows, they spoke apprehensively to one another and held a private conversation in low voices.
Perceiving their eagerness and feeling apprehensive within himself, Rāma then spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to the sage, the head of the community.
"O Blessed One, is there perhaps some past transgression on my part that is now visible, by which these ascetics are being provoked to anger?"
"Has my younger brother Lakṣmaṇa ever, through negligence, committed any act that was observed by the sages to be unbecoming of his own character?"
I trust that Sītā, who is devoted to serving you and intent on attending to me, continues to conduct herself with the propriety befitting a woman?
Then the seer, aged by years and having reached old age through asceticism,
spoke as if trembling to Rāma, who was supremely compassionate toward all beings:
O dear one, how could Vaidehī— who is of virtuous nature and likewise devoted to what is good—
ever waver, especially toward ascetics?
For your sake, this situation regarding the ascetics has come to pass;
therefore, agitated by the Rākṣasas, they speak among themselves.
A certain Rākṣasa named Khara, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, has here uprooted all the ascetics whose dwellings are in Janasthāna.
Arrogant, appearing victorious, cruel, a man-eater, haughty,
and wicked— he, O dear one, cannot tolerate you.
"O dear one, ever since you have been living in this hermitage,
the rākṣasas have begun to harass the ascetics."
For they display themselves in various forms—loathsome, cruel, and even terrifying; deformed and of such appearance that they are unpleasant to behold.
Having joined the ascetics with things that are censurable and impure,
those ignoble ones, standing before them, quickly strike down others.
Remaining hidden and unobserved in various hermitage sites,
those small-minded ones take delight there, destroying the ascetics.
When the time for the oblation has arrived, they cast aside the sacrificial ladles and vessels, douse the fires with water, and crush the jars.
Desiring to abandon the hermitages occupied by those evil-minded ones,
the sages are now urging me to depart for another land.
Therefore, O Rāma, since those wicked ones will surely display physical violence toward ascetics in the future, we shall abandon this hermitage.
Not far from here is a forest with diverse and abundant roots and fruits;
there I shall once again take up residence in that ancient hermitage along with my followers.
O dear one, harshness toward you as well would be improper;
therefore, depart from here with us if such is your intention.
O Raghava, since there is constant uncertainty for one who has a wife—
even though you are capable— your dwelling here today is indeed a source of suffering.
When the ascetic had spoken thus, Prince Rāma was unable to restrain him with further words, for he was eager to depart.
Having greeted, taken leave of, and consoled Rāghava,
that leader of the community departed for his hermitage, leaving it behind with his kinsmen.
Having seen the host of sages off from that place as they followed him, Rāma paid his respects to the Kulapati, the seer;
then, permitted by them who were well-pleased and having been instructed in his purpose, he returned to his own holy dwelling for a residence.
That lord, Rāghava, did not abandon the hermitage even for a moment when it was deserted by the sages;
for the ascetics, who maintained the virtues of the conduct of seers, constantly followed Rāghava.
When the ascetics had departed, Rāghava, reflecting deeply, did not find pleasure in dwelling there at that time for many reasons. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 109.1)
"Here I beheld Bharata, my mothers, and the citizens;
that memory follows me constantly as I grieve for them."
By the encampment of that great-souled one’s army,
and by the dung of horses and elephants, a severe desecration was caused there.
Thinking, "Therefore, let us go elsewhere," Rāghava set out,
accompanied by Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having reached the hermitage of Atri, he of great renown paid him homage;
and the blessed Atri received him in return like a son.
Having personally assigned all hospitality for him with great honor,
he comforted both the son of Sumitrā and the highly fortunate Sītā.
Having addressed his aged wife, who had arrived and been treated with honor,
he who knows the dharma and delights in the welfare of all beings comforted her.
"Accept Vaidehī," said the best of sages to the highly fortunate ascetic Anasūyā, who was a practitioner of dharma.
And he related to Rāma that story of the ascetic woman who practiced dharma,
concerning how the world had been continuously scorched by drought for ten years.
By her, roots and fruits were created and the Ganges was set in motion;
she was endowed with fierce asceticism and adorned with religious observances.
For ten thousand years, O dear one, she performed great austerities through the vows of Anasūyā, and all obstacles were warded off.
O sinless one, this night, which you have made as if it were ten nights by hurrying for the sake of the gods' work, has become like a mother to you.
Let Vaidehī approach this illustrious lady, who is always free from anger and worthy of being saluted by all living beings.
To that sage who was speaking thus, Raghava replied, "So be it," and then addressed these excellent words to Sita, who knew the dharma.
"O Princess, you have heard what has been spoken by this sage for the sake of your own welfare; go quickly now to the ascetic woman."
Go quickly to that ascetic woman who is worthy of being approached; she is known in the world by the name Anasūyā because of her deeds.
But Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, desiring the welfare of Rāghava and having heard these words, approached that wife of Atri, who was herself a knower of dharma.
She was slack, wrinkled, and aged, with hair white from old age;
her limbs were constantly trembling like a plantain tree in a strong wind.
Then Sītā, with composed mind, saluted the highly fortunate Anasūyā, who was devoted to her husband,
and announced her own name.
Having saluted that blameless female ascetic, Vaidehī,
joyful and with palms joined in reverence, inquired after her well-being.
Then, seeing the highly fortunate Sītā, who was devoted to righteousness, she spoke to her consolingly and joyfully: "By good fortune, you have regard for dharma!"
O Sītā, O proud lady, having abandoned your kinsmen, your pride, and your prosperity,
it is by good fortune that you follow Rāma, who is now confined to the forest.
Whether he dwells in a city or a forest, whether he is sinful or even unwholesome—
if a husband is dear to women, for them there are worlds of great prosperity.
Whether he be ill-behaved, addicted to sensual pleasures, or even destitute of wealth,
for women of noble character, the husband is the supreme deity.
Reflecting upon it, O Vaidehī, I see no relative more distinguished than him;
he is worthy in every respect, like imperishable ascetic merit itself.
But women who are unchaste, whose hearts are ruled by passion and who wander about with their husbands as their masters, do not understand virtue and vice in this way.
O Maithilī, those women who indeed fall under the sway of such improper conduct incur infamy as well as the loss of dharma. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.109.27)
But women like you, endowed with virtues and having perceived the higher and lower worlds, shall roam in heaven just like those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Thus addressed by Anasūyā, who was free from malice, Vaidehī honored her words and began to speak slowly. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 110.1)
"It is no wonder that you, noble lady, speak thus to me;
for this is also known to me, that for a woman, the husband is her guru."
"O noble lady, even if this husband of mine were devoid of virtuous conduct,
he must nevertheless be served by me without any duplicity."
How much more so, then, for one who is praiseworthy for his virtues, compassionate, self-controlled,
steadfast in affection, righteous in soul, devoted to his mother, and dear to his father?
The same conduct that the mighty Rāma maintains toward Kausalyā, he maintains toward all the other wives of the king as well.
Even toward women seen but once, that hero, who is devoted to the king and knows the dharma, conducts himself like a mother, having cast aside all pride.
As I was coming through this desolate forest so full of terror,
that which my mother-in-law had placed within my heart remained fixed there in its concentration.
And at the time of the giving of my hand, when I was previously instructed by my mother in the presence of the sacred fire, those words of hers have also been held fast by me.
All of that has been renewed by your words, O practitioner of dharma;
for a woman, no other austerity is ordained than service to her husband.
Sāvitrī, having performed service to her husband, is glorified in heaven;
likewise, you have attained the celestial realm through your devotion to serving your husband.
She is the most excellent among all women, and this goddess in heaven,
Rohiṇī, is not seen for even a moment without the Moon.
And such excellent women, firm in their vows toward their husbands,
are honored in the world of the gods by virtue of their own meritorious deeds.
Then Anasūyā, greatly delighted upon hearing the words spoken by Sītā,
smelled the head of the princess of Mithilā and spoke to her, gladdening her.
Indeed, I possess great ascetic power acquired through various observances;
relying on that strength, O Sītā of pure vows, I offer you my desire.
"O Maithilī, your words are appropriate and fitting;
I am pleased. Tell me, what suitable service may I do for you?
Sītā replied, "It is already done," to her who was endowed with the power of asceticism.
Thus addressed by her, she who knows the dharma became even more delighted;
"O Sītā, come now, I shall make your joy fruitful."
"O Vaidehī, here is this divine, excellent garland, clothing, and ornaments, as well as body-unguent and highly precious ointment."
"O Sītā, this which has been given by me shall adorn your limbs;
it will be suitable for you, free from blemish, and shall remain so forever."
"O daughter of Janaka, with my limbs anointed with divine unguents,
I shall adorn my husband just as Śrī adorns the imperishable Viṣṇu."
Maithilī accepted that unsurpassed gift of affection: garments, body-unguents, ornaments, and likewise garlands.
Having accepted that gift of affection, the illustrious and steadfast Sītā, with her palms joined in reverence, waited upon the lady whose wealth was asceticism.
Then Anasūyā, firm in her vows, approached Sītā as she sat nearby and began to speak some pleasant words concerning a certain story.
"O Sītā, I have heard this report reach my ears: that you were indeed won by this illustrious Rāghava at his own choice-marriage."
O Maithilī, I wish to hear that story in detail;
you ought to tell it to me exactly as it was experienced, in its entirety.
Thus addressed, Sītā then spoke to that practitioner of dharma,
saying, "Listen," and proceeded to tell her the story.
The heroic lord of Mithilā, named Janaka, who knows the dharma,
being devoted to the duty of a kṣatriya, rules the earth with justice.
While he, plough in hand, was tilling the circle of the field,
I indeed arose, O King, having pierced through the earth as the daughter of that monarch.
Seeing me with all my limbs covered in dust, King Janaka, who was intent on scattering handfuls of grain, was struck with wonder.
And by him, who was childless, having personally placed me on his lap out of affection and saying,
"This one is my daughter," he bestowed his love upon me.
And a voice, incomparable and superhuman, was indeed spoken in the sky:
"O Lord of Men, it is even so; by righteousness, she is your daughter."
Then, O lord of men, my father, the righteous ruler of Mithilā, was filled with joy,
having attained great prosperity upon obtaining me.

And I was given to the eldest queen by that performer of meritorious deeds as if she were his own beloved; and I have been treated with honor by her, who is affectionate toward me out of maternal kindness.
But seeing that old age, which is easily brought about by union with another, my father fell into deep anxiety, as dejected as a poor man who has lost his wealth.
In this world, the father of a maiden incurs insult from people who are his equals or even his inferiors,
even if he were equal to Śakra himself on earth.
Perceiving that insult to be imminent upon himself, the king entered an ocean of anxiety and, like one without a boat, could not reach the further shore.
For knowing me to be born not from a womb, that protector of the earth, though reflecting,
did not find a husband for me who was both suitable and worthy.
As that wise king reflected upon this continuously, the thought arose within him: "I shall hold a self-choice ceremony (svayaṃvara) for my daughter."
Then, at that great sacrifice, the high-souled Varuṇa out of affection gave him an excellent bow and two quivers with inexhaustible arrows.
Because of its weight, it cannot be moved by men even with great effort;
therefore, even lords of men are not able to bend it, even in their dreams.
Having obtained that bow, my father, who speaks the truth,
addressed it while previously inviting the kings to the assembly of monarchs.
"And that man who, having lifted this bow, strings it, my daughter shall become his wife; of this there is no doubt."
And having seen that excellent bow, which was like a mountain in its weight,
the kings saluted it and departed, being unable to lift it.
After a very long time, this Raghava of great splendor has arrived together with Viśvāmitra to witness the sacrifice.
Rāma, whose prowess is truth, was together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa;
and the righteous Viśvāmitra was highly honored by my father.
There he spoke to his father: "These two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are the sons of Daśaratha and are desirous of seeing the bow.
Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, he brought forth that bow.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, that heroic one bent it; having fixed the string, the valiant one instantly drew it taut.
As he was drawing it with full force, the bow snapped in two in the middle;
its sound was terrifying, like that of a falling thunderbolt.
Then, my father, who was true to his word, raised an excellent water vessel and prepared to bestow me there upon Rāma.
But at that time, Rāghava did not accept what was being offered,
as he had not yet ascertained the will of his father, the lord and ruler of Ayodhyā.
Then, having taken leave of my father-in-law, the aged King Daśaratha,
I was given by my father to Rāma, who knows his own self.
And my younger sister, the virtuous and lovely Urmilā,
was herself given by my father as a wife for Lakṣmaṇa.
Thus was I given to Rāma at that time during his svayaṃvara;
and I am devoted, in accordance with dharma, to my husband, the best among the valiant.
But Anasūyā, who knew the dharma, having heard that great story, embraced the princess of Mithilā with her arms and smelled the crown of her head. (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, 111.1)
Your speech was clear in syllables and words, wonderful, and sweet;
indeed, I have heard all that occurred at the svayaṃvara.
"I take great delight in your conversation, O sweet-spoken lady;
the glorious sun has set, ushering in the auspicious night."
The sound of birds that were scattered throughout the day for the sake of food is now heard at the time of twilight as they settle down for the sake of sleep.
And these sages, purified by their fruits and moistened by the consecration waters,
are approaching together, their bark garments drenched with water.
When the fires of the sages have been offered according to the prescribed rites,
smoke as reddish-brown as the body of a pigeon is seen, driven upward by the wind.
For the trees, though possessing few leaves, have become dense on all sides;
even in a distant region, they do not reveal the directions at all.
Nocturnal creatures roam about on all sides;
indeed, these deer of the ascetic grove lie down at the sacred bathing places.
The night has begun, O Sītā, adorned with the stars;
the moon, clothed in moonlight, is seen risen in the sky.
"Go, I give you leave; become an attendant to Rāma.
For I have been thoroughly gratified by your sweet conversation."
"Adorn yourself now before my very eyes, O Maithilī;
O child, bring me joy by gracing me with your beauty, adorned as you are with celestial ornaments."
Then Sītā, adorned like a daughter of the gods,
having bowed her head to her, went toward Rāma.
Thus Rāghava, the best among speakers, beheld Sītā adorned in that manner; and he rejoiced at the gift of affection bestowed by the ascetic woman.
Then Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, reported everything to Rāma—
the gift of affection consisting of garments, ornaments, and garlands from the ascetic woman.
Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa were filled with joy upon seeing the hospitality shown to Maithilī, which is very difficult for humans to obtain.
Then, having been honored by the ascetics and the perfected ones (siddhas), the joy of the Raghus, whose face resembles the moon, dwelt there happily for that auspicious night.
When that night had passed, those two tigers among men, having performed their ablutions and offered oblations into the sacred fires, took leave of the forest-dwelling ascetics.
Those forest-dwelling ascetics, practitioners of dharma, told them that the area of that forest was overrun by rākṣasas.
"This is the path of the great seers who gather fruits in the forest;
by this way, O Rāghava, you will be able to traverse the difficult forest."
Thus, having been granted blessings by those ascetic twice-born ones with palms joined in reverence,
Rāghava, the scorcher of foes, entered the forest together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, like the sun entering the circle of clouds.
